# Debiased Distribution Compression

**Authors:** Lingxiao Li Affiliation: MIT CSAIL Correspondence to: lingxiao@mit.edu Raaz Dwivedi Affiliation: Cornell Tech Correspondence to: dwivedi@cornell.edu Lester Mackey Affiliation: Microsoft Research New England Correspondence to: lmackey@microsoft.com

## Abstract

Modern compression methods can summarize a target distribution $\mathbb{P}$ more succinctly than i.i.d. sampling but require access to a low-bias input sequence like a Markov chain converging quickly to $\mathbb{P}$ . We introduce a new suite of compression methods suitable for compression with biased input sequences. Given $n$ points targeting the wrong distribution and quadratic time, Stein Kernel Thinning (SKT) returns $\sqrt{n}$ equal-weighted points with $\widetilde{O}(n^{-1/2})$ maximum mean discrepancy (MMD) to $\mathbb{P}$ . For larger-scale compression tasks, Low-rank SKT achieves the same feat in sub-quadratic time using an adaptive low-rank debiasing procedure that may be of independent interest. For downstream tasks that support simplex or constant-preserving weights, Stein Recombination and Stein Cholesky achieve even greater parsimony, matching the guarantees of SKT with as few as $\operatorname{poly-log}(n)$ weighted points. Underlying these advances are new guarantees for the quality of simplex-weighted coresets, the spectral decay of kernel matrices, and the covering numbers of Stein kernel Hilbert spaces. In our experiments, our techniques provide succinct and accurate posterior summaries while overcoming biases due to burn-in, approximate Markov chain Monte Carlo, and tempering.

Distribution compression is the problem of summarizing a target probability distribution $\mathbb{P}$ with a small set of representative points. Such compact summaries are particularly valuable for tasks that incur substantial downstream computation costs per summary point, like organ and tissue modeling in which each simulation consumes thousands of CPU hours (Niederer et al., 2011).

Remarkably, modern compression methods can summarize a distribution more succinctly than i.i.d. sampling. For example, kernel thinning (KT) (Dwivedi and Mackey, 2021; Dwivedi and Mackey, 2022), Compress++ (Shetty et al., 2022), recombination (Hayakawa et al., 2023), and randomly pivoted Cholesky (Epperly and Moreno, 2024) all provide $\widetilde{O}(1/m)$ approximation error using $m$ points, a significant improvement over the $\Omega(1/\sqrt{m})$ approximation provided by i.i.d. sampling from $\mathbb{P}$ . However, each of these constructions relies on access to an accurate input sequence, like an i.i.d. sample from $\mathbb{P}$ or a Markov chain converging quickly to $\mathbb{P}$ .

Much more commonly, one only has access to $n$ biased sample points approximating a distribution $\mathbb{Q}\neq\mathbb{P}$ . Such biases are a common occurrence in Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC)-based inference due to tempering (Gramacy et al., 2010, where one targets a less peaked and more dispersed distribution to achieve faster convergence,), burn-in (Cowles and Carlin, 1996, where the initial state of a Markov chain biases the distribution of chain iterates,), or approximate MCMC (Ahn et al., 2012, where one runs a cheaper approximate Markov chain to avoid the prohibitive costs of an exact MCMC algorithm, e.g.,). The Stein thinning (ST) method of Riabiz et al. (2022) was developed to provide accurate compression even when the input sample sequence provides a poor approximation to the target. ST operates by greedily thinning the input sample to minimize the maximum mean discrepancy (Gretton et al., 2012, MMD,) to $\mathbb{P}$ . However, ST is only known to provide an $O(1/\sqrt{m})$ approximation to $\mathbb{P}$ ; this guarantee is no better than that of i.i.d. sampling and a far cry from the $\widetilde{O}(1/m)$ error achieved with unbiased coreset constructions.

In this work, we address this deficit by developing new, efficient coreset constructions that provably yield better-than-i.i.d. error even when the input sample is biased. For $\mathbb{P}$ on $\mathbb{R}^{d}$ , our primary contributions are fourfold and summarized in Tab. 1. First, for the task of equal-weighted compression, we introduce Stein Kernel Thinning (SKT, Alg. 1), a strategy that combines the greedy bias correction properties of ST with the unbiased compression of KT to produce $\sqrt{n}$ summary points with error $\widetilde{O}(n^{-1/2})$ in $O(n^{2})$ time. In contrast, ST would require $\Omega(n)$ points to guarantee this error. Second, for larger-scale compression problems, we propose Low-rank SKT (Alg. 3), a strategy that combines the scalable summarization of Compress++ with a new low-rank debiasing procedure (Alg. 2) to match the SKT guarantees in sub-quadratic $o(n^{2})$ time.

Third, for the task of simplex-weighted compression, in which summary points are accompanied by weights in the simplex, we propose greedy and low-rank Stein Recombination (Alg. 5) constructions that match the guarantees of SKT with as few as $\operatorname{poly-log}(n)$ points. Finally, for the task of constant-preserving compression, in which summary points are accompanied by real-valued weights summing to $1$ , we introduce greedy and low-rank Stein Cholesky (Alg. 7) constructions that again match the guarantees of SKT using as few as $\operatorname{poly-log}(n)$ points.

Underlying these advances are new guarantees for the quality of simplex-weighted coresets (Thms. 1 and 2), the spectral decay of kernel matrices (Cor. B.1), and the covering numbers of Stein kernel Hilbert spaces (Prop. 1) that may be of independent interest. In Sec. 5, we employ our new procedures to produce compact summaries of complex target distributions given input points biased by burn-in, approximate MCMC, or tempering.

## 2 Debiased Distribution Compression

Throughout, we aim to summarize a fixed target distribution $\mathbb{P}$ on $\mathbb{R}^{d}$ using a sequence $\mathcal{S}_{n}\triangleq(x_{i})_{i=1}^{n}$ of potentially biased candidate points in $\mathbb{R}^{d}$ .11 1 Our coreset constructions will in fact apply to any sample space, but our analysis will focus on $\mathbb{R}^{d}$ . Correcting for unknown biases in $\mathcal{S}_{n}$ requires some auxiliary knowledge of $\mathbb{P}$ . For us, this knowledge comes in the form of a kernel function ${{\bm{k}}_{\mathbb{P}}}$ with known expectation under $\mathbb{P}$ . Without loss of generality, we can take this kernel mean to be identically zero.22 2 For $\mathbb{P}{{\bm{k}}_{\mathbb{P}}}\not\equiv 0$ , the kernel ${{\bm{k}}_{\mathbb{P}}}^{\prime}(x,y)={{\bm{k}}_{\mathbb{P}}}(x,y)-\mathbb{P}{{\bm{k}}_{\mathbb{P}}}(x)-\mathbb{P}{{\bm{k}}_{\mathbb{P}}}(y)+\mathbb{P}\mathbb{P}{{\bm{k}}_{\mathbb{P}}}$ satisfies $\mathbb{P}{{\bm{k}}_{\mathbb{P}}}^{\prime}\equiv 0$ and $\mmd_{{{\bm{k}}_{\mathbb{P}}}^{\prime}}=\mmd_{{{\bm{k}}_{\mathbb{P}}}}$ .

#### Assumption 1 (Mean-zero kernel).

For some $\mathfrak{p}\geq 1/2$ , $\mathbb{E}_{x\sim\mathbb{P}}[{{\bm{k}}_{\mathbb{P}}}(x,x)^{\mathfrak{p}}]<\infty$ and $\mathbb{P}{{\bm{k}}_{\mathbb{P}}}\equiv 0$ .

Given a target compression size $m$ , our goal is to output an weight vector $w\in\mathbb{R}^{n}$ with $\left\|{w}\right\|_{0}\leq m$ , $\bm{1}_{n}^{\top}w=1$ , and $o(m^{-1/2})$ (better-than-i.i.d.) maximum mean discrepancy (MMD) to $\mathbb{P}$ :

$$ \textstyle\mmd_{{{\bm{k}}_{\mathbb{P}}}}(\sum_{i=1}^{n}\!w_{i}\mathbf{\delta}_{x_{i}},\mathbb{P})\triangleq\sqrt{\sum_{i,j=1}^{n}\!w_{i}w_{j}{{\bm{k}}_{\mathbb{P}}}(x_{i},x_{j})}. $$

We consider three standard compression tasks with $\left\|{w}\right\|_{0}\leq m$ . In equal-weighted compression one selects $m$ possibly repeated points from $\mathcal{S}_{n}$ and assigns each a weight of $\frac{1}{m}$ ; because of repeats, the induced weight vector over $\mathcal{S}_{n}$ satisfies $w\in\Delta_{n-1}\cap(\frac{\mathbb{N}_{0}}{m})^{n}$ . In simplex-weighted compression we allow any $w\in\Delta_{n-1}$ , and in constant-preserving compression we simply enforce $\bm{1}_{n}^{\top}w=1$ . All three coreset types exactly preserve constants and hence satisfy standard coherence constraints.

When making big-O statements, we will treat $\mathcal{S}_{n}$ as the prefix of an infinite sequence $\mathcal{S}_{\infty}\triangleq(x_{i})_{i\in\mathbb{N}}$ . We also write ${{\bm{k}}_{\mathbb{P}}}(\mathcal{S}_{n}[\mathtt{J}],\mathcal{S}_{n}[\mathtt{J}])\triangleq[{{\bm{k}}_{\mathbb{P}}}(x_{i},x_{j})]_{i,j\in\mathtt{J}}$ for the principal kernel submatrix with indices $\mathtt{J}\subseteq[n]$ .

### 2.1 Kernel assumptions

Many practical Stein kernel constructions are available for generating mean-zero kernels for a target $\mathbb{P}$ (Chwialkowski et al., 2016; Liu et al., 2016; Gorham and Mackey, 2017; Gorham et al., 2019; Barp et al., 2019; Yang et al., 2018; Afzali and Muthukumarana, 2023). We will use the most prominent of these Stein kernels as a running example:

#### Definition 1 (Stein kernel).

Given a differentiable base kernel ${\bm{k}}$ and a symmetric positive semidefinite matrix $M$ , the Stein kernel ${{\bm{k}}_{p}}:\mathbb{R}^{d}\times\mathbb{R}^{d}\to\mathbb{R}$ for $\mathbb{P}$ with positive differentiable Lebesgue density $p$ is defined as

$$ \textstyle{{\bm{k}}_{p}}(x,y)\triangleq\frac{1}{p(x)p(y)}{\nabla_{x}\cdot\nabla_{y}\cdot(p(x)M{\bm{k}}(x,y)p(y))}. $$

While our algorithms apply to any mean zero kernel, including the aforementioned Stein kernels, the Sobolev kernels used in quasi-Monte Carlo (Kuo, 2003), and the popular centered Gaussian kernel (Chen et al., 2010; Lacoste-Julien et al., 2015), our guarantees adapt to the underlying smoothness of the kernel. Our next definition and assumption make this precise.

#### Definition 2 (Covering number).

For a kernel ${\bm{k}}:\mathbb{R}^{d}\times\mathbb{R}^{d}\to\mathbb{R}$ with $\mathcal{B}_{{\bm{k}}}\triangleq\{f\in{\mathcal{H}_{{\bm{k}}}}:\left\|{f}\right\|_{{\bm{k}}}\leq 1\}$ , a set $A\subset\mathbb{R}^{d}$ , and $\varepsilon>0$ , the covering number $\mathcal{N}_{{\bm{k}}}(A,\varepsilon)$ is the minimum cardinality of all sets $\mathcal{C}\subset\mathcal{B}_{{\bm{k}}}$ satisfying

$$ \textstyle\mathcal{B}_{{\bm{k}}}\subset\bigcup_{h\in\mathcal{C}}\{g\in\mathcal{B}_{{\bm{k}}}:\sup_{x\in A}\absolutevalue{h(x)-g(x)}\leq\varepsilon\}. $$

#### Assumption ( $\bm{{\alpha},{\beta}}$ )-kernel.

For some $\mathfrak{C}_{d}>0$ , all $r>0$ and $\varepsilon\in(0,1)$ , and $\mathcal{B}_{2}(r)\triangleq\{x\in\mathbb{R}^{d}:\left\|{x}\right\|_{2}\leq r\}$ , a kernel ${\bm{k}}$ is either $\hyperref@@ii[assum:kernel_growth]{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}{\textsc{PolyGrowth}}}({\alpha},{\beta})$ , i.e.,

$$ \textstyle\log\mathcal{N}_{{\bm{k}}}(\mathcal{B}_{2}(r),\varepsilon)\leq\mathfrak{C}_{d}(1/\varepsilon)^{{\alpha}}(r+1)^{{\beta}}, $$

with $\alpha<2$ or $\hyperref@@ii[assum:kernel_growth]{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}{\textsc{LogGrowth}}}({\alpha},{\beta})$ , i.e.,

$$ \textstyle\log\mathcal{N}_{{\bm{k}}}(\mathcal{B}_{2}(r),\varepsilon)\leq\mathfrak{C}_{d}\log(e/\vareps)^{{\alpha}}(r+1)^{{\beta}}. $$

In Cor. B.1 we show that the eigenvalues of kernel matrices with PolyGrowth and LogGrowth kernels have polynomial and exponential decay respectively. Dwivedi and Mackey (2022, Prop. 2) showed that all sufficiently differentiable kernels satisfy the PolyGrowth condition and that bounded radially analytic kernels are LogGrowth. Our next result, proved in Sec. B.2, shows that a Stein kernel ${{\bm{k}}_{p}}$ can inherit the growth properties of its base kernel even if ${{\bm{k}}_{p}}$ is itself unbounded and non-smooth.

#### Proposition 1 (Stein kernel growth rates).

A Stein kernel ${{\bm{k}}_{p}}$ with $\sup_{\|{x}\|_{2}\leq r}\|{\nabla\log p(x)}\|_{2}=O(r^{d_{\ell}})$ for $d_{\ell}\geq 0$ is

- (a) $\hyperref@@ii[assum:kernel_growth]{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}{\textsc{LogGrowth}}}(d+1,2d+\delta)$ for any $\delta>0$ if the base kernel ${\bm{k}}$ is radially analytic (Def. B.3) and

- (b) $\hyperref@@ii[assum:kernel_growth]{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}{\textsc{PolyGrowth}}}(\frac{d}{s-1},(1+\frac{d_{\ell}}{s})d)$ if the base kernel ${\bm{k}}$ is $s$ -times continuously differentiable (Def. B.2) for $s\!>\!1$ .

Notably, the popular Gaussian (Ex. B.1) and inverse multiquadric (Ex. B.2) base kernels satisfy the LogGrowth preconditions, while Matérn, B-spline, sinc, sech, and Wendland’s compactly supported kernels satisfy the PolyGrowth precondition (Dwivedi and Mackey, 2022, Prop. 3). To our knowledge, Prop. 1 and Cor. B.1 provide the first covering number bounds and eigenvalue decay rates for the typically unbounded Stein kernels ${{\bm{k}}_{p}}$ .

### 2.2 Input point desiderata

Our primary desideratum for the input points is that they can be debiased into an accurate estimate of $\mathbb{P}$ . Indeed, our high-level strategy for debiased compression is to first use ${{\bm{k}}_{\mathbb{P}}}$ to debias the input points into a more accurate approximation of $\mathbb{P}$ and then compress that approximation into a more succinct representation. Fortunately, even when the input $\mathcal{S}_{n}$ targets a distribution $\mathbb{Q}\neq\mathbb{P}$ , effective debiasing is often achievable via simplex reweighting, i.e., by solving the convex optimization problem

$$ \textstyle{w_{\textsc{OPT}}}\in\arg\min_{w\in\Delta_{n-1}}\sum_{i,j=1}^{n}w_{i}w_{j}{{\bm{k}}_{\mathbb{P}}}(x_{i},x_{j}) \textstyle\text{with }\,\mmd_{\textsc{OPT}}\triangleq\mmd_{{{\bm{k}}_{\mathbb{P}}}}(\sum_{i=1}^{n}\!{w_{\textsc{OPT}}}_{i}\mathbf{\delta}_{x_{i}},\mathbb{P}). $$

For example, Hodgkinson et al. (2020, Thm. 1b) showed that simplex reweighting can correct for biases due to off-target i.i.d. or MCMC sampling. Our next result (proved in Sec. C.2) significantly relaxes their conditions.

#### Theorem 1 (Debiasing to i.i.d. quality via simplex reweighting).

Consider a kernel ${{\bm{k}}_{\mathbb{P}}}$ satisfying Assum. 1 with ${\mathcal{H}_{{{\bm{k}}_{\mathbb{P}}}}}$ separable, and suppose $(x_{i})_{i=1}^{\infty}$ are the iterates of a homogeneous $\phi$ -irreducible geometrically ergodic Markov chain (Gallegos-Herrada et al., 2023, Thm. 1) with stationary distribution $\mathbb{Q}$ and initial distribution absolutely continuous with respect to $\mathbb{P}$ . If $\mathbb{E}_{x\sim\mathbb{P}}[\frac{\differential\mathbb{P}}{\differential\mathbb{Q}}(x)^{2\mathfrak{q}-1}{{\bm{k}}_{\mathbb{P}}}(x,x)^{\mathfrak{q}}]<\infty$ for some $\mathfrak{q}>1$ then $\mmd_{\textsc{OPT}}=O(n^{-1/2})$ in probability.

#### Remark 1.

${\mathcal{H}_{{{\bm{k}}_{\mathbb{P}}}}}$ is separable whenever ${{\bm{k}}_{\mathbb{P}}}$ is continuous (Steinwart and Christmann, 2008, Lem. 4.33).

Since $n$ points sampled i.i.d. from $\mathbb{P}$ have $\Theta(n^{-1/2})$ root mean squared MMD (see Prop. C.1), Thm. 1 shows that a debiased off-target sample can be as accurate as a direct sample from $\mathbb{P}$ . Moreover, Thm. 1 applies to many practical examples. The simplest example of a geometrically ergodic chain is i.i.d. sampling from $\mathbb{Q}$ , but geometric ergodicity has also been established for a variety of popular Markov chains including random walk Metropolis (Roberts and Tweedie, 1996, Thm. 3.2), independent Metropolis-Hastings (Atchadé and Perron, 2007, Thm. 2.2), the unadjusted Langevin algorithm (Durmus and Éric Moulines, 2017, Prop. 8), the Metropolis-adjusted Langevin algorithm (Durmus and Moulines, 2022, Thm. 1), Hamiltonian Monte Carlo (Durmus et al., 2020, Thm. 10 and Thm. 11), stochastic gradient Langevin dynamics (Li et al., 2023, Thm. 2.1), and the Gibbs sampler (Johnson, 2009). Moreover, for $\mathbb{Q}$ absolutely continuous with respect to $\mathbb{P}$ , the importance weight $\frac{\differential\mathbb{P}}{\differential\mathbb{Q}}$ is typically bounded or slowly growing when the tails of $\mathbb{Q}$ are not much lighter than those of $\mathbb{P}$ .

Remarkably, under more stringent conditions, Thm. 2 (proved in Sec. C.3) shows that simplex reweighting can decrease MMD to $\mathbb{P}$ at an even-faster-than-i.i.d. rate.

#### Theorem 2 (Better-than-i.i.d. debiasing via simplex reweighting).

Consider a kernel ${{\bm{k}}_{\mathbb{P}}}$ satisfying Assum. 1 with $\mathfrak{p}=2$ and points $(x_{i})_{i=1}^{\infty}$ drawn i.i.d. from a distribution $\mathbb{Q}$ with $\frac{\differential\mathbb{P}}{\differential\mathbb{Q}}$ bounded. If $\mathbb{E}[{{\bm{k}}_{\mathbb{P}}}(x_{1},x_{1})^{\mathfrak{q}}]<\infty$ for some $\mathfrak{q}>3$ , then $\mathbb{E}[\mmd_{\textsc{OPT}}^{2}]=o(n^{-1}).$

The work of Liu and Lee (2017, Thm. 3.3) also established $o(n^{-1/2})$ MMD error for simplex reweighting but only under a uniformly bounded eigenfunctions assumption that is often violated (Minh, 2010, Thm. 1, Zhou, 2002, Ex. 1) and difficult to verify (Steinwart and Scovel, 2012).

We highlight that our remaining results make no particular assumption about the input points but rather upper bound the excess MMD

$$ \textstyle\Delta\!\mmd_{{{\bm{k}}_{\mathbb{P}}}}(w) \textstyle\triangleq\mmd_{{{\bm{k}}_{\mathbb{P}}}}(\sum_{i\in[n]}\!w_{i}\mathbf{\delta}_{x_{i}},\mathbb{P}) \textstyle-\mmd_{\textsc{OPT}} $$

of a candidate weighting $w$ in terms of the input point radius $R_{n}\triangleq\max_{i\in[n]}\left\|{x_{i}}\right\|_{2}\vee 1$ and kernel radius $\left\|{{{\bm{k}}_{\mathbb{P}}}}\right\|_{n}\triangleq\max_{i\in[n]}{{\bm{k}}_{\mathbb{P}}}(x_{i},x_{i})$ . While these results apply to any input points, we consider the following running example of slow-growing input points throughout the paper.

#### Definition 3 (Slow-growing input points).

We say $\mathcal{S}_{n}$ is $\gamma$ -slow-growing if $R_{n}=O((\log n)^{\gamma})$ for some $\gamma\geq 0$ and $\|{{{\bm{k}}_{\mathbb{P}}}}\|_{n}=\widetilde{O}(1)$ .

Notably, $\mathcal{S}_{n}$ is $1$ -slow-growing with probability $1$ when ${{\bm{k}}_{\mathbb{P}}}(x,x)$ is polynomially bounded by $\left\|{x}\right\|_{2}$ and the input points are drawn from a homogeneous $\phi$ -irreducible geometrically ergodic Markov chain with a sub-exponential target $\mathbb{Q}$ , i.e., $\mathbb{E}[e^{c\left\|{x}\right\|_{2}}]<\infty$ for some $c>0$ (Dwivedi and Mackey, 2021, Prop. 2). For a Stein kernel ${{\bm{k}}_{p}}$ (Def. 1), by Prop. B.3, ${{\bm{k}}_{p}}(x,x)$ is polynomially bounded by $\left\|{x}\right\|_{2}$ if ${\bm{k}}(x,x)$ , $\left\|{\nabla_{x}\nabla_{y}{\bm{k}}(x,x)}\right\|_{2}$ , and $\left\|{\nabla\log p(x)}\right\|_{2}$ are all polynomially bounded by $\left\|{x}\right\|_{2}$ . Moreover, $\left\|{\nabla\log p(x)}\right\|_{2}$ is automatically polynomially bounded by $\left\|{x}\right\|_{2}$ when $\nabla\log p$ is Lipschitz or, more generally, pseudo-Lipschitz (Erdogdu et al., 2018, Eq. (2.5)).

### 2.3 Debiased compression via Stein Kernel Thinning

Off-the-shelf solvers based on mirror descent and Frank Wolfe can solve the convex debiasing program 7 in $O(n^{3})$ time by generating weights with $O(n^{-1/2}\|{{{\bm{k}}_{\mathbb{P}}}}\|_{n})$ excess MMD (Liu and Lee, 2017). We instead employ a more efficient, greedy debiasing strategy based on Stein thinning (ST). After $n$ rounds, ST outputs an equal-weighted coreset of size $n$ with $O(n^{-1/2}\|{{{\bm{k}}_{\mathbb{P}}}}\|_{n})$ excess MMD (Riabiz et al., 2022, Thm. 1). Moreover, while the original implementation of Riabiz et al. (2022) has cubic runtime, our implementation (Alg. D.1) based on sufficient statistics improves the runtime to $O(n^{2}d_{{{\bm{k}}_{\mathbb{P}}}})$ where $d_{{{\bm{k}}_{\mathbb{P}}}}$ denotes the runtime of a single kernel evaluation.33 3 Often, $d_{{{\bm{k}}_{\mathbb{P}}}}=\Theta(d)$ as in the case of Stein kernels (Sec. I.1).

The equal-weighted output of ST serves as the perfect input for the kernel thinning (KT) algorithm which compresses an equal-weighted sample of size $n$ into a coreset of any target size $m\leq n$ in $O(n^{2}d_{{{\bm{k}}_{\mathbb{P}}}})$ time. We adapt the target KT algorithm slightly to target MMD error to $\mathbb{P}$ and to include a baseline ST coreset of size $m$ in the kt-swap step (see Alg. D.3). Combining the two routines we obtain Stein Kernel Thinning (SKT), our first solution for equal-weighted debiased distribution compression:

*Algorithm 1 Stein Kernel Thinning (SKT)*

```
Input: mean-zero kernel ${{\bm{k}}_{\mathbb{P}}}$ , points $\mathcal{S}_{n}$ , output size $m$ , KT failure probability $\delta$
$n^{\prime}\leftarrow m\,2^{\lceil\log_{2}\frac{n}{m}\rceil}$
$w\leftarrow\hyperref@@ii[alg:GBC]{\textup{SteinThinning}}({{\bm{k}}_{\mathbb{P}}},\mathcal{S}_{n},n^{\prime})$
$w_{{\textup{SKT}}}\leftarrow\hyperref@@ii[alg:kt_target]{\textup{KernelThinning}}({{\bm{k}}_{\mathbb{P}}},\mathcal{S}_{n},n^{\prime},w,m,\delta)$
Return: $w_{{\textup{SKT}}}\in\!\Delta_{n-1}\cap(\frac{\mathbb{N}_{0}}{m})^{n}$ $\triangleright$ hence $\left\|{w_{{\textup{SKT}}}}\right\|_{0}\leq m$
```

Our next result, proved in Sec. D.3, shows that SKT yields better-than-i.i.d. excess MMD whenever the radii ( $R_{n}$ and $\left\|{{{\bm{k}}_{\mathbb{P}}}}\right\|_{n}$ ) and kernel covering number exhibit slow growth.

#### Theorem 3 (MMD guarantee for SKT).

Given a kernel ${{\bm{k}}_{\mathbb{P}}}$ satisfying Assums. 1 and ( α , β )-kernel, Stein Kernel Thinning (Alg. 1) outputs $w_{{\textup{SKT}}}$ in $O(n^{2}d_{{{\bm{k}}_{\mathbb{P}}}})$ time satisfying

$$ \textstyle\Delta\!\mmd_{{{\bm{k}}_{\mathbb{P}}}}(w_{{\textup{SKT}}})\!=\!O\big(\frac{\sqrt{\left\|{{{\bm{k}}_{\mathbb{P}}}}\right\|_{n}\ell_{\delta}\cdot\log n\cdot R_{n}^{{\beta}}G_{m}^{{\alpha}}}}{\min(m,\sqrt{n})}\big) $$

with probability at least $1-\delta$ , where $\ell_{\delta}\triangleq\log^{2}(\frac{e}{\delta})$ and

$$ \textstyle G_{m}\!\triangleq\!\begin{cases}1\!+\!\log m&\hyperref@@ii[assum:kernel_growth]{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}{\textsc{LogGrowth}}}({\alpha},{\beta}),\\
m&\hyperref@@ii[assum:kernel_growth]{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}{\textsc{PolyGrowth}}}({\alpha},{\beta}).\\
\end{cases} $$

#### Example 1.

Under the assumptions of Thm. 3 with $\gamma$ -slow-growing input points (Def. 3), LogGrowth ${{\bm{k}}_{\mathbb{P}}}$ , and a coreset size $m\leq\sqrt{n}$ , SKT with high probability delivers $\widetilde{O}(m^{-1})$ excess MMD, a nearly minimax optimal rate for equal-weighted coresets (Phillips and Tai, 2020, Thm. 3.1) and a significant improvement over the $\Omega(m^{-1/2})$ error rate of i.i.d. sampling.

#### Remark 2.

When $m\!\!<\!\!\sqrt{n}$ , we can uniformly subsample or, in the case of MCMC inputs, standard thin (i.e., keep only every $\frac{n}{m^{2}}$ -th point of) the input sequence down to size $m^{2}$ before running SKT to reduce runtime from $O(n^{2})$ to $O(m^{4})$ while incurring only $O(m^{-1})$ excess error. A similar remark applies to LSKT algorithm introduced in Sec. 3.

## 3 Accelerated Debiased Compression

To enable larger-scale debiased compression, we next introduce a sub-quadratic-time version of SKT built via a new low-rank debiasing scheme and the near-linear-time compression algorithm of Shetty et al. (2022).

### 3.1 Fast bias correction via low-rank approximation

At a high level, our approach to accelerated debiasing involves four components. First, we form a rank- $r$ approximation $FF^{\top}$ of the kernel matrix $K={{\bm{k}}_{\mathbb{P}}}(\mathcal{S}_{n},\mathcal{S}_{n})$ in $O(nrd_{{{\bm{k}}_{\mathbb{P}}}}+nr^{2})$ time using a weighted extension ( WeightedRPCholesky, Alg. F.1) of the randomly pivoted Cholesky algorithm of Chen et al. (2022, Alg. 2.1). Second, we correct the diagonal to form $K^{\prime}=FF^{\top}+\operatorname{diag}(K-FF^{\top})$ . Third, we solve the reweighting problem 7 with $K^{\prime}$ substituted for $K$ using $T$ iterations of accelerated entropic mirror descent (AMD, Wang et al., 2023, Alg. 14 with $\phi(w)=\sum_{i}w_{i}\log w_{i}$ ). The acceleration ensures $O(1/T^{2})$ suboptimality after $T$ iterations, and each iteration takes only $O(nr)$ time thanks to the low-rank plus diagonal approximation. Finally, we repeat this three-step procedure $Q$ times, each time using the weights outputted by the prior round to update the low-rank approximation $\widehat{K}$ . On these subsequent adaptive rounds, WeightedRPCholesky approximates the leading subspace of a weighted kernel matrix $\operatorname{diag}(\sqrt{\tilde{w}})K\operatorname{diag}(\sqrt{\tilde{w}})$ for $\tilde{w}\in\Delta_{n-1}$ before undoing the row and column reweighting. Since each round’s weights are closer to optimal, this adaptive updating has the effect of upweighting more relevant subspaces for subsequent debiasing. For added sparsity, we prune the weights outputted by the prior round using stratified residual resampling (Douc and Cappé, 2005, Resample, Alg. E.3,). Our complete Low-rank Debiasing (LD) scheme, summarized in Alg. 2, enjoys $o(n^{2})$ runtime whenever $r=o(n^{1/2})$ , $T=O(n^{1/2})$ , and $Q=O(1)$ .

*Algorithm 2 Low-rank Debiasing (LD)*

```
Input: mean-zero kernel ${{\bm{k}}_{\mathbb{P}}}$ , points $\mathcal{S}_{n}=(x_{i})_{i=1}^{n}$ , rank $r$ , AMD steps $T$ , adaptive rounds $Q$
$w^{(0)}\leftarrow(\frac{1}{n},\ldots,\frac{1}{n})\in\mathbb{R}^{n}$
for $q=1$ to $Q$ do
$\tilde{w}\leftarrow\hyperref@@ii[alg:stratified_resample]{\textup{Resample}}(w^{(q-1)},n)$
$\mathtt{I},F\leftarrow\hyperref@@ii[alg:rpc]{\textup{WeightedRPCholesky}}({{\bm{k}}_{\mathbb{P}}},\mathcal{S}_{n},\tilde{w},r)$
$K^{\prime}\leftarrow FF^{\top}+\operatorname{diag}({{\bm{k}}_{\mathbb{P}}}(\mathcal{S}_{n},\mathcal{S}_{n}))-\operatorname{diag}(FF^{\top})$
$w^{(q)}\!\leftarrow\!\hyperref@@ii[alg:agm]{\textup{AMD}}(K^{\prime},T,\tilde{w},\texttt{AGG}=\mathbbm{1}_{q>1})$
if $(w^{(q)})^{\top}K^{\prime}w^{(q)}>\tilde{w}^{\top}K^{\prime}\tilde{w}$ then $w^{(q)}\leftarrow\tilde{w}$
end for
Return: $w_{{\textup{LD}}}\leftarrow w^{(Q)}\in\!\Delta_{n-1}$
```

Moreover, our next result, proved in Sec. F.1, shows that LD provides i.i.d.-level precision whenever $T\geq\sqrt{n}$ , $Q=O(1)$ , and $r$ grows appropriately with the input radius and kernel covering number.

#### Assumption $(\bm{{\alpha},\!{\beta}})$ -params.

The kernel ${{\bm{k}}_{\mathbb{P}}}$ satisfies Assums. ( α , β )-kernel and 1, the output size and rank $m,r\!\geq\!(\frac{\mathfrak{C}_{d}R_{n}^{{\beta}}+1}{\sqrt{\log 2}}+2\sqrt{\log 2})^{2}$ , the AMD step count $T\!\geq\!\sqrt{n}$ , and the adaptive round count $Q\!=\!O(1)$ .44 4 To unify the presentation of our results, Assum. ( α , β ) -params constrains all common algorithm input parameters with the understanding that the conditions are enforced only when the input is relevant to a given algorithm.

#### Theorem 4 (Debiasing guarantee for LD).

Under Assum. ( α , β ) -params, Low-rank Debiasing (Alg. 2) takes $O((d_{{{\bm{k}}_{\mathbb{P}}}}\!+\!r\!+\!T)nr)$ time to output $w_{{\textup{LD}}}$ satisfying

$$ \textstyle\Delta\!\mmd_{{{\bm{k}}_{\mathbb{P}}}}(w_{{\textup{LD}}})\!=\!O\bigg(\!\sqrt{\frac{\|{{{\bm{k}}_{\mathbb{P}}}}\|_{n}\max(\log n,1/\delta)}{n}}+\sqrt{\frac{nH_{n,r}}{\delta}}\bigg) $$

with probability at least $1-\delta$ , for any $\delta\in(0,1)$ and $H_{n,r}$ defined in (290) that satisfies

$$ \textstyle\!H_{n,r}\!=\!\begin{cases}\!O\big(\!\sqrt{r}(\frac{R_{n}^{2\beta}}{r})^{\!\frac{1}{\alpha}}\!\big)\!&\!\hyperref@@ii[assum:kernel_growth]{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}{\textsc{PolyGrowth}}}(\alpha,\beta),\\
\!O\big(\!\sqrt{r}\exp(\!-\!\big(\!\frac{0.83\!\sqrt{r}-2.39}{\mathfrak{C}_{d}R_{n}^{\beta}}\!\big)^{\!\frac{1}{\alpha}\!})\!\big)\!&\!\hyperref@@ii[assum:kernel_growth]{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}{\textsc{LogGrowth}}}(\alpha,\beta).\end{cases} $$

#### Example 2.

Under the assumptions of Thm. 4 with $\gamma$ -slow-growing input points (Def. 3), LogGrowth ${{\bm{k}}_{\mathbb{P}}}$ , $T=\Theta(\sqrt{n})$ , and $r=(\log n)^{2({\alpha}+{\beta}\gamma)+\epsilon}$ for any $\epsilon>0$ , LD delivers $\widetilde{O}(n^{-1/2})$ excess MMD with high probability in $\widetilde{O}(n^{1.5})$ time.

### 3.2 Fast debiased compression via Low-rank Stein KT

To achieve debiased compression in sub-quadratic time, we next propose Low-rank SKT (Alg. 3). LSKT debiases the input using LD, converts the LD output into an equal-weighted coreset using Resample, and finally combines KT with the divide-and-conquer Compress++ framework (Shetty et al., 2022) to compress $n$ equal-weighted points into $\sqrt{n}$ in near-linear time.

*Algorithm 3 Low-rank Stein Kernel Thinning (LSKT)*

```
Input: mean-zero kernel ${{\bm{k}}_{\mathbb{P}}}$ , points $\mathcal{S}_{n}=(x_{i})_{i=1}^{n}$ , rank $r$ , AGM steps $T$ , adaptive rounds $Q$ , oversampling parameter $\mathfrak{g}$ , failure prob. $\delta$
$w\leftarrow\hyperref@@ii[alg:alrbc]{\textup{Low-rankDebiasing}}({{\bm{k}}_{\mathbb{P}}},\mathcal{S}_{n},r,T,Q)$
$n^{\prime}\leftarrow 4^{\left\lceil\log_{4}n\right\rceil},m\leftarrow\sqrt{n^{\prime}}$ $\triangleright$ output size $\sqrt{n}\leq m<2\sqrt{n}$
$w\leftarrow\hyperref@@ii[alg:stratified_resample]{\textup{Resample}}(w,n^{\prime})$
$w_{{\textup{LSKT}}}\leftarrow\hyperref@@ii[alg:compresspp_target]{\textup{KT-Compress++}}({{\bm{k}}_{\mathbb{P}}},\mathcal{S}_{n},n^{\prime},w,\mathfrak{g},\frac{\delta}{3})$
Return: $w_{{\textup{LSKT}}}\in\!\Delta_{n-1}\cap(\frac{\mathbb{N}_{0}}{m})^{n}$ $\triangleright$ hence $\left\|{w_{{\textup{LSKT}}}}\right\|_{0}\leq m$
```

Our next result (proved in App. F) shows that LSKT can provide better-than-i.i.d. excess MMD in $o(n^{2})$ time.

#### Theorem 5 (MMD guarantee for LSKT).

Under Assum. ( α , β ) -params, Low-rank SKT (Alg. 3) with $\mathfrak{g}\!\in[\log_{2}\log(n+1)+3.1,\log_{4}(\sqrt{n}/\log n)]$ and $\delta\in(0,1)$ outputs $w_{{\textup{LSKT}}}$ in $O((d_{{{\bm{k}}_{\mathbb{P}}}}\!+\!r\!+\!T)nr\!+\!d_{{{\bm{k}}_{\mathbb{P}}}}n^{1.5})$ time satisfying, with probability at least $1-\delta$ ,

$$ \textstyle\Delta\!\mmd_{{{\bm{k}}_{\mathbb{P}}}}(w_{{\textup{LSKT}}}) \textstyle\quad=O\left(\!\sqrt{\frac{\|{{{\bm{k}}_{\mathbb{P}}}}\|_{n}\max(1/\delta,\,\ell_{\delta}(\log n)n^{\gamma{\beta}}G_{\sqrt{n}}^{\alpha})}{n}}+\sqrt{\frac{nH_{n,r}}{\delta}}\right), $$

for $G_{m}$ , $H_{n,r}$ as in Thms. 3 and 5.

#### Example 3.

Under the assumptions of Thm. 5 with $\gamma$ -slow-growing input points (Def. 3), LogGrowth ${{\bm{k}}_{\mathbb{P}}}$ , $T=\Theta(\sqrt{n})$ , and $r=(\log n)^{2({\alpha}+{\beta}\gamma)+\epsilon}$ for any $\epsilon>0$ , LSKT delivers, with high probability, $\widetilde{O}(n^{-1/2})$ excess MMD in $\widetilde{O}(n^{1.5})$ time using a coreset of size $m\in[\sqrt{n},2\sqrt{n})$ .

## 4 Weighted Debiased Compression

The prior sections developed debiased equal-weighted coresets with better-than-i.i.d. compression guarantees. Equal-weighted coresets are typically chosen for their compatibility with unweighted downstream tasks and easy visualization. For downstream tasks that support weights, we next match the equal-weighted guarantees with significantly smaller simplex-weighted or constant-preserving coresets.

### 4.1 Simplex-weighted coresets via Stein Recombination​

*Algorithm 4 Recombination Thinning (RT)*

```
Input: mean-zero kernel ${{\bm{k}}_{\mathbb{P}}}$ , points $\mathcal{S}_{n}=(x_{i})_{i=1}^{n}$ , weights $w\in\Delta_{n-1}$ , output size $m$
$\tilde{w}\leftarrow\hyperref@@ii[alg:stratified_resample]{\textup{Resample}}(w,n)$
$\mathtt{I},F\leftarrow\hyperref@@ii[alg:rpc]{\textup{WeightedRPCholesky}}({{\bm{k}}_{\mathbb{P}}},\mathcal{S}_{n},\tilde{w},m-1)$
$w^{\prime}\leftarrow\hyperref@@ii[alg:recombbfs]{\textup{Recombination}}([F,\bm{1}_{n}]^{\top},\tilde{w})$ $\triangleright$ $[F,\bm{1}_{n}]^{\top}\!\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}$
$\triangleright$ $F^{\top}\tilde{w}=F^{\top}w^{\prime}$ , $w^{\prime}\in\Delta_{n-1}$ , and $\left\|{w^{\prime}}\right\|_{0}\leq m$
$w^{\prime\prime}\!\leftarrow\!\hyperref@@ii[alg:kt_swap_ls]{\textup{KT-Swap-LS}}({{\bm{k}}_{\mathbb{P}}},\mathcal{S}_{n},w^{\prime},\textup{SPLX})$ ; $\mathtt{J}\leftarrow\!\{i\!:w^{\prime\prime}_{i}>0\}$
$w^{\prime\prime}[\mathtt{J}]\leftarrow\mathop{\mathrm{}}{argmin}_{w^{\prime}\in\Delta_{\absolutevalue{\tJ}-1}}w^{\prime\top}{{\bm{k}}_{\mathbb{P}}}(\mathcal{S}_{n}[\mathtt{J}],\mathcal{S}_{n}[\mathtt{J}])w^{\prime}$ $\triangleright$ use any $O(\absolutevalue{\tJ}^{3})$ quadratic programming solver
Return: $w_{{\textup{RT}}}\leftarrow w^{\prime\prime}\in\Delta_{n-1}$ with $\|{w_{{\textup{RT}}}}\|_{0}\leq m$
```

Simplex-weighted coresets automatically preserve the constraints of convex integrands, support straightforward direct sampling, and, when compared with schemes involving negative weights, offer improved numerical stability in the presence of integral evaluations errors (Karvonen et al., 2019). Inspired by the coreset constructions of Hayakawa et al. (2022); Hayakawa et al. (2023), we first introduce a simplex-weighted compression algorithm, RecombinationThinning (RT, Alg. 4), suitable for summarizing a debiased input sequence. To produce a coreset given input weights $w\in\Delta_{n-1}$ , RT first prunes small weights using Resample and then uses WeightedRPCholesky to identify $m\!-\!1$ test vectors that capture most of the variability in the weighted kernel matrix. Next, Recombination (Alg. G.1) (Tchernychova, 2016, Alg. 1) identifies a sparse simplex vector $w^{\prime}$ with $\left\|{w^{\prime}}\right\|_{0}\leq m$ that exactly matches the inner product of its input with each of the test vectors. Then, we run KT-Swap-LS (Alg. G.2), a new, line-search version of kt-swap (Dwivedi and Mackey, 2021, Alg. 1b) that greedily improves MMD to $\mathbb{P}$ while maintaining both the sparsity and simplex constraint of its input. Finally, we optimize the weights of the remaining support points using any cubic-time quadratic programming solver.

In Prop. G.1 we show that RT runs in time $O((d_{{{\bm{k}}_{\mathbb{P}}}}+m)nm+m^{3}\log n)$ and nearly preserves the MMD of its input whenever $m$ grows appropriately with the kernel covering number. Combining RT with SteinThinning or Low-rankDebiasing in Alg. 5, we obtain Stein Recombination (SR) and Low-rank SR (LSR), our approaches to debiased simplex-weighted compression. Remarkably, SR and LSR can match the MMD error rates established for SKT and LSKT using substantially fewer coreset points, as our next result (proved in Sec. G.2) shows.

*Algorithm 5 (Low-rank) Stein Recombination (SR / LSR)*

```
Input: mean-zero kernel ${{\bm{k}}_{\mathbb{P}}}$ , points $\mathcal{S}_{n}$ , output size $m$ , rank $r$ , AGM steps $T$ , adaptive rounds $Q$
$w\leftarrow\begin{cases}\hyperref@@ii[alg:alrbc]{\textup{Low-rankDebiasing}}({{\bm{k}}_{\mathbb{P}}},\mathcal{S}_{n},r,T,Q)&\textup{if low-rank}\\ \hyperref@@ii[alg:GBC]{\textup{SteinThinning}}({{\bm{k}}_{\mathbb{P}}},\mathcal{S}_{n})&\textup{otherwise}\end{cases}$
$w_{\textup{SR}}\leftarrow\hyperref@@ii[alg:recomb]{\textup{RecombinationThinning}}({{\bm{k}}_{\mathbb{P}}},\mathcal{S}_{n},w,m)$
Return: $w_{\textup{SR}}\in\Delta_{n-1}$ with $\|{w_{\textup{SR}}}\|_{0}\leq m$
```

#### Theorem 6 (MMD guarantee for SR/LSR).

Under Assum. ( α , β ) -params, Stein Recombination (Alg. 5) takes $O(d_{{{\bm{k}}_{\mathbb{P}}}}n^{2}\!+\!(d_{{{\bm{k}}_{\mathbb{P}}}}\!+\!m)nm\!+\!m^{3}\log n)$ to output $w_{\textup{SR}}$ , and Low-rank SR takes $O((d_{{{\bm{k}}_{\mathbb{P}}}}\!+\!r\!+\!T)nr\!+\!(d_{{{\bm{k}}_{\mathbb{P}}}}\!+\!m)nm\!+\!m^{3}\log n)$ time to output $w_{\textup{LSR}}$ . Moreover, for any $\delta\in(0,1)$ and $H_{n,r}$ as in Thm. 4, each of the following bounds holds (separately) with probability at least $1-\delta$ :

$$ \textstyle\Delta\!\mmd_{{{\bm{k}}_{\mathbb{P}}}}\!(w_{\textup{SR}})\!=\!O\Big(\sqrt{\frac{\left\|{{{\bm{k}}_{\mathbb{P}}}}\right\|_{n}(\log n\vee\frac{1}{\delta})}{n}+\frac{nH_{n,m}}{\delta}}\Big)\ \text{and}\  \textstyle\Delta\!\mmd_{{{\bm{k}}_{\mathbb{P}}}}\!(w_{\textup{LSR}})\!=\!O\Big(\!\sqrt{\frac{\left\|{{{\bm{k}}_{\mathbb{P}}}}\right\|_{n}(\log n\vee\frac{1}{\delta})}{n}+\frac{n(H_{n,m}+H_{n,r})}{\delta}}\Big)\!. $$

#### Example 4.

Instantiate the assumptions of Thm. 6 with $\gamma$ -slow-growing input points (Def. 3), LogGrowth ${{\bm{k}}_{\mathbb{P}}}$ , and a heavily compressed coreset size $m=(\log n)^{2({\alpha}+{\beta}\gamma)+\epsilon}$ for any $\epsilon>0$ . Then SR delivers $\widetilde{O}(n^{-1/2})$ excess MMD with high probability in $O(n^{2})$ time, and LSR with $r\!=\!m$ and $T=\Theta(\sqrt{n})$ achieves the same in $\widetilde{O}(n^{1.5})$ time.

### 4.2 Constant-preserving coresets via Stein Cholesky

For applications supporting negative weights, constant-preserving coresets offer the possibility of higher accuracy at the cost of potential numerical instability and poorer robustness to errors in integral evaluation (Karvonen et al., 2019). We introduce a constant-preserving compression algorithm, CholeskyThinning (CT, Alg. 6), suitable for summarizing a debiased input sequence. CT first applies WeightedRPCholesky to a constant-regularized kernel ${{\bm{k}}_{\mathbb{P}}}(x,y)+c$ to select an initial coreset and then uses a combination of KT-Swap-LS and closed-form optimal constant-preserving reweighting to greedily refine the support and weights. The regularized kernel ensures that the coreset output by WeightedRPCholesky is of high quality when paired with the best constant-preserving weights, and our CT standalone analysis (Prop. H.1) improves upon the runtime and error guarantees of RT. In Alg. 7, we combine CT with SteinThinning or Low-rankDebiasing to obtain Stein Cholesky (SC) and Low-rank SC (LSC), our approaches to debiased constant-preserving compression. Our MMD guarantees for SC and LSC (proved in Sec. H.2) improve upon the rates of Thm. 6.

*Algorithm 6 Cholesky Thinning (CT)*

```
Input: mean-zero kernel ${{\bm{k}}_{\mathbb{P}}}$ , points $\mathcal{S}_{n}=(x_{i})_{i=1}^{n}$ , weights $w\in\Delta_{n-1}$ , output size $m$
$c\leftarrow\textsc{Average}(\text{Largest $m$ entries of }({{\bm{k}}_{\mathbb{P}}}(x_{i},x_{i}))_{i=1}^{n})$
$\mathtt{I},F\leftarrow\hyperref@@ii[alg:rpc]{\textup{WeightedRPCholesky}}({{\bm{k}}_{\mathbb{P}}}+c,\mathcal{S}_{n},w,m)$ ; $w\leftarrow\bm{0}_{n}$
$w[\mathtt{I}]\leftarrow\mathop{\mathrm{}}{argmin}_{w^{\prime}\in\mathbb{R}^{\absolutevalue{\tI}}:\sum_{i}w_{i}^{\prime}=1}w^{\prime\top}{{\bm{k}}_{\mathbb{P}}}(\mathcal{S}_{n}[\mathtt{I}],\mathcal{S}_{n}[\mathtt{I}])w^{\prime}$
$w\leftarrow\hyperref@@ii[alg:kt_swap_ls]{\textup{KT-Swap-LS}}({{\bm{k}}_{\mathbb{P}}},\mathcal{S}_{n},w,\textup{CP})$ ; $\mathtt{I}\leftarrow\{i:w_{i}\neq 0\}$
$w[\mathtt{I}]\leftarrow\mathop{\mathrm{}}{argmin}_{w^{\prime}\in\mathbb{R}^{\absolutevalue{\tI}}:\sum_{i}w_{i}^{\prime}=1}w^{\prime\top}{{\bm{k}}_{\mathbb{P}}}(\mathcal{S}_{n}[\mathtt{I}],\mathcal{S}_{n}[\mathtt{I}])w^{\prime}$
Return: $w_{{\textup{CT}}}\leftarrow w\in\mathbb{R}^{n}$ with $\|{w_{{\textup{CT}}}}\|_{0}\leq m$ , $\bm{1}_{n}^{\top}w_{{\textup{CT}}}=1$
```

*Algorithm 7 (Low-rank) Stein Cholesky (SC / LSC)*

```
Input: mean-zero kernel ${{\bm{k}}_{\mathbb{P}}}$ , points $\mathcal{S}_{n}$ , output size $m$ , rank $r$ , AGM steps $T$ , adaptive rounds $Q$
$w\leftarrow\begin{cases}\hyperref@@ii[alg:alrbc]{\textup{Low-rankDebiasing}}({{\bm{k}}_{\mathbb{P}}},\mathcal{S}_{n},r,T,Q)&\textup{if low-rank}\\ \hyperref@@ii[alg:GBC]{\textup{SteinThinning}}({{\bm{k}}_{\mathbb{P}}},\mathcal{S}_{n})&\textup{otherwise}\end{cases}$
$w_{\textup{SC}}\leftarrow\hyperref@@ii[alg:cholthin]{\textup{CholeskyThinning}}({{\bm{k}}_{\mathbb{P}}},\mathcal{S}_{n},w,m)$
Return: $w_{\textup{SC}}\in\mathbb{R}^{n}$ with $\|{w_{\textup{SC}}}\|_{0}\leq m$ and $\mathbf{1}_{n}^{\top}w_{\textup{SC}}=1$
```

Right: Using only one chain, our methods consistently outperform the Stein and standard thinning baselines and match the 6-chain oracle.*

#### Theorem 7 (MMD guarantee for SC / LSC).

Under Assum. ( α , β ) -params, Stein Cholesky (Alg. 7) takes $O(d_{{{\bm{k}}_{\mathbb{P}}}}n^{2}\!+\!(d_{{{\bm{k}}_{\mathbb{P}}}}\!+\!m)nm\!+\!m^{3})$ time to output $w_{\textup{SC}}$ , and Low-rank SC takes $O((d_{{{\bm{k}}_{\mathbb{P}}}}\!+\!r\!+\!T)nr\!+\!(d_{{{\bm{k}}_{\mathbb{P}}}}\!+\!m)nm\!+\!m^{3})$ time to output $w_{\textup{LSC}}$ . Moreover, for any $\delta\in(0,1)$ , with probability at least $1-\delta$ , each of the following bounds hold:

$$ \textstyle\Delta\!\mmd_{{{\bm{k}}_{\mathbb{P}}}}(w_{\textup{SC}})=2\mmd_{\mathrm{OPT}} \textstyle+O\big(\!\sqrt{\frac{\left\|{{{\bm{k}}_{\mathbb{P}}}}\right\|_{n}\log n}{\delta n}+\frac{H_{n,m^{\prime}}}{\delta}}\big)\ \text{and}\  \textstyle\Delta\!\mmd_{{{\bm{k}}_{\mathbb{P}}}}(w_{\textup{LSC}})=2\mmd_{\mathrm{OPT}} \textstyle+O\big(\!\sqrt{\frac{\left\|{{{\bm{k}}_{\mathbb{P}}}}\right\|_{n}(\log n\vee 1/\delta)}{\delta n}+\frac{H_{n,m^{\prime}}}{\delta}+\frac{nH_{n,r}}{\delta^{2}}}\big) $$

for $H_{n,r}$ as in Thm. 4 and $m^{\prime}\triangleq m+\log 2-2\sqrt{m\log 2+1}$ .

Instantiate the assumptions of Thm. 7 with $\gamma$ -slow-growing input points (Def. 3), LogGrowth ${{\bm{k}}_{\mathbb{P}}}$ , and a heavily compressed coreset size $m=(\log n)^{2({\alpha}+{\beta}\gamma)+\epsilon}$ for any $\epsilon>0$ . ## 5 Experiments

We next evaluate the practical utility of our procedures when faced with three common sources of bias: (1) burn-in, (2) approximate MCMC, and (3) tempering. In all experiments, we use a Stein kernel ${{\bm{k}}_{p}}$ with an inverse multiquadric (IMQ) base kernel ${\bm{k}}(x,y)\!=\!(1\!+\!\|{x\!-\!y}\|^{2}_{M}/\sigma^{2})^{-1/2}$ for $\sigma$ equal to the median pairwise $\|{\cdot}\|_{M}$ distance amongst $1000$ points standard thinned from the input. To vary output MMD precision, we first standard thin the input to size $n_{0}\in\{2^{10},2^{12},2^{14},2^{16},2^{18},2^{20}\}$ before applying any method, as discussed in Rems. 3 and 2. For low-rank or weighted coreset methods, we show results for $m\!=\!r\!=\!n^{\tau}$ . When comparing weighted coresets, we optimally reweight every coreset. We report the median over 5 independent runs for all error metrics. We implement our algorithms in JAX (Bradbury et al., 2018) and refer the reader to App. I for additional experiment details (including runtime comparison in Tab. I.1). Our open-source code is available as part of the GoodPoints Python library at https://github.com/microsoft/goodpoints.

Correcting for burn-in The initial iterates of a Markov chain are biased by its starting point and need not accurately reflect the target distribution $\mathbb{P}$ . Classical burn-in corrections use convergence diagnostics to detect and discard these iterates but typically require running multiple independent Markov chains (Cowles et al., 1999). Alternatively, our proposed debiased compression methods can be used to correct for burn-in given just a single chain.

We test this claim using an experimental setup from Riabiz et al. (2022, Sec. 4.1) and the $6$ -chain “burn-in oracle” diagnostic of Vats and Knudson (2021).55 5 The Vats and Knudson diagnostic is an improvement on the popular Gelman and Rubin (1992) diagnostic (GRD). The GRD was designed to diagnose MCMC convergence rather than burn-in but is commonly used to identify and discard burn-in points automatically through packages like coda (Plummer et al., 2006). We aim to compress a posterior $\mathbb{P}$ over the parameters in the Goodwin model of oscillatory enzymatic control ( $d\!=\!4$ ) using $n\!=\!2\!\times\!10^{6}$ points from a preconditioned Metropolis-adjusted Langevin algorithm (P-MALA) chain. We repeat this experiment with three alternative MCMC algorithms in Sec. I.3. Our primary metric is $\mmd_{{{\bm{k}}_{\mathbb{P}}}}$ to $\mathbb{P}$ with $M=I$ , but, for external validation, we also measure the energy distance (Riabiz et al., 2022, Eq. 11) to an auxiliary MCMC chain of length $n$ . Trajectory plots of the first two coordinates (Fig. 1, left) highlight the substantial burn-in period for the Goodwin chain and the ability of LSKT to mimic the 6-chain burn-in oracle using only a single chain. In Fig. 1 (right), for both the MMD metric and the auxiliary energy distance, our proposed methods consistently outperform Stein thinning and match the quality of 6-chain burn-in removal paired with unbiased compression. The spike in baseline energy distance for the constant-preserving task can be attributed to the selection of overly large weight values due to poor matrix conditioning; the simplex-weighted task does not suffer from this issue due to its regularizing nonnegativity constraint.

Correcting for approximate MCMC In posterior inference, MCMC algorithms typically require iterating over every datapoint to draw each new sample point. When datasets are large, approximating MCMC using datapoint mini-batches can reduce sampling time at the cost of persistent bias and an unknown stationary distribution that prohibits debiasing via importance sampling. Our proposed methods can correct for these biases during compression by computing full-dataset scores on a small subset of $n_{0}$ standard thinned points. To evaluate this protocol, we compress a Bayesian logistic regression posterior conditioned on the Forest Covtype dataset ( $d\!=\!54$ ) using $n\!=\!2^{24}$ approximate MCMC points from the stochastic gradient Fisher scoring sampler (Ahn et al., 2012) with batch size $32$ . Following Wang et al. (2024), we set $M\!=\!-\nabla^{2}\!\log p(x_{\textup{mode}})$ at the sample mode $x_{\textup{mode}}$ and use $2^{20}$ surrogate ground truth points from the No U-turn Sampler (Hoffman and Gelman, 2014) to evaluate energy distance. We find that our proposals improve upon standard thinning and Stein thinning for each compression task, not just in the optimized MMD metric (Fig. 2, top) but also in the auxiliary energy distance (Fig. 2, middle) and when measuring integration error for the mean (Fig. I.4).

Correcting for tempering Tempering, targeting a less-peaked and more dispersed distribution $\mathbb{Q}$ , is a popular technique to improve the speed of MCMC convergence. One can correct for the sample bias using importance sampling, but this requires knowledge of the tempered density and can introduce substantial variance (Gramacy et al., 2010). Alternatively, one can use constructions of this work to correct for tempering during compression; this requires no importance weighting and no knowledge of $\mathbb{Q}$ . To test this proposal, we compress the cardiac calcium signaling model posterior ( $d=38$ ) of Riabiz et al. (2022, Sec. 4.3) with $M=I$ and $n=3\times 10^{6}$ tempered points from a Gaussian random walk Metropolis-Hastings chain. As discussed by Riabiz et al., compression is essential in this setting as the ultimate aim is to propagate posterior uncertainty through a human heart simulator, a feat which requires over $1000$ CPU hours for each summary point retained. Our methods perform on par with Stein thinning for equal-weighted compression and yield substantial gains over Stein (and standard) thinning for the two weighted compression tasks.

## 6 Conclusions and Future Work

We have introduced and analyzed a suite of new procedures for compressing a biased input sequence into an accurate summary of a target distribution. For equal-weighted compression, Stein kernel thinning delivers $\sqrt{n}$ points with $\widetilde{O}(n^{-1/2})$ MMD in $O(n^{2})$ time, and low-rank SKT can improve this running time to $\widetilde{O}(n^{3/2})$ . For simplex-weighted and constant-preserving compression, Stein recombination and Stein Cholesky provide enhanced parsimony, matching these guarantees with as few as $\operatorname{poly-log}(n)$ points. Recent work has identified some limitations of score-based discrepancies, like Stein kernel MMDs, and developed modified objectives that are more sensitive to the relative density of isolated modes (Liu et al., 2023; Bénard et al., 2024). A valuable next step would be to extend our constructions to provide compression guarantees for these modified discrepancy measures. Other opportunities for future work include marrying the better-than-i.i.d. guarantees of this work with the non-myopic compression of Teymur et al. (2021), the control-variate compression of Chopin and Ducrocq (2021), and the online compression of Koppel et al. (2024).

## Appendix B Spectral Analysis of Kernel Matrices

### B.1 From covering numbers of kernels to eigenvalues of kernel matrices

We first introduce the general Mercer representation theorem from Steinwart and Scovel [2012], which shows the existence of a discrete spectrum of the integral operator associated with a continuous square-integrable kernel. The theorem also provides a series expansion of the kernel, i.e., the Mercer representation, in terms of the eigenvalues and eigenfunctions.

#### Lemma B.1 (General Mercer representation [Steinwart and Scovel, 2012]).

Consider a kernel ${\bm{k}}:\mathbb{R}^{d}\times\mathbb{R}^{d}\to\mathbb{R}$ that is jointly continuous in both inputs and a probability measure $\mu$ such that $\int{\bm{k}}(x,x)\differential\mu(x)<\infty$ . Then the following holds.

- (a) The inclusion ${{\mathcal{H}_{{\bm{k}}}}}\hookrightarrow{\mathcal{L}^{2}(\mu)}$ is a compact operator, i.e., $\mathcal{B}_{{\bm{k}}}$ is a compact subset of $\mathcal{L}^{2}(\mu)$ . In particular, this inclusion is continuous.

- (b) The Hilbert-space adjoint of the inclusion ${{\mathcal{H}_{{\bm{k}}}}}\hookrightarrow{\mathcal{L}^{2}(\mu)}$ is the compact operator $S_{{\bm{k}},\mu}:\mathcal{L}^{2}(\mu)\to{\mathcal{H}_{{\bm{k}}}}$ defined as $\textstyle S_{{\bm{k}},\mu}f\triangleq\int{\bm{k}}(\cdot,x)f(x)\differential\mu(x).$ (23) We also have $S_{{\bm{k}},\mu}^{*}\triangleq{{\mathcal{H}_{{\bm{k}}}}}\hookrightarrow{\mathcal{L}^{2}(\mu)}$ . Hence the operator $\textstyle T_{{\bm{k}},\mu}\triangleq S^{*}_{{\bm{k}},\mu}S_{{\bm{k}},\mu}:\mathcal{L}^{2}(\mu)\to\mathcal{L}^{2}(\mu)$ (24) is also compact.

- (c) There exist $\{\lambda_{\ell}\}_{\ell=1}^{\infty}$ with $\lambda_{1}\geq\lambda_{2}\geq\cdots\geq 0$ and $\{\phi_{\ell}\}_{\ell=1}^{\infty}\subset{\mathcal{H}_{{\bm{k}}}}$ such that $\{{\phi_{\ell}}\}_{\ell=1}^{\infty}$ is an orthonormal system in $\mathcal{L}^{2}(\mu)$ and $\{\lambda_{\ell}\}_{\ell=1}^{\infty}$ (resp. $\{{\phi_{\ell}}\}_{\ell=1}^{\infty}$ ) consists of the eigenvalues (resp. eigenfunctions) of $T_{{\bm{k}},\mu}$ with eigendecomposition, for ${f}\in\mathcal{L}^{2}(\mu)$ , $\textstyle T_{{\bm{k}},\mu}{f}=\sum_{\ell=1}^{\infty}\lambda_{\ell}\langle{f},{\phi_{\ell}}\rangle_{\mathcal{L}^{2}(\mu)}{\phi_{\ell}}$ (25) with convergence in $\mathcal{L}^{2}(\mu)$ .

- (d) We have the following series expansion $\textstyle{\bm{k}}(x,x^{\prime})$ $\textstyle=\sum_{\ell=1}^{\infty}\lambda_{i}\phi_{\ell}(x)\phi_{\ell}(x^{\prime}),$ (26) where the series convergence is absolute and uniform in $x,x^{\prime}$ on all $A\times A\subset\supp\mu\times\supp\mu$ .

#### Proof of Lem. B.1.

Part (a) and (b) follow respectively from Steinwart and Scovel [2012, Lem. 2.3 and 2.2]. Part (c) follows from part (a) and Steinwart and Scovel [2012, Lem. 2.12]. Finally, part (d) follows from Steinwart and Scovel [2012, Cor. 3.5]. ∎

We will use the following lemma regarding the restriction of covering numbers.

#### Lemma B.2 (Covering number is preserved in restriction).

For a kernel ${\bm{k}}:\mathbb{R}^{d}\times\mathbb{R}^{d}\to\mathbb{R}$ and a set $A\subset\mathbb{R}^{d}$ , we have $\mathcal{N}_{{\bm{k}}}(A,\epsilon)=\mathcal{N}_{{\bm{k}}|_{A}}(A,\epsilon)$ , for ${\bm{k}}|_{A}$ , the restricted kernel of ${\bm{k}}$ to $A$ [Paulsen and Raghupathi, 2016, Sec. 5.4].

#### Proof of Lem. B.2.

It suffices to show that a $({\bm{k}},A,\epsilon)$ cover can be converted to a cover of $({\bm{k}}|_{A},A,\epsilon)$ of the same cardinality and vice versa.

Let $\mathcal{C}\subset\mathcal{B}_{{\bm{k}}|_{A}}$ be a $({\bm{k}}|_{A},A,\epsilon)$ cover. For any $f\in\mathcal{C}$ , we have $\|{f}\|_{{\bm{k}}|_{A}}=\inf\left\{\|{\tilde{f}}\|_{{\bm{k}}}:\tilde{f}\in{\mathcal{H}_{{\bm{k}}}},\tilde{f}|_{A}=f\right\}\leq 1$ [Paulsen and Raghupathi, 2016, Corollary 5.8]. Moreover, the infimum is attained by some $\tilde{f}\in{\mathcal{H}_{{\bm{k}}}}$ such that $\|{\tilde{f}}\|_{{\bm{k}}}=\|{f}\|_{{\bm{k}}|_{A}}\leq 1$ and $\tilde{f}|_{A}=f$ . Now form $\tilde{\mathcal{C}}=\{\tilde{f}:f\in\mathcal{C}\}$ . For any $\tilde{h}\in\mathcal{B}_{{\bm{k}}}$ , there exists $f\in\mathcal{C}$ such that

$$ \textstyle\left\|{\tilde{h}|_{A}-f}\right\|_{\infty,A}\leq\epsilon\implies=\left\|{\tilde{h}-\tilde{f}}\right\|_{\infty,A}\leq\epsilon, $$

so $\tilde{\mathcal{C}}$ is a $({\bm{k}}|_{A},A,\epsilon)$ cover.

For the other direction, let $\tilde{\mathcal{C}}\subset\mathcal{B}_{{\bm{k}}}$ be a $({\bm{k}},A,\epsilon)$ cover. Define $\mathcal{C}=\{\tilde{f}|_{A}:\tilde{f}\in\tilde{\mathcal{C}}\}\subset{\mathcal{H}_{{\bm{k}}|_{A}}}$ . Since $\|{\tilde{f}|_{A}}\|_{{\bm{k}}|_{A}}\leq\|{\tilde{f}}\|_{{\bm{k}}}$ , we have $\mathcal{C}\subset\mathcal{B}_{{\bm{k}}|_{A}}$ . For any $h\in\mathcal{B}_{{\bm{k}}_{A}]}$ , again by Paulsen and Raghupathi [2016, Corollary 5.8], there exists $\tilde{h}\in{\mathcal{H}_{{\bm{k}}}}$ such that $\|{\tilde{h}}\|_{{\bm{k}}}=\|{h}\|_{{\bm{k}}|_{A}}\leq 1$ , so there exists $\tilde{f}\in\tilde{\mathcal{C}}$ such that

$$ \textstyle\left\|{\tilde{h}-\tilde{f}}\right\|_{\infty,A}\leq\epsilon\implies\left\|{h-\tilde{f}|_{A}}\right\|_{\infty,A}\leq\epsilon, $$

Hence $\mathcal{C}$ is a $({\bm{k}},A,\epsilon)$ cover. ∎

The goal for the rest of this section is to transfer the bounds of the covering number in the definition of a PolyGrowth or LogGrowth kernel from Assum. ( α , β )-kernel to bounds on entropy numbers [Steinwart and Christmann, 2008, Def. 6.20] that are closely related to eigenvalues of the integral operator (24).

#### Definition B.1 (Entropy number of a bounded linear map).

For a bounded linear operator $S:E\to F$ between normed spaces $E,F$ , for $\ell\in\mathbb{N}$ , the $\ell$ -th entropy number of $S$ is defined as

$$ \textstyle e_{\ell}(S)\triangleq\inf\left\{\epsilon>0:\exists s_{1},\ldots,s_{2^{\ell-1}}\in S(\mathcal{B}_{E})\text{ such that }S(\mathcal{B}_{E})\subset\bigcup_{i=1}^{2^{\ell-1}}\mathcal{B}_{F}(s_{i},\epsilon)\right\}. $$

The following lemma shows the relation between covering numbers and entropy numbers.

#### Lemma B.3 (Relation between covering number and entropy number).

Suppose a kernel ${\bm{k}}$ is jointly continuous and $A\subset\mathbb{R}^{d}$ is bounded. Then for any $\epsilon>0$ ,

$$ \textstyle e_{\lceil\log_{2}\mathcal{N}_{{\bm{k}}}(A,\epsilon)\rceil+1}({{\mathcal{H}_{{\bm{k}}|_{A}}}}\hookrightarrow{\ell_{\infty}(A)})\leq\epsilon. $$

#### Proof of Lem. B.3.

First, the assumption implies ${\bm{k}}|_{A}$ is a bounded kernel, so by Steinwart and Christmann [2008, Lemma 4.23], the inclusion ${{\mathcal{H}_{{\bm{k}}|_{A}}}}\hookrightarrow{\ell_{\infty}(A)}$ is continuous. By the definition of $\mathcal{N}_{{\bm{k}}|_{A}}(A,\epsilon)$ , by adding arbitrary elements into the cover if necessary, there exists a $({\bm{k}}|_{A},A,\epsilon)$ cover of $\mathcal{B}_{{\bm{k}}|_{A}}$ of cardinality $2^{\lceil\log_{2}(\mathcal{N}_{{\bm{k}}|_{A}}(A,\epsilon))\rceil}\geq\mathcal{N}_{{\bm{k}}|_{A}}(A,\epsilon)$ . Hence

$$ \textstyle e_{\lceil\log_{2}\mathcal{N}_{{\bm{k}}|_{A}}(A,\epsilon)\rceil+1}({{\mathcal{H}_{{\bm{k}}|_{A}}}}\hookrightarrow{\ell_{\infty}(A)})\leq\epsilon. $$

The claim follows since $\mathcal{N}_{{\bm{k}}|_{A}}(A,\epsilon)=\mathcal{N}_{{\bm{k}}}(A,\epsilon)$ by Lem. B.2. ∎

#### Proposition B.1 ( $\ell_{\infty}$ -entropy number bound for PolyGrowth or LogGrowth ${\bm{k}}$ ).

Suppose a kernel ${\bm{k}}$ satisfies Assum. ( α , β )-kernel. Let $\mathfrak{C}_{d}>0$ denote the constant that appears in the Assum. ( α , β )-kernel. Define

$$ \textstyle L_{\bm{k}}(r)\triangleq\frac{\mathfrak{C}_{d}}{\log 2}r^{\beta}. $$

Then for any $r>0$ and $\ell\in\mathbb{N}$ that satisfies $\ell>L_{\bm{k}}(r+1)+1$ , we have

$$ \textstyle e_{\ell}({{\mathcal{H}_{{\bm{k}}|_{\mathcal{B}_{2}(r)}}}}\hookrightarrow{\ell_{\infty}(\mathcal{B}_{2}(r))})\leq\begin{cases}\left(\frac{L_{\bm{k}}(r+1)}{\ell-1}\right)^{\frac{1}{{\alpha}}}&\text{if }{\bm{k}}\ \text{is}\ \hyperref@@ii[assum:kernel_growth]{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}{\textsc{PolyGrowth}}}(\alpha,\beta),\text{ and}\\
\exp(1-\left(\frac{\ell-1}{\krcd_\k(r+1)}\right)^{\frac{1}{\cvrw}})&\text{if }{\bm{k}}\ \text{is}\ \hyperref@@ii[assum:kernel_growth]{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}{\textsc{LogGrowth}}}(\alpha,\beta).\end{cases} $$

#### Proof of Prop. B.1.

By Lem. B.3 and the fact that $e_{\ell}$ is monotonically decreasing in $\ell$ by definition, if $\ell\geq\log_{2}\mathcal{N}_{{\bm{k}}}(\mathcal{B}_{2}(r),\epsilon)+1$ for some $\epsilon>0$ , then

$$ \textstyle e_{\ell}({{\mathcal{H}_{{\bm{k}}|_{\mathcal{B}_{2}(r)}}}}\hookrightarrow{\ell_{\infty}(\mathcal{B}_{2}(r))})\leq e_{\lceil\log_{2}\mathcal{N}_{{\bm{k}}}(\mathcal{B}_{2}(r),\epsilon)\rceil+1}({{\mathcal{H}_{{\bm{k}}|_{\mathcal{B}_{2}(r)}}}}\hookrightarrow{\ell_{\infty}(\mathcal{B}_{2}(r))})\leq\epsilon. $$

For the PolyGrowth case, by its definition, the condition $\ell\geq\log_{2}\mathcal{N}_{{\bm{k}}}(\mathcal{B}_{2}(r),\epsilon)+1$ is met if $\epsilon\in(0,1)$ and

$$ \textstyle\ell\geq\frac{\mathfrak{C}_{d}}{\log 2}(1/\epsilon)^{{\alpha}}(r+1)^{\beta}+1\Longleftrightarrow\epsilon\leq\left(\frac{L_{\bm{k}}(r+1)}{\ell-1}\right)^{\frac{1}{{\alpha}}}. $$

Hence (34) holds with $\epsilon=\left(\frac{L_{\bm{k}}(r+1)}{\ell-1}\right)^{\frac{1}{{\alpha}}}$ , as long as $\epsilon\in(0,1)$ , so $\ell$ needs to satisfy

$$ \textstyle 1 \textstyle>\left(\frac{L_{\bm{k}}(r+1)}{\ell-1}\right)^{\frac{1}{{\alpha}}}\Longleftrightarrow\ell>L_{\bm{k}}(r+1)+1. $$

Similarly, for the LogGrowth case, the condition $\ell\geq\log_{2}\mathcal{N}_{{\bm{k}}}(\mathcal{B}_{2}(r),\epsilon)+1$ is met if $\epsilon\in(0,1)$ and

$$ \textstyle\ell\geq\frac{\mathfrak{C}_{d}}{\log 2}(\log(1/\eps)+1)^{{\alpha}}(r+1)^{\beta}+1\Longleftrightarrow\epsilon\leq\exp(1-\left(\frac{\ell-1}{\krcd_\k(r+1)}\right)^{\frac{1}{\cvrw}}). $$

Hence (34) holds with $\epsilon=\exp(1-\left(\frac{\ell-1}{\krcd_\k(r+1)}\right)^{\frac{1}{\cvrw}})$ , as long as $\epsilon\in(0,1)$ , so $\ell$ needs to satisfy

$$ \textstyle 1 \textstyle>\exp(1-\left(\frac{\ell-1}{\krcd_\k(r+1)}\right)^{\frac{1}{\cvrw}})\Longleftrightarrow\ell>L_{\bm{k}}(r+1)+1. $$

∎

Next, we show that we can transfer bounds on entropy numbers to obtain bounds for the eigenvalues of kernel matrices, which will become handy when we develop sub-quadratic-time algorithms in Sec. 3. We rely on the following lemma, which summarizes the relevant facts from Steinwart and Christmann [2008, Appendix A].

#### Lemma B.4 (Eigenvalue is bounded by entropy number).

Let ${\bm{k}}$ be a jointly continuous kernel and $\mathbb{P}$ be a distribution such that $\mathbb{E}_{x\sim\mathbb{P}}[{\bm{k}}(x,x)]<\infty$ , and recall that $\lambda_{\ell}(\cdot)$ denotes the $\ell$ -th largest eigenvalue of a linear operator. Then, for all $\ell\in\mathbb{N}$ ,

$$ \textstyle\lambda_{\ell}(T_{{\bm{k}},\mathbb{P}})\leq 4e_{\ell}^{2}({{\mathcal{H}_{{\bm{k}}}}}\hookrightarrow{\mathcal{L}^{2}(\mathbb{P})}). $$

#### Proof of Lem. B.4.

For any bounded linear operator $S:\mathcal{H}_{1}\to\mathcal{H}_{2}$ between Hilbert spaces $\mathcal{H}_{1}$ and $\mathcal{H}_{2}$ , we have $a_{\ell}(S)\leq 2e_{\ell}(S)$ , where $a_{\ell}$ is the $\ell$ -th approximation number defined in Steinwart and Christmann [2008, (A.29)]. Recall the operator $S^{*}_{{\bm{k}},\mathbb{P}}={{\mathcal{H}_{{\bm{k}}}}}\hookrightarrow{\mathcal{L}^{2}(\mathbb{P})}$ from (23), which is compact (in particular bounded) by Lem. B.1(a). Thus

$$ \textstyle s_{\ell}(S^{*}_{{\bm{k}},\mathbb{P}})=a_{\ell}(S^{*}_{{\bm{k}},\mathbb{P}})\leq 2e_{\ell}(S^{*}_{{\bm{k}},\mathbb{P}}), $$

where the first equality follows from the paragraph below Steinwart and Christmann [2008, (A.29)]) and $s_{\ell}$ is $\ell$ -th singular number of an operator [Steinwart and Christmann, 2008, (A.25)]. Then using the identities mentioned under Steinwart and Christmann [2008, (A.25)] and Steinwart and Christmann [2008, (A.27)] and that all operators involved are compact by Lem. B.1(b), we have

$$ \textstyle\lambda_{\ell}(T_{{\bm{k}},\mathbb{P}})=\lambda_{\ell}(S^{*}_{{\bm{k}},\mathbb{P}}S_{{\bm{k}},\mathbb{P}})=s_{\ell}(S^{*}_{{\bm{k}},\mathbb{P}}S_{{\bm{k}},\mathbb{P}})=s^{2}_{\ell}(S^{*}_{{\bm{k}},\mathbb{P}})\leq 4e^{2}_{\ell}(S^{*}_{{\bm{k}},\mathbb{P}}). $$

∎

The previous lemma allows us to bound eigenvalues of kernel matrices by $\ell_{\infty}$ -entropy numbers.

#### Proposition B.2 (Eigenvalue of kernel matrix is bounded by $\ell_{\infty}$ -entropy number).

Let ${\bm{k}}$ be a jointly continuous kernel. Define $K\triangleq{\bm{k}}(\mathcal{S}_{n},\mathcal{S}_{n})$ for the sequence of points $\mathcal{S}_{n}=(x_{1},\ldots,x_{n})\subset\mathbb{R}^{d}$ . For any $w\in\Delta_{n-1}$ , recall the notation $\mathbb{S}_{n}^{w}=\sum_{i\in[n]}w_{i}\delta_{x_{i}}$ , $K^{w}=\operatorname{diag}(\sqrt{w})K\operatorname{diag}(\sqrt{w})$ , and $R_{n}=1+\sup_{i\in[n]}\left\|{x_{i}}\right\|_{2}$ . Then for all $\ell\in\mathbb{N}$ ,

$$ \textstyle\lambda_{\ell}(K^{w})\stackrel{{\scriptstyle(i)}}{{=}}\lambda_{\ell}(T_{{\bm{k}},\mathbb{S}_{n}^{w}})\stackrel{{\scriptstyle(ii)}}{{\leq}}4e^{2}_{\ell}({{\mathcal{H}_{{\bm{k}}}}_{|_{\mathcal{B}_{2}(R_{n}-1)}}}\hookrightarrow{\ell_{\infty}(\mathcal{B}_{2}(R_{n}-1))}). $$

#### Proof of Prop. B.2.

Without loss of generality, we assume $w_{i}>0$ for all $i\in[n]$ , since otherwise, we can consider a smaller set of points by removing the ones with zero weights.

Proof of equality (i) from display 42 Note that $\mathcal{L}^{2}(\mathbb{S}_{n}^{w})$ is isometric to $\mathbb{R}^{n}$ . Let $K\triangleq{\bm{k}}(\mathcal{S}_{n},\mathcal{S}_{n})$ denote the kernel matrix. The action of $T_{{\bm{k}},\mathbb{S}_{n}^{w}}$ is given by, for $i\in[n]$ ,

$$ \textstyle T_{{\bm{k}},\mathbb{S}_{n}^{w}}f(x_{i})=\sum_{j\in[n]}w_{j}{\bm{k}}(x_{i},x_{j})f(x_{j}), $$

so in matrix form, $T_{{\bm{k}},\mathbb{S}_{n}^{w}}f=K\operatorname{diag}(w)f$ , and hence $T_{{\bm{k}},\mathbb{S}^{w}_{n}}=K\operatorname{diag}(w)$ . If $\lambda_{\ell}$ is an eigenvalue of $K\operatorname{diag}(w)$ with eigenvector $v_{\ell}$ , then

$$ \textstyle K\operatorname{diag}(w)v_{\ell}=\lambda_{\ell}v_{\ell} \textstyle\Longleftrightarrow\operatorname{diag}(\sqrt{w})K\operatorname{diag}(w)v_{\ell}=\lambda_{\ell}\operatorname{diag}(\sqrt{w})v_{\ell} \textstyle\Longleftrightarrow\operatorname{diag}(\sqrt{w})K\operatorname{diag}(\sqrt{w})(\operatorname{diag}(\sqrt{w})v_{\ell})=\lambda_{\ell}\operatorname{diag}(\sqrt{w})v_{\ell}, $$

where we used $w_{i}>0$ for all $i\in[n]$ . Hence the eigenspectrum of $T_{{\bm{k}},\mathbb{S}_{n}^{w}}$ agrees with that of $\operatorname{diag}(\sqrt{w})K\operatorname{diag}(\sqrt{w})$ .

Proof of bound (ii) from display 42 By Lem. B.4, we have $\lambda_{\ell}(T_{{\bm{k}},\mathbb{S}_{n}^{w}})\leq 4e^{2}_{\ell}({{\mathcal{H}_{{\bm{k}}|_{\mathcal{B}_{2}(R_{n}-1)}}}}\hookrightarrow{\mathcal{L}^{2}(\mathbb{S}_{n}^{w})})$ . Finally, using Def. B.1, we have $e_{\ell}({{\mathcal{H}_{{\bm{k}}|_{\mathcal{B}_{2}(R_{n}-1)}}}}\hookrightarrow{\mathcal{L}^{2}(\mathbb{S}_{n}^{w})})\leq e_{\ell}({{\mathcal{H}_{{\bm{k}}|_{\mathcal{B}_{2}(R_{n}-1)}}}}\hookrightarrow{\ell_{\infty}(\mathcal{B}_{2}(R_{n}-1))})$ because $\mathbb{S}_{n}^{w}$ is supported in $\mathcal{B}_{2}(R_{n}-1)$ and the fact that $\|{\cdot}\|_{\mathcal{L}^{2}(\mathbb{P})}\leq\|{\cdot}\|_{\infty}$ for any $\mathbb{P}$ . ∎

Combining the tools developed so far, we have the following corollary for bounding the eigenvalues of PolyGrowth and LogGrowth kernel matrices.

#### Corollary B.1 (Eigenvalue bound for PolyGrowth or LogGrowth kernel matrix).

Suppose a kernel ${\bm{k}}$ satisfies Assum. ( α , β )-kernel. Let $\mathcal{S}_{n}=(x_{1},\ldots,x_{n})\subset\mathbb{R}^{d}$ be a sequence of points. For any $w\in\Delta_{n-1}$ , using the notation $L_{\bm{k}}$ from (32), for any $\ell>L_{\bm{k}}(R_{n})+1$ , we have

$$ \textstyle\lambda_{\ell}(K^{w})\leq\begin{cases}4\left(\frac{L_{\bm{k}}(R_{n})}{\ell-1}\right)^{\frac{2}{{\alpha}}}&\hyperref@@ii[assum:kernel_growth]{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}{\textsc{PolyGrowth}}}(\alpha,\beta)\quad\text{and}\\
4\exp(2-2\left(\frac{\ell-1}{\krcd_\k(R_{n})}\right)^{\frac{1}{\cvrw}})&\hyperref@@ii[assum:kernel_growth]{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}{\textsc{LogGrowth}}}(\alpha,\beta).\end{cases} $$

#### Proof of Cor. B.1.

The claim follows by applying Prop. B.2 and Prop. B.1. ∎

### B.2 Covering numbers and eigenvalues of Stein kernels

The goal of this section is to show that a Stein kernel ${{\bm{k}}_{p}}$ satisfies Assum. ( α , β )-kernel provided that the base kernel is sufficiently smooth and to derive the parameters ${\alpha}$ , ${\beta}$ for PolyGrowth and LogGrowth cases. Such results when put together with results from Sec. B.1 imply spectral decay rates for Stein kernel matrices.

For a Stein kernel ${{\bm{k}}_{p}}$ with preconditioning matrix $M$ , we define

$$ \textstyle\mathfrak{S}_{p}(r)\triangleq\max\left(1,\sup_{\left\|{x}\right\|_{2}\leq r}\left\|{M^{1/2}\nabla\log p(x)}\right\|_{2}\right). $$

We start by noting a useful alternative expression for a Stein kernel where we only need access to the density via the score $\nabla\log p$ .

#### Proposition B.3 (Alternative expression for Stein kernel).

The Stein kernel ${{\bm{k}}_{p}}$ has the following alternative form:

$$ \textstyle\begin{split}\textstyle{{\bm{k}}_{p}}(x,y)=\langle\nabla\log p(x),M\nabla\log p(y)\rangle{\bm{k}}(x,y)+\langle\nabla\log p(x),M\nabla_{y}{\bm{k}}(x,y)\rangle+\\
\textstyle\langle\nabla\log p(y),M\nabla_{x}{\bm{k}}(x,y)\rangle+\tr(M \nabla_x \nabla_y\k(x,y)),\end{split} $$

where $\nabla_{x}\nabla_{y}{\bm{k}}(x,y)$ denotes the $d\times d$ matrix $(\partial_{x_{i}}\partial_{y_{j}}{\bm{k}}(x,y))_{i,j\in[d]}$ .

#### Proof of Prop. B.3.

We compute

$$ \textstyle(\nabla_{x}\cdot(p(x)M{\bm{k}}(x,y)p(y)))_{j} \textstyle=\sum_{i\in[d]}M_{ij}\left(\partial_{x_{i}}p(x){\bm{k}}(x,y)p(y)+p(x)\partial_{x_{i}}{\bm{k}}(x,y)p(y)\right). \textstyle\begin{split}\textstyle\nabla_{y}\cdot\nabla_{x}\cdot(p(x)M{\bm{k}}(x,y)p(y))&\textstyle=\sum_{i,j\in[d]}M_{ij}\left(\partial_{x_{i}}p(x)\partial_{y_{j}}p(y){\bm{k}}(x,y)+\partial_{x_{i}}p(x)\partial_{y_{j}}{\bm{k}}(x,y)p(y)\right)\\
\textstyle&\textstyle+\sum_{i,j\in[d]}M_{ij}\left(p(x)\partial_{y_{j}}p(y)\partial_{x_{i}}{\bm{k}}(x,y)+p(x)\partial_{x_{i}}\partial_{y_{j}}{\bm{k}}(x,y)p(y)\right).\end{split} $$

The four terms in the last equation correspond to the four terms in (B.3). ∎

In what follows, we will make use of a matrix-valued kernel ${\bm{K}}:\mathbb{R}^{d}\times\mathbb{R}^{d}\to\mathbb{R}^{d\times d}$ which generates an RKHS ${\mathcal{H}_{{\bm{K}}}}$ of vector-valued functions. See Carmeli et al. [2006] for an introduction to vector-valued RKHS theory.

Our next goal is to build a Hilbert-space isometry between the direct sum Hilbert space ${\mathcal{H}_{{\bm{k}}}}^{\oplus d}$ and ${\mathcal{H}_{{{\bm{k}}_{p}}}}$ to represent functions in ${\mathcal{H}_{{{\bm{k}}_{p}}}}$ using functions from ${\mathcal{H}_{{\bm{k}}}}$ .

#### Lemma B.5 (Preconditioned matrix-valued RKHS from a scalar kernel).

Let ${\bm{k}}:\mathbb{R}^{d}\times\mathbb{R}^{d}\to\mathbb{R}$ be kernel and ${\mathcal{H}_{{\bm{k}}}}$ be the corresponding RKHS. Let $M\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times d}$ be an SPSD matrix. Consider the map $\iota:{\mathcal{H}_{{\bm{k}}}}^{\oplus d}\to\mathfrak{F}(\mathbb{R}^{d},\mathbb{R}^{d})$ defined by $(f_{1},\ldots,f_{d})\mapsto[x\mapsto M^{1/2}(f_{1}(x),\ldots,f_{d}(x))]$ , where ${\mathcal{H}_{{\bm{k}}}}^{\oplus d}$ is the direct-sum Hilbert space of $d$ copies of ${\mathcal{H}_{{\bm{k}}}}$ Then $\iota$ is a Hilbert-space isometry onto a vector-valued RKHS ${\mathcal{H}_{{\bm{K}}}}$ with matrix-valued reproducing kernel given by ${\bm{K}}(x,y)={\bm{k}}(x,y)M$ .

#### Proof of Lem. B.5.

Define $\gamma:\mathbb{R}^{d}\to\mathfrak{F}(\mathbb{R}^{d},{\mathcal{H}_{{\bm{k}}}}^{\oplus d})$ via

$$ \textstyle\gamma(x)(\alpha)\triangleq{\bm{k}}(x,\cdot)M^{1/2}\alpha. $$

We have

$$ \textstyle\left\|{\gamma(x)(\alpha)}\right\|_{{\mathcal{H}_{{\bm{k}}}}^{\oplus d}} \textstyle\leq\left\|{{\bm{k}}(x,\cdot)}\right\|_{{\bm{k}}}\left\|{M^{1/2}}\right\|_{2}\left\|{\alpha}\right\|_{2}, $$

so $\gamma(x)$ is bounded. Since $\gamma(x)$ is also linear, we have $\gamma(x)\in\mathfrak{B}(\mathbb{R}^{d},{\mathcal{H}_{{\bm{k}}}}^{\oplus d})$ . Let $\gamma(x)^{*}:{\mathcal{H}_{{\bm{k}}}}^{\oplus d}\to\mathbb{R}^{d}$ denote the Hilbert-space adjoint of $\gamma(x)$ . Then for any $(f_{1},\ldots,f_{d})\in{\mathcal{H}_{{\bm{k}}}}^{\oplus d}$ , $\alpha\in\mathbb{R}^{d}$ , we have

$$ \textstyle\langle\gamma(x)^{*}(f_{1},\ldots,f_{d}),\alpha\rangle \textstyle=\langle(f_{1},\ldots,f_{d}),\gamma(x)(\alpha)\rangle_{{\mathcal{H}_{{\bm{k}}}}^{\oplus d}} \textstyle=\langle(f_{1},\ldots,f_{d}),{\bm{k}}(x,\cdot)M^{1/2}\alpha\rangle_{{\mathcal{H}_{{\bm{k}}}}^{\oplus d}} \textstyle=\langle(f_{1}(x),\ldots,f_{d}(x)),M^{1/2}\alpha\rangle \textstyle=\langle M^{1/2}(f_{1}(x),\ldots,f_{d}(x)),\alpha\rangle. $$

Hence $\gamma(x)^{*}(f_{1},\ldots,f_{d})=M^{1/2}(f_{1}(x),\ldots,f_{d}(x))$ , so $\iota(f_{1},\ldots,f_{d})(x)=\gamma(x)^{*}(f_{1},\ldots,f_{d})$ . By Carmeli et al. [2006, Proposition 2.4], we see that $\iota$ is a partial isometry from ${\mathcal{H}_{{\bm{k}}}}^{\oplus d}$ onto a vector-valued RKHS space withv reproducing kernel ${\bm{K}}(x,y)=\gamma(x)^{*}\gamma(y):\mathbb{R}^{d}\to\mathbb{R}^{d}$ . For $\alpha\in\mathbb{R}^{d}$ , previous calculation implies

$$ \textstyle\gamma(x)^{*}\gamma(y)(\alpha) \textstyle=\gamma(x)^{*}({\bm{k}}(y,\cdot)M^{1/2}\alpha)=M^{1/2}{\bm{k}}(y,x)M^{1/2}\alpha={\bm{k}}(x,y)M. $$

∎

#### Lemma B.6 (Stein operator is an isometry).

Consider a Stein kernel ${{\bm{k}}_{p}}$ with base kernel ${\bm{k}}$ and preconditioning matrix $M$ . Then, the Stein operator $\mathcal{S}_{p}$ defined by $\mathcal{S}_{p}(v)\triangleq\frac{1}{p}\nabla\cdot(pv)$ is an isometry from ${\mathcal{H}_{{\bm{K}}}}$ with ${\bm{K}}\triangleq{\bm{k}}M$ to ${\mathcal{H}_{{{\bm{k}}_{p}}}}$ .

#### Proof.

This follows from Barp et al. [2022, Theorem 2.6] applied to ${\bm{K}}$ . ∎

The previous two lemmas show that $\mathcal{S}_{p}\circ\iota$ is a Hilbert space isometry from ${\mathcal{H}_{{\bm{k}}}}^{\oplus d}$ to ${\mathcal{H}_{{{\bm{k}}_{p}}}}$ . Note that $\mathcal{S}_{p}(v)=\langle\nabla\log p,h\rangle+\nabla\cdot h$ . Hence, we immediately have

$$ \textstyle{\mathcal{H}_{{{\bm{k}}_{p}}}}=\left\{\langle\nabla\log p,M^{1/2}f\rangle+\nabla\cdot(M^{1/2}f):f=(f_{1},\ldots,f_{d})\in{\mathcal{H}_{{\bm{k}}}}^{\oplus d}\right\}. $$

We next build a divergence RKHS which is one of the summands used to form ${\mathcal{H}_{{{\bm{k}}_{p}}}}$ .

#### Lemma B.7 (Divergence RKHS).

Let ${\bm{k}}:\mathbb{R}^{d}\times\mathbb{R}^{d}\to\mathbb{R}$ be a continuously differentiable kernel. Let $M$ be an SPSD matrix. Define $\nabla^{\otimes 2}\cdot(M{\bm{k}}):\mathbb{R}^{d}\times\mathbb{R}^{d}\to\mathbb{R}$ via

$$ \textstyle\nabla^{\otimes 2}\cdot(M{\bm{k}})(x,y)\triangleq\nabla_{y}\cdot\nabla_{x}\cdot(M{\bm{k}}(x,y))=\tr(M \nabla_x\nabla_y \k(x,y)). $$

Then $\nabla^{\otimes 2}\cdot(M{\bm{k}})$ is a kernel, and its RKHS ${\mathcal{H}_{\nabla^{\otimes 2}\cdot(M{\bm{k}})}}$ has the following explicit form

$$ \textstyle{\mathcal{H}_{\nabla^{\otimes 2}\cdot(M{\bm{k}})}}=\nabla\cdot{\mathcal{H}_{{\bm{K}}}}=\left\{\nabla\cdot(M^{1/2}f):f=(f_{1},\ldots,f_{d})\in{\mathcal{H}_{{\bm{k}}}}^{\oplus d}\right\}, $$

where ${\bm{K}}=M{\bm{k}}$ . Moreover, $\nabla\cdot:{\mathcal{H}_{{\bm{K}}}}\to{\mathcal{H}_{\nabla^{\otimes 2}\cdot(M{\bm{k}})}}$ is an isometry.

#### Proof of Lem. B.7.

First of all, by Steinwart and Christmann [2008, Corollary 4.36], every $f\in{\mathcal{H}_{{\bm{k}}}}$ is continuously differentiable, so $\partial_{x_{i}}f$ exists. By Lem. B.5, $\nabla\cdot{\mathcal{H}_{{\bm{K}}}}$ is well-defined and the right equality in (58) holds.

Define $\gamma:\mathbb{R}^{d}\to\mathfrak{F}(\mathbb{R},{\mathcal{H}_{{\bm{K}}}})$ via

$$ \textstyle\gamma(x)(t) \textstyle\triangleq t\sum_{i=1}^{d}\partial_{x_{i}}{\bm{K}}(x,\cdot)e_{i}, $$

where $e_{i}\in\mathbb{R}^{d}$ is the $i$ th standard basis vector in $\mathbb{R}^{d}$ ; by Barp et al. [2022, Lemma C.8] we have $\partial_{x_{i}}{\bm{K}}(x,\cdot)e_{i}\in{\mathcal{H}_{{\bm{K}}}}$ . Note that

$$ \textstyle\left\|{\gamma(x)(t)}\right\|_{{\bm{K}}} \textstyle=\absolutevalue{t}\left\|{\sum_{i=1}^{d}\partial_{x_{i}}{\bm{K}}(x,\cdot)e_{i}}\right\|_{{\bm{K}}}, $$

so $\gamma(x)\in\mathfrak{B}(\mathbb{R},{\mathcal{H}_{{\bm{K}}}})$ . The adjoint $\gamma(x)^{*}\in\mathfrak{B}({\mathcal{H}_{{\bm{K}}}},\mathbb{R})$ must satisfy, for any $h\in{\mathcal{H}_{{\bm{K}}}}$ ,

$$ \textstyle t\gamma(x)^{*}h \textstyle=\langle h,\gamma(x)(t)\rangle_{{\bm{K}}}=\left\langle h,t\sum_{i=1}^{d}\partial_{x_{i}}{\bm{K}}(x,\cdot)e_{i}\right\rangle_{{\bm{K}}}=t\nabla\cdot h, $$

where we used the fact [Barp et al., 2022, Lemma C.8] that, for $c\in\mathbb{R}^{d}$ , $h\in{\mathcal{H}_{{\bm{K}}}}$ , $\langle\partial_{x_{i}}{\bm{K}}(x,\cdot)c,h\rangle=c^{\top}\partial_{x_{i}}h(x)$ . So we find $\gamma(x)^{*}(h)=\nabla\cdot h(x)$ . By Carmeli et al. [2006, Proposition 2.4], the map $A:{\mathcal{H}_{{\bm{K}}}}\to\mathfrak{F}(\mathbb{R}^{d},\mathbb{R})$ defined by $A(h)(x)=\gamma^{*}(x)(h)=\nabla\cdot h(x)$ , i.e., $A=\nabla\cdot$ , is a partial isometry from ${\mathcal{H}_{{\bm{K}}}}$ to an RKHS ${\mathcal{H}_{\nabla\cdot{\bm{K}}}}$ with reproducing kernel

$$ \textstyle\gamma(x)^{*}\gamma(y)=\nabla\cdot\left(\sum_{i=1}^{d}\partial_{x_{i}}{\bm{K}}(x,\cdot)e_{i}\right)(y)=\nabla_{y}\cdot\nabla_{x}\cdot{\bm{K}}(x,y)=\nabla^{\otimes 2}\cdot(M{\bm{k}})(x,y). $$

∎

The following lemma shows that we can project a covering of $\mathcal{B}_{{\bm{k}}}$ consisting of arbitrary functions to a covering using functions only in $\mathcal{B}_{{\bm{k}}}$ while inflating the covering radius by at most 2.

#### Lemma B.8 (Projection of coverings into RKHS balls).

Let ${\bm{k}}$ be a kernel, $A\subset\mathbb{R}^{d}$ be a set, and $\epsilon>0$ . Let $\mathcal{C}$ be a set of functions such that for any $f\in\mathcal{B}_{{\bm{k}}}$ , there exists $g\in\mathcal{C}$ such that $\left\|{f-g}\right\|_{\infty,A}\leq\epsilon$ . Then

$$ \textstyle\mathcal{N}_{{\bm{k}}}(A,2\epsilon)\leq\absolutevalue{\cC}. $$

#### Proof.

We will build a $({\bm{k}},A,2\epsilon)$ covering $\mathcal{C}^{\prime}$ as follows. For any $h\in\mathcal{C}$ , if there exists $h^{\prime}\in\mathcal{B}_{{\bm{k}}}$ with $\left\|{h^{\prime}-h}\right\|_{\infty,A}\leq\epsilon$ , then we include $h^{\prime}$ in $\mathcal{C}^{\prime}$ . By construction, $\absolutevalue{\cC'}\leq\absolutevalue{\cC}$ . Then, for any $f\in\mathcal{B}_{{\bm{k}}}$ , by assumption, there exists $g\in\mathcal{C}$ such that $\left\|{f-g}\right\|_{\infty,A}\leq\epsilon$ . By construction, there exists $g^{\prime}\in\mathcal{C}^{\prime}$ such that $\left\|{g^{\prime}-g}\right\|_{\infty,A}\leq\epsilon$ . Thus

$$ \textstyle\left\|{f-g^{\prime}}\right\|_{\infty,A}\leq\left\|{f-g}\right\|_{\infty,A}+\left\|{g-g^{\prime}}\right\|_{\infty,A}\leq 2\epsilon. $$

Hence $C^{\prime}$ is a $({\bm{k}},A,2\epsilon)$ covering. ∎

We are now ready to bound the covering numbers of ${{\bm{k}}_{p}}$ by those of ${\bm{k}}$ and $\nabla^{\otimes 2}\cdot(M{\bm{k}})$ . Our key insight towards this end is that any element in ${\mathcal{H}_{{{\bm{k}}_{p}}}}$ can be decomposed as a sum of functions originated from ${\mathcal{H}_{{\bm{k}}}}$ and a function from the divergence RKHS ${\mathcal{H}_{\nabla^{\otimes 2}\cdot(M{\bm{k}})}}$ .

#### Lemma B.9 (Upper bounding covering number of Stein kernel with that of its base kernel).

Let ${{\bm{k}}_{p}}$ be a Stein kernel with density $p$ and preconditioning matrix $M$ . For any $A\subset\mathbb{R}^{d}$ , $\epsilon_{1},\epsilon_{2}>0$ ,

$$ \textstyle\mathcal{N}_{{{\bm{k}}_{p}}}(A,\epsilon)\leq\mathcal{N}_{{\bm{k}}}(A,\epsilon_{1})^{d}\mathcal{N}_{\nabla^{\otimes 2}\cdot(M{\bm{k}})}(A,\epsilon_{2}), $$

for $\epsilon=2(\sqrt{d}\epsilon_{1}\sup_{x\in A}\left\|{M^{1/2}\nabla\log p(x)}\right\|+\epsilon_{2})$ .

#### Proof of Lem. B.9.

Let $\mathcal{C}_{\bm{k}}$ be a $({\bm{k}},A,\epsilon_{1})$ covering and $\mathcal{C}_{\nabla^{\otimes 2}\cdot(M{\bm{k}})}$ be a $(\nabla^{\otimes 2}\cdot(M{\bm{k}}),A,\epsilon_{2})$ covering. Define $b\triangleq M^{1/2}\nabla\log p$ . Form

$$ \textstyle\mathcal{C}\triangleq\left\{\langle b,\tilde{f}\rangle+\tilde{g}:\tilde{f}=(\tilde{f}_{1},\ldots,\tilde{f}_{d})\in(\mathcal{C}_{\bm{k}})^{d},\tilde{g}\in\mathcal{C}_{\nabla^{\otimes 2}\cdot(M{\bm{k}})}\right\}\subset\mathfrak{F}(\mathbb{R}^{d},\mathbb{R}). $$

Then $\absolutevalue{\cC}\leq\absolutevalue{\cC_{\k}}^{d}\absolutevalue{\cC_{\divmk}}$ . Let ${\bm{K}}\triangleq{\bm{k}}M$ . For any $h\in\mathcal{B}_{{{\bm{k}}_{p}}}$ , by (56), we can find $f=(f_{1},\ldots,f_{d})\in{\mathcal{H}_{{\bm{k}}}}^{\oplus d}$ with $f_{i}\in{\mathcal{H}_{{\bm{k}}}}$ such that

$$ \textstyle h=\mathcal{S}_{p}\circ\iota(f)=\langle\nabla\log p,M^{1/2}f\rangle+\nabla\cdot(M^{1/2}f)=\langle b,f\rangle+\nabla\cdot(M^{1/2}f). $$

Since $\iota$ and $\mathcal{S}_{p}$ are isometries, we have $f\in\mathcal{B}_{{\mathcal{H}_{{\bm{k}}}}^{\oplus d}}$ . Since, for each $i$ ,

$$ \textstyle\left\|{f_{i}}\right\|_{{\bm{k}}}\leq\sqrt{\sum_{j=1}^{d}\left\|{f_{j}}\right\|_{{\bm{k}}}^{2}}=\left\|{f}\right\|_{{\mathcal{H}_{{\bm{k}}}}^{\oplus d}}\leq 1, $$

we have $f_{i}\in\mathcal{B}_{{\bm{k}}}$ . By Lem. B.7, $\nabla\cdot:{\mathcal{H}_{{\bm{K}}}}\to{\mathcal{H}_{\nabla^{\otimes 2}\cdot(M{\bm{k}})}}$ is also an isometry, so $\nabla\cdot(M^{1/2}f)\in\mathcal{B}_{\nabla^{\otimes 2}\cdot(M{\bm{k}})}$ . Thus there exist $\tilde{f}_{i}\in\mathcal{C}_{\bm{k}}$ for each $i$ and $\tilde{g}\in\mathcal{C}_{\nabla^{\otimes 2}\cdot(M{\bm{k}})}$ such that

$$ \textstyle\left\|{f_{i}-\tilde{f}_{i}}\right\|_{\infty,A}\leq\epsilon_{1},\quad\left\|{\nabla\cdot(M^{1/2}f)-\tilde{g}}\right\|_{\infty,A}\leq\epsilon_{2}. $$

Let

$$ \textstyle\tilde{h}(x)\triangleq\langle b,\tilde{f}\rangle+\tilde{g}\in\mathcal{C}. $$

Then for $x\in A$ ,

$$ \textstyle\absolutevalue{h(x) - \tilde h(x)} \textstyle=\absolutevalue{\langle b(x), f(x)-\tilde f(x)\rangle+ \div(M^{1/2}f(x)) - \tilde g(x)} \textstyle\leq\left\|{b(x)}\right\|\sqrt{\sum_{i=1}^{d}(f_{i}(x)-\tilde{f}_{i}(x))^{2}}+\absolutevalue{\div(M^{1/2}f(x)) - \tilde g(x)} \textstyle\leq\sqrt{d}\epsilon_{1}\left\|{b(x)}\right\|+\epsilon_{2}. $$

Hence

$$ \textstyle\left\|{h-\tilde{h}}\right\|_{\infty,A} \textstyle\leq\sqrt{d}\epsilon_{1}\sup_{x\in A}\left\|{b(x)}\right\|+\epsilon_{2}\triangleq\epsilon_{3}. $$

Note that $\mathcal{C}$ that we constructed is not necessarily contained in $\mathcal{B}_{{{\bm{k}}_{p}}}$ . By Lem. B.8, we can get a $({{\bm{k}}_{p}},A,2\epsilon_{3})$ covering and we are done. ∎

#### Corollary B.2 (Log-covering number bound for Stein kernel).

Let ${{\bm{k}}_{p}}$ be a Stein kernel and $A\subset\mathbb{R}^{d}$ . For any $r>0$ , $\epsilon>0$ ,

$$ \textstyle\log\mathcal{N}_{{{\bm{k}}_{p}}}(A,\epsilon)\leq d\log\mathcal{N}_{{\bm{k}}}\left(A,\frac{\epsilon}{4\sqrt{d}\mathfrak{S}_{p}(r)}\right)+\log\mathcal{N}_{\nabla^{\otimes 2}\cdot(M{\bm{k}})}\left(A,\frac{\epsilon}{4}\right), $$

where $\mathfrak{S}_{p}$ is defined in (47).

#### Proof.

This is direct from Lem. B.9 with $\epsilon_{1}=\frac{\epsilon}{4\sqrt{d}\mathfrak{S}_{p}(r)}$ , $\epsilon_{2}=\frac{\epsilon}{4}$ . ∎

#### B.2.1 Case of differentiable base kernel

#### Definition B.2 ( $s$ -times continuously differentiable kernel).

A kernel ${\bm{k}}$ is $s$ -times continuously differentiable for $s\in\mathbb{N}$ if all partial derivatives $\partial^{\alpha,\alpha}{\bm{k}}$ exist and are continuous for all multi-indices $\alpha\in\mathbb{N}_{0}^{d}$ with $\absolutevalue{\alpha}\leq s$ .

#### Proposition B.4 (Covering number bound for ${{\bm{k}}_{p}}$ with differentiable base kernel).

Suppose ${{\bm{k}}_{p}}$ is a Stein kernel with an $s$ -times continuously differentiable base kernel ${\bm{k}}$ for $s\geq 2$ . Then there exist a constant $\mathfrak{C}_{d}>0$ depending only on $(s,d,{\bm{k}},M)$ such that for any $r>0,\epsilon\in(0,1)$ ,
