$$ \textstyle\log\mathcal{N}_{{{\bm{k}}_{p}}}(\mathcal{B}_{2}(r),\epsilon)\leq\mathfrak{C}_{d}r^{d}\mathfrak{S}_{p}^{d/s}(r)(1/\epsilon)^{d/(s-1)}. $$

#### Proof of Prop. B.4.

Since ${\bm{k}}$ is $s$ -times continuously differentiable, the divergence kernel $\nabla^{\otimes 2}\cdot(M{\bm{k}})$ is $(s-1)$ -times continuously differentiable. By Dwivedi and Mackey [2022, Proposition 2(b)], there exists constants $c_{1},c_{2}$ depending only on $(s,d,{\bm{k}},M)$ such that, for any $r>0$ , $\epsilon_{1},\epsilon_{2}>0$ ,

$$ \textstyle\log\mathcal{N}_{{\bm{k}}}\left(\mathcal{B}_{2}(r),\epsilon_{1}\right) \textstyle\leq c_{1}r^{d}(1/\epsilon)^{d/s}, \textstyle\log\mathcal{N}_{\nabla^{\otimes 2}\cdot(M{\bm{k}})}\left(\mathcal{B}_{2}(r),\epsilon_{2}\right) \textstyle\leq c_{2}r^{d}(1/\epsilon)^{d/(s-1)}. $$

By Cor. B.2 with $A=\mathcal{B}_{2}(r)$ , we have, for any $r>0$ and $\epsilon\in(0,1)$ ,

$$ \textstyle\log\mathcal{N}_{{{\bm{k}}_{p}}}(\mathcal{B}_{2}(r),\epsilon) \textstyle\leq c_{1}dr^{d}(4\sqrt{d}\mathfrak{S}_{p}(r))^{d/s}(1/\epsilon)^{d/\epsilon}+c_{2}r^{d}(4/\epsilon)^{d/(s-1)} \textstyle\leq\mathfrak{C}_{d}r^{d}\mathfrak{S}_{p}^{d/s}(r)(1/\epsilon)^{d/(s-1)} $$

for some $\mathfrak{C}_{d}>0$ depending only on $(s,d,{\bm{k}},M)$ . ∎

#### B.2.2 Case of radially analytic base kernel

For a symmetric positive definite $M\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times d}$ , we define, for $x\in\mathbb{R}^{d}$ ,

$$ \textstyle\left\|{x}\right\|_{M}\triangleq\sqrt{x^{\top}M^{-1}x}. $$

#### Definition B.3 (Radially analytic kernel).

A kernel ${\bm{k}}$ is radially analytic if ${\bm{k}}$ satisfies ${\bm{k}}(x,y)=\kappa(\left\|{x-y}\right\|_{M}^{2})$ for a symmetric positive definite matrix $M\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times d}$ and a function $\kappa:\mathbb{R}_{\geq 0}\to\mathbb{R}$ real-analytic everywhere with convergence radius $R_{\kappa}>0$ such that there exists a constant $C_{\kappa}>0$ for which

$$ \textstyle\absolutevalue{\frac{1}{j!}\kappa_+^{(j)}(0)}\leq C_{\kappa}(2/R_{\kappa})^{j},\text{ for all }j\in\mathbb{N}_{0}, $$

where $\kappa_{+}^{(j)}$ indicates the $j$ -th right-sided derivative of $\kappa$ .

#### Example B.1 (Gaussian kernel).

Consider the Gaussian kernel ${\bm{k}}(x,y)=\kappa(\left\|{x-y}\right\|_{M}^{2})$ with $\kappa(t)=e^{-\frac{t}{2\sigma^{2}}}$ where $\sigma>0$ . Note the exponential function is real-analytic everywhere, and so is $\kappa$ . Since $\kappa(t)=\sum_{j=0}^{\infty}\frac{(-t/2\sigma^{2})^{j}}{j}$ , we find $\frac{1}{j!}\kappa^{(j)}(0)=\frac{(-1)^{j}}{j(2\sigma^{2})^{j}}$ . Hence (82) holds with $C_{\kappa}=1$ and $R_{\kappa}=2\inf_{j\geq 0}(j(2\sigma^{2})^{j})^{1/j}=4\sigma^{2}$ .

#### Example B.2 (IMQ kernel).

Consider the inverse multiquadric kernel ${\bm{k}}(x,y)=\kappa(\left\|{x-y}\right\|_{M}^{2})$ with $\kappa(t)=(c^{2}+t)^{-\beta}$ where $c,\beta>0$ . By Sun and Zhou [2008, Example 3], $\kappa$ is real-analytic everywhere with $C_{\kappa}=c^{-2\beta}(2\beta+1)^{\beta+1}$ and $R_{\kappa}=c^{2}$ .

A simple calculation yields the following lemma.

#### Proposition B.5 (Expression for ${{\bm{k}}_{p}}$ with a radially analytic base kernel).

Suppose a Stein kernel ${{\bm{k}}_{p}}$ has a symmetric positive definite preconditioning matrix and a base kernel ${\bm{k}}(x,y)=\kappa(\left\|{x-y}\right\|_{M}^{2})$ where $\kappa$ is twice-differentiable. Then

$$ \textstyle\begin{split}\textstyle{{\bm{k}}_{p}}(x,y)=\langle\nabla\log p(x),M\nabla\log p(y)\rangle\kappa(\left\|{x-y}\right\|_{M}^{2})-\\
\textstyle 2\kappa^{\prime}_{+}(\left\|{x-y}\right\|_{M}^{2})\langle x-y,\nabla\log p(x)-\nabla\log p(y)\rangle-\\
\textstyle 4\kappa^{\prime\prime}_{+}(\left\|{x-y}\right\|_{M}^{2})\left\|{x-y}\right\|_{M}^{2}-2d\kappa^{\prime}_{+}(\left\|{x-y}\right\|_{M}^{2}).\end{split} $$

In particular,

$$ \textstyle{{\bm{k}}_{p}}(x,x) \textstyle=\left\|{M^{1/2}\nabla\log p(x)}\right\|_{2}^{2}\kappa(0)-2d\kappa^{\prime}_{+}(0). $$

#### Proof of Prop. B.5.

From ${\bm{k}}(x,y)=\kappa(\left\|{x-y}\right\|_{M}^{2})=\kappa((x-y)^{\top}M^{-1}(x-y))$ , we compute, using (57),

$$ \textstyle\nabla_{y}{\bm{k}}(x,y) \textstyle=-2\kappa^{\prime}_{+}(\left\|{x-y}\right\|_{M}^{2})M^{-1}(x-y) \textstyle\nabla_{x}\nabla_{y}{\bm{k}}(x,y) \textstyle=-2\kappa^{\prime}_{+}(\left\|{x-y}\right\|_{M}^{2})M^{-1}-4\kappa^{\prime\prime}_{+}(\left\|{x-y}\right\|_{M}^{2})M^{-1}(x-y)((x-y)M^{-1})^{\top} \textstyle\nabla^{\otimes 2}\cdot(M{\bm{k}})(x,y) \textstyle=\tr(M \nabla_x \nabla_y \k(x,y))=-4\kappa^{\prime\prime}_{+}(\left\|{x-y}\right\|_{M}^{2})\left\|{x-y}\right\|_{M}^{2}-2d\kappa^{\prime}_{+}(\left\|{x-y}\right\|_{M}^{2}). $$

The form (B.5) then follows from applying Prop. B.3. ∎

We next show that the divergence kernel $\nabla^{\otimes 2}\cdot(M{\bm{k}})$ is radially analytic given that ${\bm{k}}$ is.

#### Lemma B.10 (Convergence radius of divergence kernel).

Let ${\bm{k}}$ be a radially analytic kernel with the corresponding real-analytic function $\kappa$ , convergence radius $R_{\kappa}$ with constant $C_{\kappa}$ , and a symmetric positive definite matrix $M$ . Then

$$ \textstyle\nabla^{\otimes 2}\cdot(M{\bm{k}})(x,y)=\kappa_{\nabla^{\otimes 2}\cdot(M{\bm{k}})}(\left\|{x-y}\right\|_{M}^{2}), $$

where $\kappa_{\nabla^{\otimes 2}\cdot(M{\bm{k}})}:\mathbb{R}_{\geq 0}\to\mathbb{R}$ is the real-analytic function defined as

$$ \textstyle\kappa_{\nabla^{\otimes 2}\cdot(M{\bm{k}})}(t)\triangleq-4\kappa^{\prime\prime}_{+}(t)t-2d\kappa^{\prime}_{+}(t). $$

Moreover, $\kappa_{\nabla^{\otimes 2}\cdot(M{\bm{k}})}$ has convergence radius with constant

$$ \textstyle R_{\kappa_{\nabla^{\otimes 2}\cdot(M{\bm{k}})}}=\frac{R_{\kappa}}{4d+8},\quad C_{\kappa_{\nabla^{\otimes 2}\cdot(M{\bm{k}})}}=4dC_{\kappa}/R_{\kappa}. $$

#### Proof of Lem. B.10.

The first statement regarding the form of $\kappa_{\nabla^{\otimes 2}\cdot(M{\bm{k}})}$ directly follows from (86). Next, iterative differentiation yields, for $j\in\mathbb{N}_{0}$ ,

$$ \textstyle\kappa_{\nabla^{\otimes 2}\cdot(M{\bm{k}})}^{(j)}(t)=-(2d+4j)\kappa^{(j+1)}_{+}(t)-4\kappa^{(j+2)}_{+}(t)t. $$

Thus

$$ \textstyle\absolutevalue{\frac{1}{j!}\kappa_{\divmk}^{(j)}(0)} \textstyle=\frac{2d+4j}{j!}\kappa^{(j+1)}_{+}(0) \textstyle=\frac{(2d+4j)(j+1)}{(j+1)!}\kappa^{(j+1)}_{+}(0) \textstyle\leq(2d+4j)(j+1)C_{\kappa}(2/R_{\kappa})^{j+1}. $$

For $j\geq 1$ ,

$$ \textstyle\absolutevalue{\frac{1}{j!}\kappa_{\divmk}^{(j)}(0)} \textstyle\leq(2C_{\kappa}/R_{\kappa})\left(((2d+4j)(j+1))^{1/j}2/R_{\kappa}\right)^{j} \textstyle\leq(2C_{\kappa}/R_{\kappa})\left((2(2d+4)\cdot 2/R_{\kappa}\right)^{j}. $$

where we used the fact that $((2d+4j)(j+1))^{1/j}$ is decreasing in $j$ . For $j=0$ , (93) is just $2dC_{\kappa}\cdot 2/R_{\kappa}$ . Hence $\kappa_{\nabla^{\otimes 2}\cdot(M{\bm{k}})}$ is analytic with $C_{\kappa_{\nabla^{\otimes 2}\cdot(M{\bm{k}})}}=4dC_{\kappa}/R_{\kappa}$ and $R_{\kappa_{\nabla^{\otimes 2}\cdot(M{\bm{k}})}}=\frac{R_{\kappa}}{4d+8}$ . ∎

We will use the following lemma repeatedly.

#### Lemma B.11 (Covering number of radially analytic kernel with $M$ -metric).

Let ${\bm{k}}_{0}$ be a radially analytic kernel with ${\bm{k}}_{0}(x,y)=\kappa(\left\|{x-y}\right\|_{2}^{2})$ . For any symmetric positive definite $M\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times d}$ , consider the radially analytic kernel ${\bm{k}}(x,y)\triangleq\kappa(\left\|{x-y}\right\|^{2}_{M})$ . Then for any $A\subset\mathbb{R}^{d}$ and $\epsilon>0$ , we have

$$ \textstyle\mathcal{N}_{{\bm{k}}}(M^{-1/2}(A),\epsilon)=\mathcal{N}_{{\bm{k}}_{0}}(A,\epsilon). $$

In particular, for any $r>0$ ,

$$ \textstyle\mathcal{N}_{{\bm{k}}}(\mathcal{B}_{2}(r),\epsilon)\leq\mathcal{N}_{{\bm{k}}_{0}}(\mathcal{B}_{2}(r\|{M^{1/2}}\|_{2}),\epsilon). $$

#### Proof.

Note that ${\bm{k}}(x,y)={\bm{k}}_{0}(M^{-1/2}x,M^{-1/2}y)$ . By Paulsen and Raghupathi [2016, Theorem 5.7], ${\mathcal{H}_{{\bm{k}}}}=\{f\circ M^{-1/2}:f\in{\mathcal{H}_{{\bm{k}}_{0}}}\}$ , and moreover $\mathcal{B}_{{\bm{k}}}=\{f\circ M^{-1}:f\in\mathcal{B}_{{\bm{k}}_{0}}\}$ . Let $\mathcal{C}_{0}$ be a $({\bm{k}}_{0},A,\epsilon)$ covering. Form $\mathcal{C}=\{h\circ M^{-1/2}:h\in\mathcal{C}_{0}\}\subset\mathcal{B}_{{\bm{k}}}$ . For any element $f\circ M^{-1/2}\in\mathcal{B}_{{\bm{k}}}$ where $f\in\mathcal{B}_{{\bm{k}}_{0}}$ , there exists $h\in\mathcal{C}_{0}$ such that $\left\|{f-h}\right\|_{\infty,A}\leq\epsilon$ . Thus

$$ \textstyle\left\|{f\circ M^{-1/2}-h\circ M^{-1/2}}\right\|_{\infty,M^{-1/2}(A)}=\left\|{f-h}\right\|_{\infty,A}\leq\epsilon. $$

Thus $\mathcal{N}_{{\bm{k}}}(M^{-1/2}(A),\epsilon)\leq\mathcal{N}_{{\bm{k}}_{0}}(A,\epsilon)$ . By considering $M^{-1}$ in place of $M$ , we get our desired equality.

For the second statement, by letting $A=M^{1/2}\mathcal{B}_{2}(r)$ , we have

$$ \textstyle\mathcal{N}_{{\bm{k}}}(\mathcal{B}_{2}(r),\epsilon)=\mathcal{N}_{{\bm{k}}_{0}}(M^{1/2}\mathcal{B}_{2}(r),\epsilon)\leq\mathcal{N}_{{\bm{k}}_{0}}(\mathcal{B}_{2}(r\|{M^{1/2}}\|_{2}),\epsilon), $$

where we use the fact that $M^{1/2}\mathcal{B}_{2}(r)\subset\mathcal{B}_{2}(r\|{M^{1/2}}\|_{2})$ . ∎

In the next lemma, we rephrase the result from Sun and Zhou [2008, Theorem 2] for bounding the covering number of a radially analytic kernel.

#### Lemma B.12 (Covering number bound for radially analytic kernel).

Let ${\bm{k}}$ be a radially analytic kernel with ${\bm{k}}(x,y)=\kappa(\left\|{x-y}\right\|_{2}^{2})$ . Then, there exist a polynomial $P(r)$ of degree $2d$ and a constant $C$ depending only on $(\kappa,d)$ such that for any $r>0$ , $\epsilon\in(0,1/2)$ ,

$$ \textstyle\log\mathcal{N}_{{\bm{k}}}(\mathcal{B}_{2}(r),\epsilon)\leq P(r)(\log(1/\eps)+C)^{d+1}. $$

#### Proof of Lem. B.12.

Let $R_{\kappa},C_{\kappa}$ denote the constants for $\kappa$ as in (82). By and Sun and Zhou [2008, Theorem 2] with $R=1$ , $D=2r$ , and Lem. B.2, for $\epsilon\in(0,1/2)$ , we have

$$ \textstyle\log\mathcal{N}_{{\bm{k}}}(\mathcal{B}_{2}(r),\epsilon)\leq N_{2}(\mathcal{B}_{2}(r),r^{\dagger}/2)\left(4\log(1/\eps)+2+4\log(16\sqrt{C_\kappa}+1)\right)^{d+1}, $$

where $r^{\dagger}=\min(\frac{\sqrt{R_{\kappa}}}{2d},\sqrt{R_{\kappa}+(2r)^{2}}-2r)$ , and $N_{2}(\mathcal{B}_{2}(r),r^{\dagger}/2)$ is the covering number of $\mathcal{B}_{2}(r)$ as a subset of $\mathbb{R}^{d}$ , which can be further bounded by [Wainwright, 2019, (5.8)]

$$ \textstyle N_{2}(\mathcal{B}_{2}(r),r^{\dagger}/2) \textstyle\leq\left(1+\frac{4r}{r^{\dagger}}\right)^{d}. $$

If $r^{\dagger}=\sqrt{R_{\kappa}+(2r)^{2}}-2r$ , then $\frac{r}{r^{\dagger}}=\frac{r}{\sqrt{R_{\kappa}+(2r)^{2}}-2r}=\frac{r(\sqrt{R_{\kappa}+(2r)^{2}}+2r)}{R_{\kappa}}\leq\frac{r(\sqrt{R_{\kappa}}+4r)}{R_{\kappa}}$ which is a quadratic polynomial in $r$ . Hence for a constant $C>0$ and a polynomial $P(r)$ of degree $2d$ that depend only on $(\kappa,d)$ , we have the claim. ∎

#### Proposition B.6 (Covering number bound for ${{\bm{k}}_{p}}$ with radially analytic base kernel).

Suppose ${{\bm{k}}_{p}}$ is a Stein kernel with a preconditioning matrix $M$ and a radially analytic base kernel ${\bm{k}}$ based on a real-analytic function $\kappa$ . Then there exist a constant $C>0$ and a polynomial $P(r)$ of degree $2d$ depending only on $(\kappa,d,M)$ such that for any $r>0,\epsilon\in(0,1)$ ,

$$ \textstyle\log\mathcal{N}_{{{\bm{k}}_{p}}}(\mathcal{B}_{2}(r),\epsilon)\leq\left(\log\frac{\mathfrak{S}_{p}(r)}{\epsilon}+C\right)^{d+1}P(r). $$

#### Proof of Prop. B.6.

Recall ${\bm{k}}(x,y)=\kappa(\left\|{x-y}\right\|^{2}_{M})$ . Consider ${\bm{k}}_{0}(x,y)\triangleq\kappa(\left\|{x-y}\right\|_{2}^{2})$ . For $\epsilon_{1}\in(0,1/2)$ , by Lem. B.11, we have

$$ \textstyle\log\mathcal{N}_{{\bm{k}}}(\mathcal{B}_{2}(r/\|{M^{1/2}}\|_{2}),\epsilon_{1})\leq\log\mathcal{N}_{{\bm{k}}_{0}}(\mathcal{B}_{2}(r),\epsilon_{1}/2). $$

Thus by Lem. B.12, there exists a polynomial $P_{{\bm{k}}}(r)$ of degree $2d$ and a constant $C_{{\bm{k}}}$ depending only on $(\kappa,d,M)$ such that

$$ \textstyle\log\mathcal{N}_{{\bm{k}}}(\mathcal{B}_{2}(r),\epsilon_{1})\leq P_{{\bm{k}}}(r)(\log(1/\eps_1)+C_{{\bm{k}}})^{d+1} $$

Similarly, for $\epsilon_{2}\in(0,1/2)$ , by Lem. B.10 and Lem. B.12, we have, for a constant $C_{\nabla^{\otimes 2}\cdot(M{\bm{k}})}>0$ and a polynomial $P_{\nabla^{\otimes 2}\cdot(M{\bm{k}})}(r)$ of degree $2d$ that depend only on $(\kappa,d,M)$ ,

$$ \textstyle\log\mathcal{N}_{\nabla^{\otimes 2}\cdot(M{\bm{k}})}(\mathcal{B}_{2}(r),\epsilon_{2})\leq P_{\nabla^{\otimes 2}\cdot(M{\bm{k}})}(r)(\log(1/\eps_2)+C_{\nabla^{\otimes 2}\cdot(M{\bm{k}})})^{d+1}. $$

For a given $\epsilon\in(0,1)$ , let $\epsilon_{1}=\frac{\epsilon}{4\sqrt{d}\mathfrak{S}_{p}(r)}$ and $\epsilon_{2}=\frac{\epsilon}{4}$ . Then since $\mathfrak{S}_{p}\geq 1$ , we have $\epsilon_{1},\epsilon_{2}\in(0,1/2)$ . By Cor. B.2 with $A=\mathcal{B}_{2}(r)$ , we obtain, for a constants $C>0$ and a polynomial $P(r)$ of degree $2d$ that depend only on $(\kappa,d,M)$ ,

$$ \textstyle\log\mathcal{N}_{{{\bm{k}}_{p}}}(\mathcal{B}_{2}(r),\epsilon)\leq P(r)(\log(1/\eps)+\log\mathfrak{S}_{p}(r)+C)^{d+1}. $$

Hence (103) is shown. ∎

When $\log\mathfrak{S}_{p}(r)$ grows polynomially in $r$ , we apply Prop. B.6 to immediately obtain the following.

#### Corollary B.3.

Under the assumption of Prop. B.6, suppose $\mathfrak{S}_{p}(r)=O(\textup{poly}(r))$ . Then for any $\delta>0$ , there exists $\mathfrak{C}_{d}>0$ such that

$$ \textstyle\log\mathcal{N}_{{{\bm{k}}_{p}}}(\mathcal{B}_{2}(r),\epsilon)\leq\mathfrak{C}_{d}\log(e/\eps)^{d+1}(r+1)^{2d+\delta}. $$

#### Proof of Cor. B.3.

This immediately follows from Prop. B.6 by using $\delta>0$ to absorb the $\log\mathfrak{S}_{p}(r)=O(r^{\delta})$ term. ∎

#### B.2.3 Proof of Prop. 1: Proposition 1 (Stein kernel growth rates).

This follows from Props. B.4 and B.3, and by noticing that if $\sup_{\left\|{x}\right\|_{2}\leq r}\left\|{\nabla\log p(x)}\right\|_{2}$ is bounded by a degree $d_{\ell}$ polynomial, then so is

$$ \textstyle\mathfrak{S}_{p}(r)=\sup_{\left\|{x}\right\|_{2}\leq r}\left\|{M^{1/2}\nabla\log p(x)}\right\|_{2}\leq\left\|{M^{1/2}}\right\|_{2}\sup_{\left\|{x}\right\|_{2}\leq r}\left\|{\nabla\log p(x)}\right\|_{2}. $$

∎

## Appendix C Analysis of Debiasing Benchmarks

We start with a result on the MMD quality of i.i.d. sample points in Sec. C.1, followed by the proofs of our i.i.d.-like and better-than-i.i.d. guarantees for debiasing from Thms. 1 and 2 in Secs. C.2 and C.3 respectively.

### C.1 MMD of unbiased i.i.d. sample points

We start by showing that sequence of $n$ points sampled i.i.d. from $\mathbb{P}$ achieves $\Theta(n^{-1})$ squared $\mmd_{{{\bm{k}}_{\mathbb{P}}}}$ to $\mathbb{P}$ in expectation.

#### Proposition C.1 (MMD of unbiased i.i.d. sample points).

Let ${{\bm{k}}_{\mathbb{P}}}$ be a kernel satisfying Assum. 1 with $\mathfrak{p}\geq 1$ . Let $\mathcal{S}_{n}=(x_{i})_{i\in[n]}$ be $n$ i.i.d. samples from $\mathbb{P}$ . Then

$$ \textstyle\mathbb{E}[\mmd_{{{\bm{k}}_{\mathbb{P}}}}(\mathbb{S}_{n},\mathbb{P})^{2}]=\frac{\mathbb{E}_{x\sim\mathbb{P}}[{{\bm{k}}_{\mathbb{P}}}(x,x)]}{n}. $$

#### Proof of Prop. C.1.

We compute

$$ \textstyle\mathbb{E}[\mmd_{{{\bm{k}}_{\mathbb{P}}}}(\mathbb{S}_{n},\mathbb{P})^{2}] \textstyle=\mathbb{E}[\sum_{i,j\in[n]}\frac{1}{n^{2}}{{\bm{k}}_{\mathbb{P}}}(x_{i},x_{j})]=\frac{1}{n^{2}}\sum_{i,j\in[n]}\mathbb{E}[{{\bm{k}}_{\mathbb{P}}}(x_{i},x_{j})]=\frac{1}{n}\mathbb{E}[{{\bm{k}}_{\mathbb{P}}}(x_{1},x_{1})], $$

where we used the fact that ${{\bm{k}}_{\mathbb{P}}}$ is mean-zero with respect to $\mathbb{P}$ and the independence of $x_{i},x_{j}$ for $i\neq j$ . ∎

### C.2 Proof of Thm. 1: Theorem 1 (Debiasing to i.i.d. quality via simplex reweighting).

We make use of the self-normalized importance sampling weights $w_{j}^{\textup{SNIS}}=\frac{\differential\mathbb{P}}{\differential\mathbb{Q}}(x_{j})/\sum_{i\in[n]}\frac{\differential\mathbb{P}}{\differential\mathbb{Q}}(x_{i})$ for $j\in[n]$ in our proofs. Notice that $(w_{1}^{\textup{SNIS}},\ldots,w_{n}^{\textup{SNIS}})^{\top}\in\Delta_{n-1}$ and hence

$$ \textstyle\mmd_{\textsc{OPT}}\leq\mmd_{{{\bm{k}}_{\mathbb{P}}}}(w_{i}^{\textup{SNIS}}\delta_{x_{i}},\mathbb{P})=\frac{\|{\sum_{i=1}^{n}\frac{\differential\mathbb{P}}{\differential\mathbb{Q}}(x_{i}){{\bm{k}}_{\mathbb{P}}}(x_{i},\cdot)}\|_{{{\bm{k}}_{\mathbb{P}}}}}{\sum_{i=1}^{n}\frac{\differential\mathbb{P}}{\differential\mathbb{Q}}(x_{i})}=\frac{\|{\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\frac{\differential\mathbb{P}}{\differential\mathbb{Q}}(x_{i}){{\bm{k}}_{\mathbb{P}}}(x_{i},\cdot)}\|_{{{\bm{k}}_{\mathbb{P}}}}}{\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\frac{\differential\mathbb{P}}{\differential\mathbb{Q}}(x_{i})}. $$

Introduce the bounded in probability notation $X_{n}=O_{p}(g_{n})$ to mean $\Pr(\abs{X_n/g_n}> C_\eps)\leq\epsilon$ for all $n\geq N_{\epsilon}$ for any $\epsilon>0$ . Then we claim that under the conditions assumed in Thm. 1,

$$ \textstyle\|{\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\frac{\differential\mathbb{P}}{\differential\mathbb{Q}}(x_{i}){{\bm{k}}_{\mathbb{P}}}(x_{i},\cdot)}\|_{{{\bm{k}}_{\mathbb{P}}}}=O_{p}(n^{-\frac{1}{2}})\quad\text{and}\quad\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\frac{\differential\mathbb{P}}{\differential\mathbb{Q}}(x_{i})\to 1\ \text{almost surely,}\  $$

so that by Slutsky’s theorem [Wellner, 2013, Ex. 1.4.7], we have $\mmd_{\textsc{OPT}}=O_{p}(n^{-\frac{1}{2}})$ as desired. We prove the claims in 113 in two main steps: (a) first, we construct a weighted RKHS and then (b) establish a central limit theorem (CLT) that allows us to conclude both claims from 113

#### Constructing a weighted and separable RKHS

Define the kernel ${{\bm{k}}_{\mathbb{Q}}}(x,y)\triangleq\frac{\differential\mathbb{P}}{\differential\mathbb{Q}}(x){{\bm{k}}_{\mathbb{P}}}(x,y)\frac{\differential\mathbb{P}}{\differential\mathbb{Q}}(y)$ with Hilbert space ${\mathcal{H}_{{{\bm{k}}_{\mathbb{Q}}}}}=\frac{\differential\mathbb{P}}{\differential\mathbb{Q}}{\mathcal{H}_{{{\bm{k}}_{\mathbb{P}}}}}$ and the elements $\xi_{i}\triangleq{{\bm{k}}_{\mathbb{Q}}}(x_{i},\cdot)=\frac{\differential\mathbb{P}}{\differential\mathbb{Q}}(x_{i}){{\bm{k}}_{\mathbb{P}}}(x_{i},\cdot)\frac{\differential\mathbb{P}}{\differential\mathbb{Q}}(\cdot)\in{\mathcal{H}_{{{\bm{k}}_{\mathbb{Q}}}}}$ for each $i\in\mathbb{N}$ . By Paulsen and Raghupathi [2016, Prop. 5.20], any element in ${\mathcal{H}_{{{\bm{k}}_{\mathbb{Q}}}}}$ is represented by $\frac{\differential\mathbb{P}}{\differential\mathbb{Q}}f$ for some $f\in{\mathcal{H}_{{{\bm{k}}_{\mathbb{P}}}}}$ and moreover, $f\mapsto\frac{\differential\mathbb{P}}{\differential\mathbb{Q}}f$ preserves inner product between the two RKHSs, i.e., $\left\langle f,g\right\rangle_{{{\bm{k}}_{\mathbb{P}}}}=\langle{\frac{\differential\mathbb{P}}{\differential\mathbb{Q}}f,\frac{\differential\mathbb{P}}{\differential\mathbb{Q}}g}\rangle_{{{\bm{k}}_{\mathbb{Q}}}}$ for $f,g\in{\mathcal{H}_{{{\bm{k}}_{\mathbb{P}}}}}$ , which in turn implies $\|{f}\|_{{{\bm{k}}_{\mathbb{P}}}}=\|{\frac{\differential\mathbb{P}}{\differential\mathbb{Q}}f}\|_{{{\bm{k}}_{\mathbb{Q}}}}$ . As a result, we also have that

$$ \textstyle\|{\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\frac{\differential\mathbb{P}}{\differential\mathbb{Q}}(x_{i}){{\bm{k}}_{\mathbb{P}}}(x_{i},\cdot)}\|_{{{\bm{k}}_{\mathbb{P}}}}=\|{\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\frac{\differential\mathbb{P}}{\differential\mathbb{Q}}(x_{i}){{\bm{k}}_{\mathbb{P}}}(x_{i},\cdot)\frac{\differential\mathbb{P}}{\differential\mathbb{Q}}(\cdot)}\|_{{{\bm{k}}_{\mathbb{Q}}}}=\|{\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\xi_{i}}\|_{{{\bm{k}}_{\mathbb{Q}}}}. $$

Since ${\mathcal{H}_{{{\bm{k}}_{\mathbb{P}}}}}$ is separable, there exists a dense countable subset $(f_{n})_{n\in\mathbb{N}}\subset{\mathcal{H}_{{{\bm{k}}_{\mathbb{P}}}}}$ . For any $\frac{\differential\mathbb{P}}{\differential\mathbb{Q}}f\in{\mathcal{H}_{{{\bm{k}}_{\mathbb{Q}}}}}$ , there exists $\{n_{k}\}_{k\in\mathbb{N}}$ such that $\lim_{k\to\infty}\|{f_{n_{k}}-f}\|_{{{\bm{k}}_{\mathbb{P}}}}=0$ . Since $\|{\frac{\differential\mathbb{P}}{\differential\mathbb{Q}}f_{n_{k}}-\frac{\differential\mathbb{P}}{\differential\mathbb{Q}}f}\|_{{{\bm{k}}_{\mathbb{Q}}}}=\|{\frac{\differential\mathbb{P}}{\differential\mathbb{Q}}(f_{n_{k}}-f)}\|_{{{\bm{k}}_{\mathbb{Q}}}}=\left\|{f_{n_{k}}-f}\right\|_{{{\bm{k}}_{\mathbb{P}}}}$ due to inner-product preservation, we thus have $\lim_{k\to\infty}\|{\frac{\differential\mathbb{P}}{\differential\mathbb{Q}}f_{n_{k}}-\frac{\differential\mathbb{P}}{\differential\mathbb{Q}}f}\|_{{{\bm{k}}_{\mathbb{Q}}}}=\lim_{k\to\infty}\|{f_{n_{k}}-f}\|_{{{\bm{k}}_{\mathbb{P}}}}0$ , so $(\frac{\differential\mathbb{P}}{\differential\mathbb{Q}}f_{n})_{n\in\mathbb{N}}$ is dense in ${\mathcal{H}_{{{\bm{k}}_{\mathbb{Q}}}}}$ , showing that ${\mathcal{H}_{{{\bm{k}}_{\mathbb{Q}}}}}$ is separable.

#### Harris recurrence of the chain $(x_{i})_{i\in\mathbb{N}}$

Let $\mu_{1}$ denote the distribution of $x_{1}$ . Since $\mathcal{S}_{\infty}=(x_{i})_{i=1}^{\infty}$ is a homogeneous $\phi$ -irreducible geometrically ergodic Markov chain with stationary distribution $\mathbb{Q}$ , it is also positive [Meyn and Tweedie, 2012, Ch. 10] by definition and aperiodic by Douc et al. [2018, Lem. 9.3.9]. Moreover, since $\mathcal{S}_{\infty}$ is $\phi$ -irreducible, aperiodic, and geometrically ergodic in the sense of Gallegos-Herrada et al. [2023, Thm. 1] and $\mu_{1}$ is absolutely continuous with respect to $\mathbb{P}$ , we will assume, without loss of generality, that $\mathcal{S}_{\infty}$ is Harris recurrent [Meyn and Tweedie, 2012, Ch. 9], since, by Qin [2023, Lem. 9], $\mathcal{S}_{\infty}$ is equal to a geometrically ergodic Harris chain with probability $1$ .

#### CLT for $\frac{1}{\sqrt{n}}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\xi_{i}$

We now show that $\frac{1}{\sqrt{n}}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\xi_{i}$ converges to a Gaussian random element taking values in ${\mathcal{H}_{{{\bm{k}}_{\mathbb{Q}}}}}$ . We separate the proof in two parts: first when the initial distribution $\mu_{1}=\mathbb{Q}$ and next when $\mu_{1}\neq\mathbb{Q}$ .

Case 1: $\mu_{1}=\mathbb{Q}$ When $\mu_{1}=\mathbb{Q}$ , $\mathcal{S}_{\infty}$ is a strictly stationary chain. By Bradley [2005, Thm. 3.7 and (1.11)], since $\mathcal{S}_{\infty}$ is geometrically ergodic, its strong mixing coefficients $(\tilde{\alpha}_{i})_{i\in\mathbb{N}}$ satisfy $\tilde{\alpha}_{i}\leq C\rho^{i}$ for some $C>0$ and $\rho\in[0,1)$ and all $i\in\mathbb{N}$ . Since each $\xi_{i}$ is a measurable function of $x_{i}$ , the strong mixing coefficients $(\alpha_{i})_{i\in\mathbb{N}}$ of $(\xi_{i})_{i\in\mathbb{N}}$ satisfy $\alpha_{i}\leq\tilde{\alpha}_{i}\leq C\rho^{i}$ for each $i\in\mathbb{N}$ . Consequently, $\sum_{i\in\mathbb{N}}i^{2/\delta}\alpha_{i}<\infty$ for $\delta=2\mathfrak{q}-2>0$ . Note that we also have

$$ \textstyle\mathbb{E}_{z\sim\mathbb{Q}}[\|{{{\bm{k}}_{\mathbb{Q}}}(z,\cdot)}\|_{{{\bm{k}}_{\mathbb{Q}}}}^{2+\delta}]=\mathbb{E}_{z\sim\mathbb{Q}}[{{\bm{k}}_{\mathbb{Q}}}(z,z)^{\mathfrak{q}}]=\mathbb{E}_{z\sim\mathbb{Q}}[\frac{\differential\mathbb{P}}{\differential\mathbb{Q}}(z)^{2\mathfrak{q}}{{\bm{k}}_{\mathbb{P}}}(z,z)^{\mathfrak{q}}]=\mathbb{E}_{x\sim\mathbb{P}}[\frac{\differential\mathbb{P}}{\differential\mathbb{Q}}(x)^{2\mathfrak{q}-1}{{\bm{k}}_{\mathbb{P}}}(x,x)^{\mathfrak{q}}]<\infty, $$

$\mathbb{E}_{x_{i}\sim\mathbb{Q}}[\xi_{i}]=\mathbb{E}_{x_{i}\sim\mathbb{P}}[{{\bm{k}}_{\mathbb{P}}}(x_{i},\cdot)]=0$ and that ${\mathcal{H}_{{{\bm{k}}_{\mathbb{Q}}}}}$ is separable. Since $\mathcal{S}_{\infty}$ is a strictly stationary chain, we conclude that $(\xi_{i})_{i\in\mathbb{N}}$ is a strictly stationary centered sequence of ${\mathcal{H}_{{{\bm{k}}_{\mathbb{Q}}}}}$ -valued random variables satisfying the conditions needed to invoke Merlevède et al. [1997, Cor. 1], and hence $\sum_{i=1}^{n}\xi_{i}/\sqrt{n}$ converges in distribution to a Gaussian random element taking values in ${\mathcal{H}_{{{\bm{k}}_{\mathbb{Q}}}}}$ .

Case 2: $\mu_{1}\neq\mathbb{Q}$ Since $\mathcal{S}_{\infty}$ is positive Harris and $\sum_{i=1}^{n}\xi_{i}/\sqrt{n}$ satisfies a CLT for the initial distribution $\mu_{1}=\mathbb{Q}$ , Meyn and Tweedie [2012, Prop. 17.1.6] implies that $\sum_{i=1}^{n}\xi_{i}/\sqrt{n}$ also satisfies the same CLT for any initial distribution $\mu_{1}$ .

Putting the pieces together for 113 Since, for any initial distribution for $x_{1}$ , the sequence $(\sum_{i=1}^{n}\xi_{i}/\sqrt{n})_{n\in\mathbb{N}}$ converges in distribution and that ${\mathcal{H}_{{{\bm{k}}_{\mathbb{Q}}}}}$ is separable and (by virtue of being a Hilbert space) complete, Prokhorov’s theorem [Billingsley, 2013, Thm. 5.2] implies that the sequence is also tight, i.e., $\|{\sum_{i=1}^{n}\xi_{i}}\|_{{{\bm{k}}_{\mathbb{Q}}}}/\sqrt{n}=O_{p}(1)$ . Consequently,

$$ \textstyle\|{\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\frac{\differential\mathbb{P}}{\differential\mathbb{Q}}(x_{i}){{\bm{k}}_{\mathbb{P}}}(x_{i},\cdot)}\|_{{{\bm{k}}_{\mathbb{P}}}}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\lx@cref{creftype~refnum}{eq:relating_the_norms}}}{{=}}\|{\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\xi_{i}}\|_{{{\bm{k}}_{\mathbb{Q}}}}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{n}}\cdot\|{\frac{\sum_{i=1}^{n}\xi_{i}}{\sqrt{n}}}\|_{{{\bm{k}}_{\mathbb{Q}}}}=O_{p}(n^{-\frac{1}{2}}), $$

as desired for the first claim in 113. Moreover, the strong law of large numbers for positive Harris chains [Meyn and Tweedie, 2012, Thm. 17.0.1(i)] implies that $\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i\in[n]}\frac{\differential\mathbb{P}}{\differential\mathbb{Q}}(x_{i})$ converges almost surely to $\mathbb{E}_{z\sim\mathbb{Q}}[\frac{\differential\mathbb{P}}{\differential\mathbb{Q}}(z)]=1$ as desired for the second claim in 113. ∎

### C.3 Proof of Thm. 2: Theorem 2 (Better-than-i.i.d. debiasing via simplex reweighting).

We start with Thm. C.1, proved in Sec. C.4, that bounds $\mmd_{\textsc{OPT}}$ in terms of the eigenvalues of the integral operator of the kernel ${{\bm{k}}_{\mathbb{P}}}$ . Our proof makes use of a weight construction from Liu and Lee [2017, Theorem 3.2], but is a non-trivial generalization of their proof as we no longer assume uniform bounds on the eigenfunctions, and instead leverage truncated variations of Bernstein’s inequality (Lems. C.2 and C.3) to establish suitable concentration bounds.

#### Theorem C.1 (Debiasing via i.i.d. simplex reweighting).

Consider a kernel ${{\bm{k}}_{\mathbb{P}}}$ satisfying Assum. 1 with $\mathfrak{p}=2$ . Let $(\lambda_{\ell})_{\ell=1}^{\infty}$ be the decreasing sequence of eigenvalues of $T_{{{\bm{k}}_{\mathbb{P}}},\mathbb{P}}$ defined in (24). Let $\mathcal{S}_{n}$ be a sequence of $n\in 2\mathbb{N}$ i.i.d. random variables with law $\mathbb{Q}$ such that $\mathbb{P}$ is absolutely continuous with respect to $\mathbb{Q}$ and $\|{\frac{\differential\mathbb{P}}{\differential\mathbb{Q}}}\|_{\infty}\leq M$ for some $M>0$ . Futhermore, assume there exist constants $\delta_{n},B_{n}>0$ such that $\Pr\left(\|{{{\bm{k}}_{\mathbb{P}}}}\|_{n}>B_{n}\right)<\delta_{n}$ . Then for all $L\in\mathbb{N}$ such that $\lambda_{L}>0$ , we have

$$ \textstyle\mathbb{E}[\mmd^{2}_{{{\bm{k}}_{\mathbb{P}}}}(\mathbb{S}_{n}^{{w_{\textsc{OPT}}}},\mathbb{P})]\leq\frac{8M}{n}\left(\frac{2M}{n}\frac{\mathbb{E}_{x\sim\mathbb{P}}[{{\bm{k}}^{2}_{\mathbb{P}}}(x,x)]}{\lambda_{L}}+\sum_{\ell>L}\lambda_{\ell}\right)+\epsilon_{n}\mathbb{E}[{{\bm{k}}^{2}_{\mathbb{P}}}(x_{1},x_{1})], $$

where

$$ \textstyle\epsilon_{n}^{2}\triangleq n\exp(\frac{-3n}{16\Mis B_{n}/\lambda_L} )+2\exp(\frac{-n}{16\Mis^2})+2\exp(-\frac{n}{64M^2(\bE_{x\sim\bP}[\kp(x,x)]+B_n/12)/\lambda_L})+\delta_{n}. $$

Given Thm. C.1, Thm. 2 follows, i.e., we have $\mathbb{E}[\mmd^{2}_{{{\bm{k}}_{\mathbb{P}}}}(\mathbb{S}_{n}^{{w_{\textsc{OPT}}}},\mathbb{P})]=o(n^{-1})$ , as long as we can show (i) $\mathbb{E}[{{\bm{k}}^{2}_{\mathbb{P}}}(x_{1},x_{1})]<\infty$ , which in turn holds when $\mathfrak{q}>3$ as assumed in Thm. 2, and (ii) find sequences $(B_{n})_{n=1}^{\infty}$ , $(\delta_{n})_{n=1}^{\infty}$ , and $(L_{n})_{n=1}^{\infty}$ such that $\Pr(\kpnormSn> B_n)<\delta_{n}$ for all $n$ and the following conditions are met:

- (a) $\frac{\mathbb{E}_{x\sim\mathbb{P}}[{{\bm{k}}^{2}_{\mathbb{P}}}(x,x)]}{\lambda_{L_{n}}}=o(n)$ ;

- (b) $\frac{B_{n}}{\lambda_{L_{n}}}=O(n^{\beta})$ , for some $\beta<1$ ;

- (c) $\sum_{\ell>L_{n}}\lambda_{\ell}=o(1)$ ;

- (d) $\delta_{n}=o(n^{-2})$ .

We now proceed to establish these conditions under the assumptions of Thm. 2.

Condition (d) By the de La Vallée Poussin Theorem [Chandra, 2015, Thm. 1.3] applied to the $\mathbb{Q}$ -integrable function $x\mapsto{{\bm{k}}_{\mathbb{P}}}(x,x)^{\mathfrak{q}}$ (which is a uniformly integrable family with one function), there exists a convex increasing function $G$ such that $\lim_{t\to\infty}\frac{G(t)}{t}=\infty$ and $\mathbb{E}[G({{\bm{k}}_{\mathbb{P}}}(x_{1},x_{1})^{\mathfrak{q}})]<\infty$ . Thus,

$$ \textstyle\Pr(\kp(x_1,x_1) > n^{3/\fq})=\Pr(\kp(x_1,x_1)^{\fq} > n^3) \textstyle=\Pr(G(\kp(x_1,x_1))^\fq> G(n^3)) \textstyle\leq\frac{\mathbb{E}[G({{\bm{k}}_{\mathbb{P}}}(x_{1},x_{1}))^{\mathfrak{q}}]}{G(n^{3})}=o(n^{-3}), $$

where the last step uses $\lim_{t\to\infty}\frac{G(t)}{t}=\infty$ . Hence by the union bound,

$$ \textstyle\Pr(\kpnormSn> n^{3/\fq})=\Pr(\max_{i\in[n]}\kp(x_i,x_i) > n^{3/\fq})\leq n\Pr(\kp(x_1,x_1) > n^{3/\fq})=o(n^{-2}). $$

Hence if we set $B_{n}=n^{\tau}$ for $\tau\triangleq 3/\mathfrak{q}<1$ , there exists $(\delta_{n})_{n=1}^{\infty}$ such that $\delta_{n}=o(n^{-2})$ . This fulfills (d) and that $\Pr(\kpnormSn> B_n)<\delta_{n}$ .

To prove remaining conditions, without loss of generality, we assume that $\lambda_{\ell}>0$ for all $\ell\in\mathbb{N}$ , since otherwise we can choose $L_{n}$ to be, for all $n$ , the largest $\ell$ such that $\lambda_{\ell}>0$ . Then $\sum_{\ell>L_{n}}\lambda_{L_{n}}=0$ and all other conditions are met.

Condition (c) If $L_{n}\to\infty$ , then (c) is fulfilled since $\sum_{\ell}{\lambda_{\ell}}<\infty$ , which follows from Lem. B.1(d) and that

$$ \textstyle\sum_{\ell}\lambda_{\ell}=\sum_{\ell=1}^{\infty}\lambda_{i}\mathbb{E}_{x\sim\mathbb{P}}[\phi_{\ell}(x)^{2}]=\sum_{\ell=1}^{\infty}\lambda_{i}\mathbb{E}_{x\sim\mathbb{P}}[\phi_{\ell}(x)^{2}]=\mathbb{E}_{x\sim\mathbb{P}}[\sum_{\ell=1}^{\infty}\lambda_{i}\phi_{\ell}(x)^{2}]=\mathbb{E}_{x\sim\mathbb{P}}[{{\bm{k}}_{\mathbb{P}}}(x,x)]<\infty. $$

Conditions (a) and (b) Note that the condition (a) is subsumed by (b) since $\mathbb{E}_{x\sim\mathbb{P}}[{{\bm{k}}^{2}_{\mathbb{P}}}(x,x)]<\infty$ . It remains to choose $(L_{n})_{n=1}^{\infty}$ to satisfy (b) such that $\lim_{n\to\infty}L_{n}=\infty$ . Define $L_{n}\triangleq\max\{\ell\in\mathbb{N}:\lambda_{\ell}\geq n^{\frac{\tau-1}{2}}\}$ . Then $L_{n}$ is well-defined for $n\geq(\frac{1}{\lambda_{1}})^{\frac{2}{1-\tau}}$ , since for such $n$ we have $\lambda_{1}\geq n^{\frac{\tau-1}{2}}$ . Hence for $n\geq(\frac{1}{\lambda_{1}})^{\frac{2}{1-\tau}}$ , we have

$$ \textstyle\frac{B_{n}}{\lambda_{L_{n}}}\leq\frac{n^{\tau}}{n^{\frac{\tau-1}{2}}}=n^{\frac{\tau+1}{2}}, $$

so (b) is satisfied with $\beta=\frac{\tau+1}{2}<1$ . Since $\tau<1$ , $L_{n}$ is non-decreasing in $n$ and $n^{\frac{\tau-1}{2}}$ decreases to $0$ . Since each $\lambda_{\ell}>0$ , we therefore have $\lim_{n\to\infty}L_{n}=\infty$ . ∎

### C.4 Proof of Thm. C.1: Theorem C.1 (Debiasing via i.i.d. simplex reweighting).

We will slowly build up towards proving Thm. C.1. First notice $\mathbb{E}_{x\sim\mathbb{P}}[{{\bm{k}}^{2}_{\mathbb{P}}}(x,x)]<\infty$ implies $\mathbb{E}_{x\sim\mathbb{P}}[{{\bm{k}}_{\mathbb{P}}}(x,x)]<\infty$ , so Lem. B.1 holds. Fix any $L\in\mathbb{N}$ satisfying $\lambda_{L}>0$ . Since $n$ is even, we can define $\mathcal{D}_{0}\triangleq[n/2]$ and $\mathcal{D}_{1}\triangleq[n]\setminus\mathcal{D}_{0}$ . We will use $\mathcal{S}_{\mathcal{D}_{0}}$ and $\mathcal{S}_{\mathcal{D}_{1}}$ to denote the subsets of $\mathcal{S}_{n}$ with indices in $\mathcal{D}_{0}$ and $\mathcal{D}_{1}$ respectively. Let $(\phi_{\ell})_{\ell=1}^{\infty}\subset{\mathcal{H}_{{{\bm{k}}_{\mathbb{P}}}}}$ be eigenfunctions corresponding to the eigenvalues $(\lambda_{\ell})_{\ell=1}^{\infty}$ by Lem. B.1(c), so that $({\phi_{\ell}})_{\ell=1}^{\infty}$ is an orthonormal system of $\mathcal{L}^{2}(\mathbb{P})$ .

We start with a useful lemma.

#### Lemma C.1 ( ${\mathcal{H}_{{{\bm{k}}_{\mathbb{P}}}}}$ consists of mean-zero functions).

Let ${{\bm{k}}_{\mathbb{P}}}$ be a kernel satisfying Assum. 1. Then for any $f\in{\mathcal{H}_{{{\bm{k}}_{\mathbb{P}}}}}$ , we have $\mathbb{P}f=0$ .

#### Proof.

Fix $f\in{\mathcal{H}_{{{\bm{k}}_{\mathbb{P}}}}}$ . By Steinwart and Christmann [2008, Thm 4.26], $f$ is $\mathbb{P}$ integrable. Consider the linear operator $I$ that maps $f\mapsto\mathbb{P}f$ . Since

$$ \textstyle\absolutevalue{I(f)}=\absolutevalue{\bP f}\leq\mathbb{P}\absolutevalue{f}=\int\absolutevalue{\langle f, \kp(x,\cdot)\rangle_{\kp}}\differential\mathbb{P}\leq\int\left\|{f}\right\|_{{{\bm{k}}_{\mathbb{P}}}}\sqrt{{{\bm{k}}_{\mathbb{P}}}(x,x)}\differential\mathbb{P}=\left\|{f}\right\|_{{{\bm{k}}_{\mathbb{P}}}}\mathbb{E}_{x\sim\mathbb{P}}[{{\bm{k}}_{\mathbb{P}}}(x,x)^{\frac{1}{2}}]. $$

Hence $I$ is a continuous linear operator, so by the Riez representation theorem [Steinwart and Christmann, 2008, Thm. A.5.12], there exists $g\in{\mathcal{H}_{{{\bm{k}}_{\mathbb{P}}}}}$ such that $I(h)=\langle h,g\rangle_{{{\bm{k}}_{\mathbb{P}}}}$ for any $h\in{\mathcal{H}_{{{\bm{k}}_{\mathbb{P}}}}}$ .

By Steinwart and Christmann [2008, Thm. 4.21], the set

$$ \textstyle H_{\text{pre}}\triangleq\left\{\sum_{i=1}^{n}\alpha_{i}{{\bm{k}}_{\mathbb{P}}}(\cdot,x_{i}):n\in\mathbb{N},(\alpha_{i})_{i\in[n]}\subset\mathbb{R},(x_{i})_{i\in[n]}\subset\mathbb{R}^{d}\right\} $$

is dense in ${\mathcal{H}_{{{\bm{k}}_{\mathbb{P}}}}}$ . Note that $H_{\text{pre}}$ consists of mean zero functions under $\mathbb{P}$ by linearity. So there exists $f_{n}$ converging to $f$ in ${\mathcal{H}_{{{\bm{k}}_{\mathbb{P}}}}}$ where each $f_{n}$ has $\mathbb{P}f_{n}=I(f_{n})=\langle f_{n},g\rangle_{{{\bm{k}}_{\mathbb{P}}}}=0$ . Since

$$ \textstyle\lim_{n\to\infty}\absolutevalue{\langle f, g \rangle_{\kp} - \langle f_n, g \rangle_{\kp}}=\lim_{n\to\infty}\absolutevalue{\langle f - f_n, g \rangle_{\kp}}\leq\lim_{n\to\infty}\left\|{f-f_{n}}\right\|_{{{\bm{k}}_{\mathbb{P}}}}\left\|{g}\right\|_{{{\bm{k}}_{\mathbb{P}}}}=0, $$

we have $\mathbb{P}f=\langle f,g\rangle_{{{\bm{k}}_{\mathbb{P}}}}=0$ . ∎

In particular, the assumption $\mathbb{E}_{x\sim\mathbb{P}}[{{\bm{k}}^{2}_{\mathbb{P}}}(x,x)]<\infty$ of Thm. C.1 implies $\mathbb{E}_{x\sim\mathbb{P}}[{{\bm{k}}_{\mathbb{P}}}(x,x)^{\frac{1}{2}}]<\infty$ , so Lem. C.1 holds.

Step 1. Build control variate weights

Fix any $L\geq 1$ and $h\in{\mathcal{H}_{{{\bm{k}}_{\mathbb{P}}}}}$ , and let $\hat{h}_{\mathcal{D}_{0}}$ denote the eigen-expansion truncated approximation of $h$ based on $\mathcal{D}_{0}$ ,

$$ \textstyle\hat{h}_{\mathcal{D}_{0}}(x)\triangleq\sum_{\ell=1}^{L}\hat{\beta}_{\ell,0}\phi_{\ell}(x)\quad\text{for}\quad\hat{\beta}_{\ell,0}\triangleq\frac{2}{n}\sum_{i\in\mathcal{D}_{0}}h(x_{i})\phi_{\ell}(x_{i})\xi(x_{i}). $$

Then

$$ \textstyle\mathbb{E}[\hat{\beta}_{\ell,0}] \textstyle=\mathbb{E}\left[\frac{2}{n}\sum_{i\in\mathcal{D}_{0}}h(x_{i})\phi_{\ell}(x_{i})\xi(x_{i})\right]=\langle{h},{\phi_{\ell}}\rangle_{\mathcal{L}^{2}(\mathbb{P})}. $$

Next, define the control variate

$$ \textstyle\hat{Z}_{0}[h]=\frac{2}{n}\sum_{i\in D_{1}}\left(\xi(x_{i})(h(x_{i})-\hat{h}_{\mathcal{D}_{0}}(x_{i}))\right). $$

which satisfies

$$ \textstyle\mathbb{E}[\hat{Z_{0}}[h]]=\mathbb{E}_{x\sim\mathbb{P}}\left[h(x)-\sum_{\ell=1}^{L}\mathbb{E}[\hat{\beta}_{\ell,0}]\phi_{\ell}(x)\right]=0, $$

since functions in ${\mathcal{H}_{{{\bm{k}}_{\mathbb{P}}}}}$ have mean $0$ with respect to $\mathbb{P}$ (Lem. C.1). Similarly, we define $\hat{Z_{1}}[h]$ by swapping $\mathcal{D}_{0}$ and $\mathcal{D}_{1}$ . Then we form $\hat{Z}[h]\triangleq\frac{\hat{Z}_{0}[h]+\hat{Z}_{1}[h]}{2}$ . We can rewrite $\hat{Z}[h]$ as a quadrature rule over $\mathcal{S}_{n}$ [Liu and Lee, 2017, Lemma B.6]

$$ \textstyle\hat{Z}[h]=\sum_{i\in[n]}w_{i}h(x_{i}), $$

where $w_{i}$ is defined as (whose randomness depends on the randomness in $\mathcal{S}_{n}$ )

$$ \textstyle w_{i}\triangleq\left\{\begin{array}[]{cc}\frac{1}{n}\xi(x_{i})-\frac{2}{n^{2}}\sum_{j\in\mathcal{D}_{1}}\xi(x_{i})\xi(x_{j})\langle\Phi_{L}(x_{i}),\Phi_{L}(x_{j})\rangle,\forall i\in\mathcal{D}_{0},\\
\frac{1}{n}\xi(x_{i})-\frac{2}{n^{2}}\sum_{j\in\mathcal{D}_{0}}\xi(x_{i})\xi(x_{j})\langle\Phi_{L}(x_{i}),\Phi_{L}(x_{j})\rangle,\forall i\in\mathcal{D}_{1},\end{array}\right. $$

and $\Phi_{L}(x)\triangleq(\phi_{1}(x),\ldots,\phi_{L}(x))$ .

Step 2. Show $\mathbb{E}[\mmd^{2}_{{{\bm{k}}_{\mathbb{P}}}}(\mathbb{S}_{n}^{w},\mathbb{P})]=o(n^{-1})$

We first bound the variance of the control variate $\hat{Z}_{0}[h]$ for $h=\phi_{\ell^{\prime}}$ for $\ell^{\prime}\in\mathbb{N}$ . Let us fix $\ell^{\prime}\in\mathbb{N}$ . From (129), we compute

$$ \textstyle\mathbb{E}[\hat{Z}_{0}[h]^{2}]=\frac{4}{n^{2}}\mathbb{E}\left[\left(\sum_{i\in\mathcal{D}_{1}}\xi(x_{i})(h(x_{i})-\hat{h}_{\mathcal{D}_{0}}(x_{i}))\right)^{2}\right] \textstyle=\frac{4}{n^{2}}\mathbb{E}\left[\sum_{i\in\mathcal{D}_{1}}\xi(x_{i})^{2}(h(x_{i})-\hat{h}_{\mathcal{D}_{0}}(x_{i}))^{2}\right] \textstyle=\frac{2}{n}\mathbb{E}[\mathbb{E}_{x\sim\mathbb{Q}}[\xi(x)^{2}(h(x)-\hat{h}_{\mathcal{D}_{0}}(x))^{2}|\mathcal{S}_{\mathcal{D}_{0}}]] \textstyle=\frac{2}{n}\mathbb{E}[\mathbb{E}_{x\sim\mathbb{P}}[\xi(x)(h(x)-\hat{h}_{\mathcal{D}_{0}}(x))^{2}|\mathcal{S}_{\mathcal{D}_{0}}]] \textstyle\leq\frac{2M}{n}\mathbb{E}[\mathbb{E}_{x\sim\mathbb{P}}[(h(x)-\hat{h}_{\mathcal{D}_{0}}(x))^{2}|\mathcal{S}_{\mathcal{D}_{0}}]], $$

where in the second equality, the cross terms are zero due to the independence of points $x_{i}$ and the equality 130. By the definition of $\hat{h}_{\mathcal{D}_{0}}$ , we compute

$$ \textstyle\mathbb{E}_{x\sim\mathbb{P}}[(h(x)-\hat{h}_{\mathcal{D}_{0}}(x))^{2}|\mathcal{S}_{\mathcal{D}_{0}}] \textstyle=\mathbb{E}_{x\sim\mathbb{P}}\left[\left(\phi_{\ell^{\prime}}(x)-\sum_{\ell\leq L}\hat{\beta}_{\ell,0}\phi_{\ell}(x)\right)^{2}\middle|\mathcal{S}_{\mathcal{D}_{0}}\right] \textstyle=\mathbb{E}_{x\sim\mathbb{P}}\left[\phi_{\ell^{\prime}}^{2}(x)+\sum_{\ell\leq L}\hat{\beta}^{2}_{\ell,0}\phi^{2}_{\ell}(x)-2\phi_{\ell^{\prime}}(x)\sum_{\ell\leq L}\hat{\beta}_{\ell,0}\phi_{\ell}(x)\middle|\mathcal{S}_{\mathcal{D}_{0}}\right] \textstyle=1+\sum_{\ell\leq L}\hat{\beta}^{2}_{\ell,0}-2\sum_{\ell\leq L}\hat{\beta}_{\ell,0}\mathbbm{1}_{\ell^{\prime}=\ell} \textstyle=1+\sum_{\ell\leq L}\hat{\beta}^{2}_{\ell,0}-2\hat{\beta}_{\ell^{\prime},0}\mathbbm{1}_{\ell^{\prime}\leq L}, $$

where we use the fact that $({\phi_{\ell}})_{\ell=1}^{\infty}$ is an orthonormal system in $\mathcal{L}^{2}(\mathbb{P})$ . By (128) with $h=\phi_{\ell^{\prime}}$ , we have $\mathbb{E}[\hat{\beta}_{\ell^{\prime},0}]=1$ . On the other hand, we can bound, again using the orthonormality of $({\phi_{\ell}})_{\ell=1}^{\infty}$ ,

$$ \textstyle\mathbb{E}[\hat{\beta}^{2}_{\ell,0}]=\mathbb{E}\left[\left(\frac{2}{n}\sum_{i\in\mathcal{D}_{0}}\phi_{\ell}(x_{i})\phi_{\ell^{\prime}}(x_{i})\xi(x_{i})\right)^{2}\right]=\frac{4}{n^{2}}\mathbb{E}\left[\sum_{i\in\mathcal{D}_{0}}(\phi_{\ell}(x_{i})\phi_{\ell^{\prime}}(x_{i})\xi(x_{i}))^{2}\right]\leq\frac{2M}{n}\mathbb{E}_{x\sim\mathbb{P}}[(\phi_{\ell}(x)\phi_{\ell^{\prime}}(x))^{2}]. $$

Thus for all $\ell^{\prime}\in\mathbb{N}$ ,

$$ \textstyle\mathbb{E}[\hat{Z}_{0}[\phi_{\ell^{\prime}}]^{2}]\leq\frac{2M}{n}\left(1+\frac{2M}{n}\sum_{\ell\leq L}\mathbb{E}_{x\sim\mathbb{P}}[(\phi_{\ell}(x)\phi_{\ell^{\prime}}(x))^{2}]-2\mathbbm{1}_{\ell^{\prime}\leq L}\right)\leq\frac{2M}{n}\left(\frac{2M}{n}\sum_{\ell\leq L}\mathbb{E}_{x\sim\mathbb{P}}[(\phi_{\ell}(x)\phi_{\ell^{\prime}}(x))^{2}]+\mathbbm{1}_{\ell^{\prime}>L}\right). $$

Since $\hat{Z}[h]=\frac{\hat{Z}_{0}[h]+\hat{Z}_{1}[h]}{2}$ and $(\frac{a+b}{2})^{2}\leq\frac{a^{2}+b^{2}}{2}$ for $a,b\in\mathbb{R}$ , and, by symmetry, $\mathbb{E}[\hat{Z}_{0}[h]^{2}]=\mathbb{E}[\hat{Z}_{1}[h]^{2}]$ , we have

$$ \textstyle\mathbb{E}[\hat{Z}[\phi_{\ell^{\prime}}]^{2}] \textstyle\leq\frac{2M}{n}\left(\frac{2M}{n}\sum_{\ell\leq L}\mathbb{E}_{x\sim\mathbb{P}}[(\phi_{\ell}(x)\phi_{\ell^{\prime}}(x))^{2}]+\mathbbm{1}_{\ell^{\prime}>L}\right). $$

Now we have

$$ \textstyle\mathbb{E}[\mmd^{2}_{{{\bm{k}}_{\mathbb{P}}}}(\mathbb{S}_{n}^{w},\mathbb{P})]=\mathbb{E}\left[\sum_{i,j\in[n]}w_{i}w_{j}{{\bm{k}}_{\mathbb{P}}}(x_{i},x_{j})\right] \textstyle=\mathbb{E}\left[\sum_{i,j\in[n]}w_{i}w_{j}\sum_{\ell^{\prime}=1}^{\infty}\lambda_{\ell^{\prime}}\phi_{\ell^{\prime}}(x_{i})\phi_{\ell^{\prime}}(x_{j})\right] \textstyle=\mathbb{E}\left[\sum_{\ell^{\prime}=1}^{\infty}\sum_{i,j\in[n]}w_{i}w_{j}\lambda_{\ell^{\prime}}\phi_{\ell^{\prime}}(x_{i})\phi_{\ell^{\prime}}(x_{j})\right] \textstyle=\mathbb{E}\left[\sum_{\ell^{\prime}=1}^{\infty}\lambda_{\ell^{\prime}}\left(\sum_{i\in[n]}w_{i}\phi_{\ell^{\prime}}(x_{i})\right)^{2}\right] \textstyle=\sum_{\ell^{\prime}=1}^{\infty}\lambda_{\ell^{\prime}}\mathbb{E}\left[\left(\sum_{i\in[n]}w_{i}\phi_{\ell^{\prime}}(x_{i})\right)^{2}\right]=\sum_{\ell^{\prime}=1}^{\infty}\lambda_{\ell^{\prime}}\mathbb{E}[\hat{Z}[\phi_{\ell^{\prime}}]^{2}], $$

where the second and third equalities are due to the absolute convergence of the Mercer series (Lem. B.1(d)), the fourth equality follows from Tonelli’s theorem [Steinwart and Christmann, 2008, Thm. A.3.10], and the last step is due to (131). Plugging in (144), we have

$$ \textstyle\mathbb{E}[\mmd^{2}_{{{\bm{k}}_{\mathbb{P}}}}(\mathbb{S}_{n}^{w},\mathbb{P})] \textstyle\leq\frac{2M}{n}\left(\frac{2M}{n}\sum_{\ell^{\prime}=1}^{\infty}\sum_{\ell\leq L}\lambda_{\ell^{\prime}}\mathbb{E}_{x\sim\mathbb{P}}[(\phi_{\ell}(x)\phi_{\ell^{\prime}}(x))^{2}]+\sum_{\ell>L}\lambda_{\ell}\right). $$

Since the eigenvalues are nonnegative and non-increasing, we can write, by (26),

$$ \textstyle{{\bm{k}}^{2}_{\mathbb{P}}}(x,x) \textstyle=\left(\sum_{\ell=1}^{\infty}\lambda_{\ell}\phi_{\ell}(x)^{2}\right)^{2}\geq\sum_{\ell^{\prime}=1}^{\infty}\sum_{\ell\leq L}\lambda_{\ell^{\prime}}\lambda_{\ell}(\phi_{\ell}(x)\phi_{\ell^{\prime}}(x))^{2}\geq\lambda_{L}\sum_{\ell^{\prime}=1}^{\infty}\sum_{\ell\leq L}\lambda_{\ell^{\prime}}(\phi_{\ell}(x)\phi_{\ell^{\prime}}(x))^{2}. $$

Thus by Tonelli’s theorem [Steinwart and Christmann, 2008, Thm. A.3.10],

$$ \textstyle\sum_{\ell^{\prime}=1}^{\infty}\sum_{\ell\leq L}\lambda_{\ell^{\prime}}\mathbb{E}_{x\sim\mathbb{P}}[(\phi_{\ell}(x)\phi_{\ell^{\prime}}(x))^{2}] \textstyle=\mathbb{E}_{x\sim\mathbb{P}}\left[\sum_{\ell^{\prime}=1}^{\infty}\sum_{\ell\leq L}\lambda_{\ell^{\prime}}(\phi_{\ell}(x)\phi_{\ell^{\prime}}(x))^{2}\right]\leq\frac{\mathbb{E}_{x\sim\mathbb{P}}[{{\bm{k}}^{2}_{\mathbb{P}}}(x,x)]}{\lambda_{L}}. $$

Finally, we have

$$ \textstyle\mathbb{E}[\mmd^{2}_{{{\bm{k}}_{\mathbb{P}}}}(\mathbb{S}^{w}_{n},\mathbb{P})] \textstyle\leq\frac{2M}{n}\left(\frac{2M}{n}\frac{\mathbb{E}_{x\sim\mathbb{P}}[{{\bm{k}}^{2}_{\mathbb{P}}}(x,x)]}{\lambda_{L}}+\sum_{\ell>L}\lambda_{\ell}\right). $$

Step 3. Meet the non-negative constraint

We now show that the weights (C.4) are nonnegative and sum close to one with high probability. For $i\in\mathcal{D}_{0}$ , we have

$$ \textstyle w_{i}=\frac{1}{n}\xi(x_{i})\left(1-T_{i}\right)\quad\text{for}\quad T_{i}\triangleq\frac{2}{n}\sum_{j\in\mathcal{D}_{1}}\xi(x_{j})\langle\Phi_{L}(x_{i}),\Phi_{L}(x_{j})\rangle. $$

Our first goal is to derive an upper bound for $\Pr\left(\min_{i\in\mathcal{D}_{0}}w_{i}<0\right)$ . Define the event

$$ \textstyle E_{n}\triangleq\left\{\|{{{\bm{k}}_{\mathbb{P}}}}\|_{n}\leq B_{n}\right\}, $$

so $\Pr(E_n^c)<\delta_{n}$ by the assumption on $\|{{{\bm{k}}_{\mathbb{P}}}}\|_{n}$ . Then

$$ \textstyle\Pr\left(\min_{i\in[n]}w_{i}<0,E_{n}\right) \textstyle=\Pr\left(\max_{i\in[n]}T_{i}>1,E_{n}\right)\leq n\Pr(T_1\ind{E_n} > 1), $$

where we applied the union bound and used the fact that $T_{i}\mathbbm{1}_{E_{n}}$ has the same law for different $i$ . To further bound $\Pr(T_1\ind{E_n} > 1)$ , we will use the following lemma.

#### Lemma C.2 (Truncated Bernstein inequality).

Let $X_{1},\ldots,X_{n}$ be i.i.d. random variables with $\mathbb{E}[X_{1}]=0$ and $\mathbb{E}[X_{1}^{2}]<\infty$ . For any $B>0$ , $t>0$ ,

$$ \textstyle\Pr\left(\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i\in[n]}X_{i}\mathbbm{1}_{X_{i}\leq B}>t\right)\leq\exp\left(\frac{-nt^{2}}{2(\mathbb{E}[X_{1}^{2}]+\frac{Bt}{3})}\right). $$

#### Proof of Lem. C.2.

Fix any $B>0$ and $t>0$ and define, for each $i\in[n]$ , $Y_{i}\triangleq X_{i}\mathbbm{1}_{X_{i}\leq B}.$ Then $Y_{i}\leq B$ ,

$$ \textstyle\mathbb{E}[Y_{i}] \textstyle=\mathbb{E}[X_{i}\mathbbm{1}_{X_{i}\leq B}]\leq\mathbb{E}[X_{i}\mathbbm{1}_{X_{i}\leq B}]+\mathbb{E}[X_{i}\mathbbm{1}_{X_{i}>B}]=\mathbb{E}[X_{i}]=0,\quad\text{and}\quad \textstyle\mathbb{E}[Y_{i}^{2}] \textstyle=\mathbb{E}[X_{i}^{2}\mathbbm{1}_{X_{i}\leq B}]\leq\mathbb{E}[X_{i}^{2}]=\mathbb{E}[X_{1}^{2}]. $$

Now we can invoke the non-positivity of $\mathbb{E}[Y_{i}]$ , the one-sided Bernstein inequality [Wainwright, 2019, Prop. 2.14], and the relation $\mathbb{E}[Y_{i}^{2}]\leq\mathbb{E}[X_{1}^{2}]$ to conclude that

$$ \textstyle\Pr\left(\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i\in[n]}Y_{i}>t\right) \textstyle\leq\Pr\left(\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i\in[n]}\left(Y_{i}-\mathbb{E}[Y_{i}]\right)>t\right)\leq\exp\left(\frac{-nt^{2}}{2(\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i\in[n]}\mathbb{E}[Y_{i}^{2}]+\frac{Bt}{3})}\right)\leq\exp\left(\frac{-nt^{2}}{2(\mathbb{E}[X_{1}^{2}]+\frac{Bt}{3})}\right). $$

∎

For $j\in\mathcal{D}_{1}$ , define $X_{j}\triangleq\xi(x_{j})\langle\Phi_{L}(x_{1}),\Phi_{L}(x_{j})\rangle$ and note that

$$ \textstyle\mathbb{E}[X_{j}|x_{1}] \textstyle=\mathbb{E}_{x\sim\mathbb{Q}}[\xi(x)\langle\Phi_{L}(x_{1}),\Phi_{L}(x)\rangle|x_{1}]=\mathbb{E}_{x\sim\mathbb{P}}[\langle\Phi_{L}(x_{1}),\Phi_{L}(x)\rangle|x_{1}]=0 \textstyle\mathbb{E}[X_{j}^{2}|x_{1}] \textstyle=\mathbb{E}[\xi(x_{j})^{2}\langle\Phi_{L}(x_{1}),\Phi_{L}(x_{j})\rangle^{2}|x_{1}]\leq M\mathbb{E}_{x\sim\mathbb{P}}[\langle\Phi_{L}(x_{1}),\Phi_{L}(x)\rangle^{2}|x_{1}] \textstyle=M\mathbb{E}_{x\sim\mathbb{P}}\left[\sum_{\ell,\ell^{\prime}\leq L}\phi_{\ell}(x_{1})\phi_{\ell^{\prime}}(x_{1})\phi_{\ell}(x)\phi_{\ell^{\prime}}(x)\middle|x_{1}\right] \textstyle=M\sum_{\ell,\ell^{\prime}\leq L}\phi_{\ell}(x_{1})\phi_{\ell^{\prime}}(x_{1})\mathbb{E}_{x\sim\mathbb{P}}\left[\phi_{\ell}(x)\phi_{\ell^{\prime}}(x)\right] \textstyle=M\left\|{\Phi_{L}(x_{1})}\right\|_{2}^{2}. $$

Since $\lambda_{1}\geq\lambda_{2}\geq\cdots\geq 0$ , for any $x\in\mathbb{R}^{d}$ , we can bound $\left\|{\Phi_{L}(x)}\right\|_{2}^{2}$ via

$$ \textstyle\left\|{\Phi_{L}(x)}\right\|_{2}^{2} \textstyle=\sum_{\ell\leq L}\phi_{\ell}(x)^{2}\leq\frac{\sum_{\ell\leq L}\lambda_{\ell}\phi_{\ell}(x)^{2}}{\lambda_{L}}\leq\frac{\sum_{\ell=1}^{\infty}\lambda_{\ell}\phi_{\ell}(x)^{2}}{\lambda_{L}}=\frac{{{\bm{k}}_{\mathbb{P}}}(x,x)}{\lambda_{L}}, $$

where we applied Lem. B.1(d) for the last equality. Thus

$$ \textstyle\absolutevalue{X_j}\leq M\left\|{\Phi_{L}(x_{1})}\right\|_{2}\left\|{\Phi_{L}(x_{j})}\right\|_{2}\leq M\left\|{\Phi_{L}(x_{1})}\right\|_{2}\sqrt{\frac{{{\bm{k}}_{\mathbb{P}}}(x_{j},x_{j})}{\lambda_{L}}}, $$

so if we let $B\triangleq\sqrt{\frac{B_{n}}{\lambda_{L}}}M\left\|{\Phi_{L}(x_{1})}\right\|_{2},$ then

$$ \textstyle E_{n}=\left\{\sup_{i\in[n]}{{\bm{k}}_{\mathbb{P}}}(x_{i},x_{i})\leq B_{n}\right\}\subset\bigcap_{j\in\mathcal{D}_{1}}\{\absolutevalue{X_j}\leq B\}. $$

Since $T_{1}=\frac{2}{n}\sum_{j\in\mathcal{D}_{1}}X_{j}$ , we have inclusions of events

$$ \textstyle\{T_{1}\mathbbm{1}_{E_{n}}>1\} \textstyle=\{T_{1}>1\}\cap E_{n}\subset\left\{\frac{2}{n}\sum_{j\in\mathcal{D}_{1}}X_{j}\mathbbm{1}_{X_{j}\leq B}>1\right\}. $$

Thus Lem. C.2 with $t=1$ and conditioned on $x_{1}$ implies

$$ \textstyle\Pr\left(T_{1}\mathbbm{1}_{E_{n}}>1\middle|x_{1}\right) \textstyle\leq\Pr\left(\frac{2}{n}\sum_{j\in\mathcal{D}_{1}}X_{j}\mathbbm{1}_{X_{j}\leq B}>1\middle|x_{1}\right) \textstyle\leq\exp\left(\frac{-n}{4(M\left\|{\Phi_{L}(x_{1})}\right\|_{2}^{2}+\sqrt{\frac{B_{n}}{\lambda_{L}}}M\left\|{\Phi_{L}(x_{1})}\right\|_{2}/3)}\right). $$

On event $\{{{\bm{k}}_{\mathbb{P}}}(x_{1},x_{1})\leq B_{n}\}$ , by (165), we have

$$ \textstyle\left\|{\Phi_{L}(x_{1})}\right\|_{2}\leq\sqrt{\frac{B_{n}}{\lambda_{L}}}. $$

Hence

$$ \textstyle\Pr\left(T_{1}\mathbbm{1}_{E_{n}}>1\middle|x_{1}\right)\mathbbm{1}_{{{\bm{k}}_{\mathbb{P}}}(x_{1},x_{1})\leq B_{n}}\leq\exp\left(\frac{-n}{\frac{16}{3}M\frac{B_{n}}{\lambda_{L}}}\right). $$

On the other hand, $\{{{\bm{k}}_{\mathbb{P}}}(x_{1},x_{1})>B_{n}\}\notin E_{n}$ , so

$$ \textstyle\Pr\left(T_{1}\mathbbm{1}_{E_{n}}>1\middle|x_{1}\right)\mathbbm{1}_{{{\bm{k}}_{\mathbb{P}}}(x_{1},x_{1})>B_{n}}=0 $$

Thus

$$ \textstyle\Pr(T_1\ind{E_n} > 1)=\mathbb{E}[\Pr(T_1\ind{E_n} > 1\vert x_1)]\leq\exp\left(\frac{-n}{\frac{16}{3}M\frac{B_{n}}{\lambda_{L}}}\right). $$

Combining the last inequality with (155), we have:

$$ \textstyle\Pr\left(\min_{i\in[n]}w_{i}<0,E_{n}\right) \textstyle\leq n\exp\left(\frac{-n}{\frac{16}{3}M\frac{B_{n}}{\lambda_{L}}}\right). $$

Step 4. Meet the sum-to-one constraint

Let

$$ \textstyle S\triangleq\sum_{i\in\mathcal{D}_{0}}w_{i}=\sum_{i\in\mathcal{D}_{0}}\frac{1}{n}\xi(x_{i})\left(1-\frac{2}{n}\sum_{j\in\mathcal{D}_{1}}\xi(x_{j})\langle\Phi_{L}(x_{i}),\Phi_{L}(x_{j})\rangle\right). $$

We now derive a bound for $\Pr(S < 1/2 - t/2)$ for $t\in(0,1)$ . Let

$$ \textstyle S_{1}\triangleq\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i\in\mathcal{D}_{0}}\xi(x_{i}),\quad S_{2}\triangleq-\frac{2}{n^{2}}\sum_{i\in\mathcal{D}_{0}}\sum_{j\in\mathcal{D}_{1}}\xi(x_{i})\xi(x_{j})\langle\Phi_{L}(x_{i}),\Phi_{L}(x_{j})\rangle, $$

so $S=S_{1}+S_{2}$ . Note that $\mathbb{E}[S_{1}]=1/2$ and $\mathbb{E}[S_{2}]=0$ since $\mathcal{D}_{0}$ and $\mathcal{D}_{1}$ are disjoint. Let $E_{n}$ be the same event defined as in (154). For $t_{1}\in(0,t/2)$ to be determined later and $t_{2}\triangleq t/2-t_{1}$ , we have, by the union bound

$$ \textstyle\Pr(S < 1/2 - t/2, E_n)\leq\Pr(S_1 < 1/2 - t_1, E_n)+\Pr(S_2 < -t_2, E_n). $$

By Hoeffding’s inequality and the assumption $\xi(x)\leq M$ , we have

$$ \textstyle\Pr(S_1 < 1/2 - t_1, E_n)\leq\Pr\left(\frac{2}{n}\sum_{i\in\mathcal{D}_{0}}\frac{\xi(x_{i})}{2}-1/2<-t_{1}\right) \textstyle\leq\exp\left(\frac{-2(n/2)t_{1}^{2}}{(M/2)^{2}}\right)=\exp\left(\frac{-4nt_{1}^{2}}{M^{2}}\right). $$

To give a concentration bound for $\Pr(S_2 < -t_2, E_n)$ , we will use the following lemma.

#### Lemma C.3 (U-statistic Bernstein’s inequality).

Let $h:\mathcal{X}\times\mathcal{X}\to\mathbb{R}$ be a function bounded above by $b>0$ . Assume $n\in 2\mathbb{N}$ and let $x_{1},\ldots,x_{n}$ be i.i.d. random variables taking values in $\mathcal{X}$ . Denote $m_{h}\triangleq\mathbb{E}[h(x_{1},x_{2})]$ and $\sigma_{h}^{2}\triangleq\operatorname{Var}[h(x_{1},x_{2})]$ . Let $\mathcal{D}_{0}=[n/2]$ and $\mathcal{D}_{1}=[n]\setminus[n/2]$ . Define

$$ \textstyle U\triangleq\frac{1}{(n/2)^{2}}\sum_{i\in\mathcal{D}_{0}}\sum_{j\in\mathcal{D}_{1}}h(x_{i},x_{j}). $$

Then

$$ \textstyle\Pr(U - m_h > t)\leq\exp\left(\frac{-nt^{2}}{4(\sigma_{h}^{2}+\frac{bt}{3})}\right). $$

#### Proof of Lem. C.3.

We adapt the proof from Pitcan [2017, Section 3] as follows. Let $k\triangleq n/2$ . Define $V:\mathcal{X}^{n}\to\mathbb{R}$ as

$$ \textstyle V(x_{1},\ldots,x_{n})\triangleq\frac{1}{k}\sum_{i\in[k]}h(x_{i},x_{i+k}). $$

Then note that

$$ \textstyle U \textstyle=\frac{1}{k!}\sum_{\sigma\in\operatorname{perm}(k)}V_{\sigma}, \textstyle V_{\sigma} \textstyle\triangleq V(x_{\sigma_{1}},\ldots,x_{\sigma_{k}}), $$

where $\operatorname{perm}(k)$ is the set of all permutations of $[k]$ ; this is because every $h(x_{i},x_{j})$ term for $i\in\mathcal{D}_{0},j\in\mathcal{D}_{1}$ will appear in the summation an equal number of times. For a fixed $\sigma\in\operatorname{perm}(k)$ , the random variable $V(x_{\sigma_{1}},\ldots,x_{\sigma_{k}},x_{k+1},\ldots,x_{n})$ is a sum of $k$ i.i.d. terms $h(x_{\sigma_{i}},x_{i+k})$ . Denote $V=V(x_{1},\ldots,x_{n})$ . For any $s>0$ , we have, by independence,

$$ \textstyle\mathbb{E}[e^{s(V-m_{h})}] \textstyle=\mathbb{E}\left[\exp(\frac{s}{k}\sum_{i\in[k]} (h(x_i,x_{i+[k]})-m_h))\right] \textstyle=\left(\mathbb{E}\left[\exp(\frac{s}{k} (h(x_1,x_{2})-m_h))\right]\right)^{k} $$

By the one-sided Bernstein’s lemma Wainwright [2019, Prop. 2.14] applied to $\frac{h(x_{1},x_{2})}{k}$ which is upper bounded by $\frac{b}{k}$ with variance $\frac{\sigma^{2}_{h}}{k^{2}}$ , we have

$$ \textstyle\mathbb{E}\left[\exp(s \frac{h(x_1,x_2) - m_h}{k})\right] \textstyle\leq\exp(\frac{s^2\sigma_h^2/2}{k(k - \frac{bs}{3})}), $$

for $s\in[0,3k/b)$ . Next, by Markov’s inequality and Jensen’s inequality,

$$ \textstyle\Pr(U-m_h > t) \textstyle=\Pr(e^{s(U-m_h)} > e^{st})\leq\mathbb{E}[e^{s(U-m_{h})}]e^{-st} \textstyle=\mathbb{E}\left[\exp(\frac{1}{(n/2)!} \sum_{\sigma\in\perm(n/2)} s(V_\sigma-m_h))\right]e^{-st} \textstyle\leq\mathbb{E}\left[\frac{1}{(n/2)!}\sum_{\sigma\in\operatorname{perm}(n/2)}\exp(s(V_\sigma-m_h))\right]e^{-st} \textstyle=\mathbb{E}[e^{s(V-m_{h})}]e^{-st}. $$

Therefore,

$$ \textstyle\Pr(U-m_h > t) \textstyle\leq\exp(\frac{s^2\sigma_h^2}{2(k-\frac{bs}{3})}-st). $$

Now, we get the desired bound if we pick $s=\frac{k^{2}t}{k\sigma_{h}^{2}+\frac{ktb}{3}}\in[0,3k/b)$ and simplify. ∎

Let

$$ \textstyle h(x,x^{\prime}) \textstyle\triangleq\xi(x)\xi(x^{\prime})\langle\Phi_{L}(x),\Phi_{L}(x^{\prime})\rangle \textstyle\bar{h}(x,x^{\prime}) \textstyle\triangleq h(x,x^{\prime})\mathbbm{1}_{h(x,x^{\prime})\leq M^{2}\frac{B_{n}}{\lambda_{L}}}. $$

Then

$$ \textstyle\Pr(S_2 < -t_2, E_n) \textstyle=\Pr\left(\frac{1}{(n/2)^{2}}\sum_{i\in\mathcal{D}_{0}}\sum_{j\in\mathcal{D}_{1}}h(x_{i},x_{j})>2t_{2},E_{n}\right) \textstyle\leq\Pr\left(\frac{1}{(n/2)^{2}}\sum_{i\in\mathcal{D}_{0}}\sum_{j\in\mathcal{D}_{1}}\bar{h}(x_{i},x_{j})>2t_{2}\right), $$

where the last inequality used the fact that, for $i\in\mathcal{D}_{0},j\in\mathcal{D}_{1}$ ,

$$ \textstyle E_{n}\subset\left\{\max({{\bm{k}}_{\mathbb{P}}}(x_{i},x_{i}),{{\bm{k}}_{\mathbb{P}}}(x_{j},x_{j}))\leq B_{n}\right\}\subset\left\{h(x_{i},x_{j})\leq M^{2}\frac{B_{n}}{\lambda_{L}}\right\}, $$

using (165). We further compute

$$ \textstyle m_{\bar{h}} \textstyle=\mathbb{E}[\bar{h}(x_{1},x_{2})]\leq\mathbb{E}[h(x_{1},x_{2})]=\mathbb{E}[\xi(x_{1})\xi(x_{2})\langle\Phi_{L}(x_{1}),\Phi_{L}(x_{2})\rangle] \textstyle=\sum_{\ell\leq L}\mathbb{E}[\xi(x_{1})\xi(x_{2})\phi_{\ell}(x_{1})\phi_{\ell}(x_{2})] \textstyle=\sum_{\ell\leq L}(\mathbb{E}_{x\sim\mathbb{P}}[\phi_{\ell}(x)])^{2}=0, $$

and

$$ \textstyle\sigma^{2}_{\bar{h}} \textstyle=\operatorname{Var}[\bar{h}(x_{1},x_{2})]\leq\mathbb{E}[\bar{h}(x_{1},x_{2})^{2}]\leq\mathbb{E}[h(x_{1},x_{2})^{2}] \textstyle=\mathbb{E}\left[\left(\xi(x_{1})\xi(x_{2})\langle\Phi_{L}(x_{1}),\Phi_{L}(x_{2})\rangle\right)^{2}\right] \textstyle\leq M^{2}\mathbb{E}_{(x,x^{\prime})\sim\mathbb{P}\times\mathbb{P}}[\langle\Phi_{L}(x),\Phi_{L}(x^{\prime})\rangle^{2}] \textstyle=M^{2}\mathbb{E}_{(x,x^{\prime})\sim\mathbb{P}\times\mathbb{P}}\left[\sum_{\ell,\ell^{\prime}\leq L}\phi_{\ell}(x)\phi_{\ell^{\prime}}(x)\phi_{\ell}(x^{\prime})\phi_{\ell^{\prime}}(x^{\prime})\right] \textstyle=M^{2}\sum_{\ell,\ell^{\prime}\leq L}(\mathbb{E}[\phi_{\ell}(x)\phi_{\ell^{\prime}}(x)])^{2}=LM^{2}. $$

Since $\mathbb{E}_{x\sim\mathbb{P}}[{{\bm{k}}_{\mathbb{P}}}(x,x)]=\sum_{\ell}\lambda_{\ell}\geq L\lambda_{L}$ , we have $L\leq\frac{\left\|{{{\bm{k}}_{\mathbb{P}}}}\right\|^{2}_{\mathcal{L}^{2}(\mathbb{P})}}{\lambda_{L}}$ , so that $\sigma_{\bar{h}}^{2}\leq\frac{M^{2}\left\|{{{\bm{k}}_{\mathbb{P}}}}\right\|^{2}_{\mathcal{L}^{2}(\mathbb{P})}}{\lambda_{L}}$ . Applying Lem. C.3 to $\bar{h}$ , which is bounded by $M^{2}\frac{B_{n}}{\lambda_{L}}$ and using the fact that $m_{\bar{h}}\leq 0$ , we have

$$ \textstyle\Pr\left(\frac{1}{(n/2)^{2}}\sum_{i\in\mathcal{D}_{0}}\sum_{j\in\mathcal{D}_{1}}\bar{h}(x_{i},x_{j})>2t_{2}\right) \textstyle\leq\Pr\left(\frac{1}{(n/2)^{2}}\sum_{i\in\mathcal{D}_{0}}\sum_{j\in\mathcal{D}_{1}}\bar{h}(x_{i},x_{j})-m_{\bar{h}}>2t_{2}\right) \textstyle\leq\exp\left(\frac{-n(2t_{2})^{2}}{4\left(\frac{M^{2}\left\|{{{\bm{k}}_{\mathbb{P}}}}\right\|^{2}_{\mathcal{L}^{2}(\mathbb{P})}}{\lambda_{L}}+2M^{2}\frac{B_{n}}{\lambda_{L}}t_{2}/3\right)}\right). $$

Thus combining (179), (196), (207), we get

$$ \textstyle\Pr(S < 1/2 - t/2, E_n)\leq\exp\left(\frac{-4nt_{1}^{2}}{M^{2}}\right)+\exp\left(\frac{-nt_{2}^{2}}{\left(\frac{M^{2}\left\|{{{\bm{k}}_{\mathbb{P}}}}\right\|^{2}_{\mathcal{L}^{2}(\mathbb{P})}}{\lambda_{L}}+2M^{2}\frac{B_{n}}{\lambda_{L}}t_{2}/3\right)}\right). $$

Finally, by symmetry and the union bound, for $t\in(0,1)$ , $t\in(0,t/2)$ and $t_{2}=t/2-t_{1}$ , we have

$$ \textstyle\Pr\left(\sum_{i\in[n]}w_{i}<1-t,E_{n}\right) \textstyle\leq\Pr\left(\sum_{i\in\mathcal{D}_{0}}w_{i}<1/2-t/2,E_{n}\right)+\Pr\left(\sum_{i\in\mathcal{D}_{1}}w_{i}<1/2-t/2,E_{n}\right) \textstyle=2\Pr(S < 1/2 - t/2, E_n) \textstyle\leq 2\left(\exp\left(\frac{-4nt_{1}^{2}}{M^{2}}\right)+\exp\left(\frac{-nt_{2}^{2}}{\left(\frac{M^{2}\left\|{{{\bm{k}}_{\mathbb{P}}}}\right\|^{2}_{\mathcal{L}^{2}(\mathbb{P})}}{\lambda_{L}}+2M^{2}\frac{B_{n}}{\lambda_{L}}t_{2}/3\right)}\right)\right). $$

Step 5. Putting it all together

Define the event

$$ \textstyle F_{n} \textstyle=\left\{\min_{i\in[n]}w_{i}\geq 0,\sum_{i\in[n]}w_{i}\geq\frac{1}{2}\right\}. $$

Then, by the union bound,

$$ \textstyle\Pr(F_n^c) \textstyle\leq\Pr(\min_{i\in[n]} w_i < 0, E_n)+\Pr(\sum_{i\in[n]} w_i < \frac{1}{2}, E_n)+\Pr(E_n^c). $$

Applying (175) and (211) to bound the last expression with $t=1/2$ , $t_{1}=t_{2}=1/8$ , we have $\Pr(F_n^c)\leq\epsilon_{n}^{2}$ for $\epsilon_{n}$ defined in 118. On the event $F_{n}$ , if we define $w^{+}\in\Delta_{n-1}$ via

$$ \textstyle w^{+}_{i}\triangleq\frac{w_{i}}{\sum_{i\in[n]}w_{i}}, $$

then $w^{+}_{i}=\alpha w_{i}$ for $i\in[n]$ and $\alpha\triangleq\frac{1}{\sum_{i\in[n]}w_{i}}\leq 2$ . Let $\tilde{w}\in\Delta_{n-1}$ be the weight defined by $\tilde{w}_{1}=1$ and $\tilde{w}_{i}=0$ for $i>1$ .

Since ${w_{\textsc{OPT}}}$ is the best simplex weight, we have $\mmd_{{{\bm{k}}_{\mathbb{P}}}}^{2}(\mathbb{S}^{{w_{\textsc{OPT}}}}_{n},\mathbb{P})\leq\min(\mmd_{{{\bm{k}}_{\mathbb{P}}}}^{2}(\mathbb{S}^{w^{+}}_{n},\mathbb{P}),\mmd_{{{\bm{k}}_{\mathbb{P}}}}^{2}(\mathbb{S}^{\tilde{w}}_{n},\mathbb{P}))$ . Hence

$$ \textstyle\mathbb{E}\left[\mmd^{2}_{{{\bm{k}}_{\mathbb{P}}}}(\mathbb{S}^{{w_{\textsc{OPT}}}}_{n},\mathbb{P})\right] \textstyle=\mathbb{E}\left[\mmd^{2}_{{{\bm{k}}_{\mathbb{P}}}}(\mathbb{S}^{{w_{\textsc{OPT}}}}_{n},\mathbb{P})\mathbbm{1}_{F_{n}}\right]+\mathbb{E}\left[\mmd^{2}_{{{\bm{k}}_{\mathbb{P}}}}(\mathbb{S}^{{w_{\textsc{OPT}}}}_{n},\mathbb{P})\mathbbm{1}_{F_{n}^{c}}\right] \textstyle\leq\mathbb{E}\left[\mmd^{2}_{{{\bm{k}}_{\mathbb{P}}}}(\mathbb{S}^{w^{+}}_{n},\mathbb{P})\mathbbm{1}_{F_{n}}\right]+\mathbb{E}\left[\mmd^{2}_{{{\bm{k}}_{\mathbb{P}}}}(\mathbb{S}^{\tilde{w}}_{n},\mathbb{P})\mathbbm{1}_{F_{n}^{c}}\right]. $$

For the first term, we have the bound

$$ \textstyle\mathbb{E}\left[\mmd^{2}_{{{\bm{k}}_{\mathbb{P}}}}(\mathbb{S}^{w^{+}}_{n},\mathbb{P})\mathbbm{1}_{F_{n}}\right] \textstyle=\mathbb{E}\left[\sum_{i,j\in[n]}w_{i}^{+}w_{j}^{+}{{\bm{k}}_{\mathbb{P}}}(x_{i},x_{j})\mathbbm{1}_{F_{n}}\right]=\mathbb{E}\left[\alpha^{2}\sum_{i,j\in[n]}w_{i}w_{j}{{\bm{k}}_{\mathbb{P}}}(x_{i},x_{j})\mathbbm{1}_{F_{n}}\right] \textstyle\leq 4\mathbb{E}\left[\sum_{i,j\in[n]}w_{i}w_{j}{{\bm{k}}_{\mathbb{P}}}(x_{i},x_{j})\right]\leq\frac{8M}{n}\left(\frac{2M}{n}\frac{\mathbb{E}_{x\sim\mathbb{P}}[{{\bm{k}}^{2}_{\mathbb{P}}}(x,x)]}{\lambda_{L}}+\sum_{\ell>L}\lambda_{\ell}\right), $$

where we applied (152) for the last inequality. For the second term, by the Cauchy-Schwartz inequality,

$$ \textstyle\mathbb{E}\left[\mmd^{2}_{{{\bm{k}}_{\mathbb{P}}}}(\mathbb{S}^{\tilde{w}}_{n},\mathbb{P})\mathbbm{1}_{F_{n}^{c}}\right] \textstyle\leq\sqrt{\Pr(F_n^c)}\sqrt{\mathbb{E}\left[\left(\sum_{i,j\in[n]}{{\bm{k}}_{\mathbb{P}}}(x_{i},x_{j})\tilde{w}_{i}\tilde{w}_{j}\right)^{2}\right]} \textstyle\leq\sqrt{\Pr(F_n^c)}\sqrt{\mathbb{E}[{{\bm{k}}_{\mathbb{P}}}(x_{1},x_{1})^{2}]}. $$

Putting everything together we obtain (117). ∎

## Appendix D Stein Kernel Thinning

In this section, we detail our Stein thinning implementation in Sec. D.1, our kernel thinning implementation and analysis in Sec. D.2, and our proof of Thm. 3 in Sec. D.3.

### D.1 Stein Thinning with sufficient statistics

For an input point set of size $n$ , the original implementation of Stein Thinning of Riabiz et al. [2022] takes $O(nm^{2})$ time to output a coreset of size $m$ . In Alg. D.1, we show that this runtime can be improved to $O(nm)$ using sufficient statistics. The idea is to maintain a vector $g\in\mathbb{R}^{n}$ such that $g=2{{\bm{k}}_{\mathbb{P}}}(\mathbb{S}_{n},\mathbb{S}_{n})w$ where $w$ is the weight representing the current coreset.

*Algorithm D.1 SteinThinning (ST) with sufficient statistics*

```
Input: kernel ${{\bm{k}}_{\mathbb{P}}}$ with zero-mean under $\mathbb{P}$ , input points $\mathcal{S}_{n}=(x_{i})_{i\in[n]}$ , output size $m$
$w\leftarrow\bm{0}\in\mathbb{R}^{n}$
$j\leftarrow\mathop{\mathrm{}}{argmin}_{i\in[n]}{{\bm{k}}_{\mathbb{P}}}(x_{i},x_{i})$
$w_{j}\leftarrow 1$
$g\leftarrow 2{{\bm{k}}_{\mathbb{P}}}(\mathcal{S}_{n},x_{j})$ $\triangleright$ maintain sufficient statistics $g=2{{\bm{k}}_{\mathbb{P}}}(\mathcal{S}_{n},\mathcal{S}_{n})w$
for $t=1$ to $m-1$ do
$j\leftarrow\mathop{\mathrm{}}{argmin}_{i\in[n]}\{tg_{i}+{{\bm{k}}_{\mathbb{P}}}(x_{i},x_{i})\}$
$w\leftarrow\frac{t}{t+1}w+\frac{1}{t+1}e_{j}$
$g\leftarrow\frac{t}{t+1}g+\frac{2}{t+1}{{\bm{k}}_{\mathbb{P}}}(\mathcal{S}_{n},x_{j})$
end for
Return: $w$
```

### D.2 Kernel Thinning targeting $\mathbb{P}$

*Algorithm D.2 KernelThinning (KT) (adapted from Dwivedi and Mackey [2022, Alg. 1])*

```
Input: kernel ${{\bm{k}}_{\mathbb{P}}}$ with zero-mean under $\mathbb{P}$ , input points $\mathcal{S}_{n}=(x_{i})_{i\in[n]}$ , multiplicity $n^{\prime}$ with $\log_{2}\frac{n^{\prime}}{m}\in\mathbb{N}$ , weight $w\in\Delta_{n-1}\cap(\frac{\mathbb{N}_{0}}{n^{\prime}})^{n}$ , output size $m$ with $\frac{n^{\prime}}{m}\in 2^{\mathbb{N}}$ , failure probability $\delta$
$\mathtt{S}\leftarrow$ index sequence where $k\in[n]$ appears $n^{\prime}w_{k}$ times
$\mathfrak{t}\leftarrow\log_{2}\frac{n^{\prime}}{m}\in\mathbb{N}$
$(\mathtt{I}^{(\ell)})_{\ell\in[2^{\mathfrak{t}}]}\leftarrow\textsc{kt-split}({{\bm{k}}_{\mathbb{P}}},\mathcal{S}_{n}[\mathtt{S}],\mathfrak{t},\delta/n^{\prime})$ $\triangleright$ kt-split is from Dwivedi and Mackey [2022, Algorithm 1a] and we set $\delta_{i}=\delta$ for all $i$
$\mathtt{I}^{(\ell)}\leftarrow\mathtt{S}[\mathtt{I}^{(\ell)}]$ for each $\ell\in[2^{\mathfrak{t}}]$
$\mathtt{I}\leftarrow\hyperref@@ii[alg:kt_swap_target]{\textup{KT-Swap}}({{\bm{k}}_{\mathbb{P}}},\mathcal{S}_{n},(\mathtt{I}^{(\ell)})_{\ell\in[2^{\mathfrak{t}}]})$
$w_{{\textup{KT}}}\leftarrow\text{simplex weight corresponding to }\mathtt{I}$ $\triangleright$ $w_{i}=\frac{\text{number of occurrences of }i\text{ in }\mathtt{I}}{\absolutevalue{\tI}}$
Return: $w_{{\textup{KT}}}\in\Delta_{n-1}\cap(\frac{\mathbb{N}_{0}}{m})^{n}$ $\triangleright$ Hence $\left\|{w_{{\textup{KT}}}}\right\|_{0}\leq m$
```

*Algorithm D.3 KT-Swap (modified Dwivedi and Mackey [2022, Alg. 1b] to minimize $\mmd$ to $\mathbb{P}$ )*

```
Input: kernel ${{\bm{k}}_{\mathbb{P}}}$ with zero-mean under $\mathbb{P}$ , input points $\mathcal{S}_{n}=(x_{i})_{i\in[n]}$ , candidate coreset indices $(\mathtt{I}^{(\ell)})_{\ell\in[L]}$
$m\leftarrow\absolutevalue{\tI^{(0)}}$ $\triangleright$ all candidate coresets are of the same size
$\mathtt{I}\leftarrow\mathtt{I}^{(\ell^{*})}$ for $\ell^{*}\in\mathop{\mathrm{}}{argmin}_{\ell\in[L]}\mmd_{{{\bm{k}}_{\mathbb{P}}}}(\mathcal{S}_{n}[\mathtt{I}^{(\ell)}],\mathbb{P})$ $\triangleright$ select the best kt-split coreset
$\mathtt{I}_{{\textup{ST}}}\leftarrow$ index sequence of $\hyperref@@ii[alg:GBC]{\textup{SteinThinning}}({{\bm{k}}_{\mathbb{P}}},\mathcal{S}_{n},m)$ $\triangleright$ add Stein thinning baseline
$\mathtt{C}=\{\mathtt{I},\mathtt{I}_{{\textup{ST}}}\}$ $\triangleright$ shortlisted candidates
for $\mathtt{I}\in\mathtt{C}$ do
$g\leftarrow\bm{0}\in\mathbb{R}^{n}$ $\triangleright$ maintain sufficient statistics $g=\sum_{j\in[m]}{{\bm{k}}_{\mathbb{P}}}(x_{\mathtt{I}_{j}},\mathcal{S}_{n})$
$\mathtt{Kdiag}\leftarrow({{\bm{k}}_{\mathbb{P}}}(x_{i},x_{i}))_{i\in[n]}$
for $j=1$ to $m$ do
$g\leftarrow g+{{\bm{k}}_{\mathbb{P}}}(x_{\mathtt{I}_{j}},\mathcal{S}_{n})$
end for
for $j=1$ to $m$ do
$\Delta=2(g-{{\bm{k}}_{\mathbb{P}}}(x_{\mathtt{I}_{j}},\mathcal{S}_{n}))+\mathtt{Kdiag}$ $\triangleright$ this is the change in $\mmd^{2}_{{{\bm{k}}_{\mathbb{P}}}}(\mathcal{S}_{n}[\mathtt{I}],\mathbb{P})$ if we were to replace $\mathtt{I}_{j}$
$k\leftarrow\mathop{\mathrm{}}{argmin}_{i\in[n]}\Delta_{i}$
$g=g-{{\bm{k}}_{\mathbb{P}}}(x_{\mathtt{I}_{j}},\mathcal{S}_{n})+{{\bm{k}}_{\mathbb{P}}}(x_{k},\mathcal{S}_{n})$
$\mathtt{I}_{j}\leftarrow k$
end for
end for
Return: $\mathtt{I}=\mathop{\mathrm{}}{argmin}_{\mathtt{I}\in\mathtt{C}}\mmd_{{{\bm{k}}_{\mathbb{P}}}}(\mathcal{S}_{n}[\mathtt{I}],\mathbb{P})$
```

Our KernelThinning implementation is detailed in Alg. D.2. Since we are able to directly compute $\mmd_{{{\bm{k}}_{\mathbb{P}}}}(\mathbb{S}_{n}^{w},\mathbb{P})$ , we use KT-Swap (Alg. D.3) in place of the standard kt-swap subroutine [Dwivedi and Mackey, 2022, Algorithm 1b] to choose candidate points to swap in so as to greedily minimize $\mmd_{{{\bm{k}}_{\mathbb{P}}}}(\mathbb{S}_{n}^{w},\mathbb{P})$ . To facilitate our subsequent SKT analysis, we restate the guarantees of kt-split [Dwivedi and Mackey, 2022, Theorem 2] in the sub-Gaussian format of [Shetty et al., 2022, Definition 3].

#### Lemma D.1 (Sub-Gaussian guarantee for kt-split).

Let $\mathcal{S}_{n}$ be a sequence of $n$ points and ${\bm{k}}$ a kernel. For any $\delta\in(0,1)$ and $m\in\mathbb{N}$ such that $\log_{2}\frac{n}{m}\in\mathbb{N}$ , consider the kt-split algorithm [Dwivedi and Mackey, 2022, Algorithm 1a] with ${{\bm{k}}_{\textup{split}}}={\bm{k}}$ , thinning parameter $\mathfrak{t}=\log_{2}\frac{n}{m}$ , and $\delta_{i}=\frac{\delta}{n}$ to compress $\mathcal{S}_{n}$ to $2^{\mathfrak{t}}$ coresets $\{\mathcal{S}^{(i)}_{\textup{out}}\}_{i\in[2^{\mathfrak{t}}]}$ where each $\mathcal{S}^{(i)}_{\textup{out}}$ has $m$ points. Denote the signed measure $\phi^{(i)}\triangleq\frac{1}{n}\sum_{x\in\mathcal{S}_{n}}\delta_{x}-\frac{2^{\mathfrak{t}}}{n}\sum_{x\in\mathcal{S}^{(i)}_{\textup{out}}}\delta_{x}$ . Then for each $i\in[2^{\mathfrak{t}}]$ , on an event $\mathcal{E}_{\textup{equi}}^{(i)}$ with $\mathbb{P}(\mathcal{E}_{\textup{equi}}^{(i)})\geq 1-\frac{\delta}{2}$ , $\phi^{(i)}=\tilde{\phi}^{(i)}$ for a random signed measure $\tilde{\phi}^{(i)}$ 66 6 This is the signed measure returned by repeated applications of self-balancing Hilbert walk (SBHW) [Dwivedi and Mackey, 2021, Algorithm 3]. Although SBHW returns an element of ${\mathcal{H}_{{\bm{k}}}}$ , by tracing the algorithm, the returned output is equivalent to a signed measure via the correspondence $\sum_{i\in[n]}c_{i}{\bm{k}}(x_{i},\cdot)\Leftrightarrow\sum_{i\in[n]}c_{i}\delta_{x_{i}}$ . The usage of signed measures is consistent with Shetty et al. [2022]. such that, for any $\delta^{\prime}\in(0,1)$ ,

$$ \textstyle\Pr\left(\left\|{\tilde{\phi}^{(i)}{\bm{k}}}\right\|_{{\mathcal{H}_{{\bm{k}}}}}\geq a_{n,m}+v_{n,m}\sqrt{\log(\frac{1}{\delta'})}\right)\leq\delta^{\prime}, $$

where

$$ \textstyle a_{n,m} \textstyle\triangleq\frac{1}{m}\left(2+\sqrt{\frac{8}{3}\|{{\bm{k}}}\|_{n}\log(\frac{6(\log_2\frac{n}{m})m}{\delta})\log(4\cvrnum{\k}(\balleuc(R_{n}), m^{-1}))}\right), \textstyle v_{n,m} \textstyle\triangleq\frac{1}{m}\sqrt{\frac{8}{3}\|{{\bm{k}}}\|_{n}\log(\frac{6(\log_2\frac{n}{m})m}{\delta})}. $$

#### Proof of Lem. D.1.

Fix $i\in[2^{\mathfrak{t}}]$ , $\delta\in(0,1)$ and $n,m\in\mathbb{N}$ such that $\mathfrak{t}=\log_{2}\frac{n}{m}\in\mathbb{N}$ . Define $\phi\triangleq\phi^{(i)}$ . By the proof of Dwivedi and Mackey [2022, Thms. 1 and 2], there exists an event $\mathcal{E}_{\textup{equi}}$ with $\Pr(\Eequi^c)\leq\frac{\delta}{2}$ such that, on this event, $\phi=\tilde{\phi}$ where $\tilde{\phi}$ is a signed measure such that, for any $\delta^{\prime}\in(0,1)$ , with probability at least $1-\delta^{\prime}$ ,

$$ \textstyle\left\|{\tilde{\phi}{\bm{k}}}\right\|_{{\mathcal{H}_{{\bm{k}}}}}\leq\inf_{\epsilon\in(0,1),A:\mathcal{S}_{n}\subset A}2\epsilon+\frac{2^{\mathfrak{t}}}{n}\sqrt{\frac{8}{3}\|{{\bm{k}}}\|_{n}\log(\frac{6\ft n}{2^\ft\delta})\left[\log\frac{4}{\delta^{\prime}}+\log\mathcal{N}_{{\bm{k}}}(A,\epsilon)\right]}. $$

Note that on $\mathcal{E}_{\textup{equi}}$ , $\left\|{\tilde{\phi}{\bm{k}}}\right\|_{{\mathcal{H}_{{\bm{k}}}}}=\left\|{\phi{\bm{k}}}\right\|_{{\mathcal{H}_{{\bm{k}}}}}$ . We choose $A=\mathcal{B}_{2}(R_{n})$ and $\epsilon=\frac{2^{\mathfrak{t}}}{n}=m^{-1}$ , so that, with probability at least $1-\delta^{\prime}$ , using the fact that $\sqrt{a+b}\leq\sqrt{a}+\sqrt{b}$ for $a,b\geq 0$ ,

$$ \textstyle\left\|{\tilde{\phi}{\bm{k}}}\right\|_{{\mathcal{H}_{{\bm{k}}}}} \textstyle\leq\frac{2^{\mathfrak{t}+1}}{n}+\frac{2^{\mathfrak{t}}}{n}\sqrt{\frac{8}{3}\|{{\bm{k}}}\|_{n}\log(\frac{6\ft n}{2^\ft\delta})\left[\log\frac{4}{\delta^{\prime}}+\log\mathcal{N}_{{\bm{k}}}(\mathcal{B}_{2}(R_{n}),m^{-1})\right]} \textstyle\leq\frac{2^{\mathfrak{t}+1}}{n}+\frac{2^{\mathfrak{t}}}{n}\sqrt{\frac{8}{3}\|{{\bm{k}}}\|_{n}\log(\frac{6\ft n}{2^\ft\delta})}\left[\sqrt{\log\frac{1}{\delta^{\prime}}}+\sqrt{\log 4\mathcal{N}_{{\bm{k}}}(\mathcal{B}_{2}(R_{n}),m^{-1})}\right] \textstyle\leq a_{n,m}+v_{n,m}\sqrt{\log(\frac{1}{\delta'})}, $$

for $a_{n,m}$ , $v_{n,m}$ in Lem. D.1. ∎

#### Corollary D.1 (MMD guarantee for kt-split).

Let $\mathcal{S}_{\infty}$ be an infinite sequence of points in $\mathbb{R}^{d}$ and ${\bm{k}}$ a kernel. For any $\delta\in(0,1)$ and $n,m\in\mathbb{N}$ such that $\log_{2}\frac{n}{m}\in\mathbb{N}$ , consider the kt-split algorithm [Dwivedi and Mackey, 2022, Algorithm 1a] with parameters ${{\bm{k}}_{\textup{split}}}={\bm{k}}$ and $\delta_{i}=\frac{\delta}{n}$ to compress $\mathcal{S}_{n}$ to $2^{\mathfrak{t}}$ coresets $\{\mathcal{S}_{\textup{out}}^{(i)}\}_{i\in[2^{\mathfrak{t}}]}$ where $\mathfrak{t}={\log_{2}\frac{n}{m}}$ , each with $m$ points. Then for any $i\in[2^{\mathfrak{t}}]$ , with probability at least $1-\delta$ ,

$$ \textstyle\mmd_{{\bm{k}}}(\mathbb{S}_{n},\mathbb{S}^{(i)}_{\textup{out}}) \textstyle\leq\frac{1}{m}\left(2+\sqrt{\frac{8}{3}\|{{\bm{k}}}\|_{n}\log(\frac{6(\log_2\frac{n}{m})m}{\delta})\left(\log\mathcal{N}_{{\bm{k}}}(\mathcal{B}_{2}(R_{n}),m^{-1})+\log\frac{8}{\delta}\right)}\right). $$

#### Proof of Cor. D.1.

Fix $i\in[2^{\mathfrak{t}}]$ . By taking $\delta^{\prime}=\frac{\delta}{2}$ in 225, we obtain (228). This occurs with probability

$$ \textstyle\Pr(\mmd_{\k}(\bS_n, \bS^{(i)}_{\out}) < a_{n,m} + v_{n,m} \sqrt{\log(\frac{1}{\delta'})}) \textstyle= \textstyle 1-\Pr\left(\mmd_{{\bm{k}}}(\mathbb{S}_{n},\mathbb{S}^{(i)}_{\textup{out}})\geq a_{n,m}+v_{n,m}\sqrt{\log(\frac{1}{\delta'})}\right) \textstyle\geq \textstyle 1-\Pr\left(\mathcal{E}_{\textup{equi}}^{(i)},\mmd_{{\bm{k}}}(\mathbb{S}_{n},\mathbb{S}^{(i)}_{\textup{out}})\geq a_{n,m}+v_{n,m}\sqrt{\log(\frac{1}{\delta'})}\right)-\Pr\left({\mathcal{E}_{\textup{equi}}^{(i)}}^{c}\right) \textstyle\geq \textstyle 1-\Pr\left(\left\|{\tilde{\phi}^{(i)}{\bm{k}}}\right\|_{{\mathcal{H}_{{\bm{k}}}}}\geq a_{n,m}+v_{n,m}\sqrt{\log(\frac{1}{\delta'})}\right)-\Pr({\Eequi^{(i)}}^c) \textstyle\geq \textstyle 1-\frac{\delta}{2}-\frac{\delta}{2}=1-\delta. $$

∎

### D.3 Proof of Thm. 3: Theorem 3 (MMD guarantee for SKT).

Thm. 3 follows directly from Assum. ( α , β )-kernel and the following result for a kernel with generic covering number.

#### Theorem D.1.

Let ${{\bm{k}}_{\mathbb{P}}}$ be a kernel satisfying Assum. 1. Let $\mathcal{S}_{\infty}$ be an infinite sequence of points. Then for a prefix sequence $\mathcal{S}_{n}$ of $n$ points, $m\in[n]$ , and $n^{\prime}\triangleq m2^{\left\lceil\log_{2}\frac{n}{m}\right\rceil}$ , SKT outputs $w_{{\textup{SKT}}}$ in $O(n^{2}d_{{{\bm{k}}_{\mathbb{P}}}})$ time that satisfies, with probability at least $1-\delta$ ,

$$ \textstyle\Delta\!\mmd_{{{\bm{k}}_{\mathbb{P}}}}(w_{{\textup{SKT}}})\leq\sqrt{\left(\frac{1+\log n^{\prime}}{n^{\prime}}\right)\|{{{\bm{k}}_{\mathbb{P}}}}\|_{n}}+\frac{1}{m}\left(2+\sqrt{\frac{8}{3}\|{{\bm{k}}}\|_{n}\log(\frac{6(\log_2\frac{n'}{m})m}{\delta})\left(\log\mathcal{N}_{{\bm{k}}}(\mathcal{B}_{2}(R_{n}),m^{-1})+\log\frac{8}{\delta}\right)}\right). $$

#### Proof of Thm. D.1.

The runtime of SKT comes from the fact that all of SteinThinning (with output size $n$ ), kt-split, and KT-Swap take $O(d_{{{\bm{k}}_{\mathbb{P}}}}n^{2})$ time.

By Riabiz et al. [2022, Theorem 1], SteinThinning (which is a deterministic algorithm) from $n$ points to $n^{\prime}$ points has the following guarantee

$$ \textstyle\mmd^{2}_{{{\bm{k}}_{\mathbb{P}}}}(\mathbb{S}_{n}^{w^{\dagger}},\mathbb{P})\leq\mmd^{2}_{{{\bm{k}}_{\mathbb{P}}}}(\mathbb{S}_{n}^{{w_{\textsc{OPT}}}},\mathbb{P})+\left(\frac{1+\log n^{\prime}}{n^{\prime}}\right)\|{{{\bm{k}}_{\mathbb{P}}}}\|_{n}, $$

where we denote the output weight of SteinThinning as $w^{\dagger}$ . Using $\sqrt{a+b}\leq\sqrt{a}+\sqrt{b}$ for $a,b\geq 0$ , we have

$$ \textstyle\mmd_{{{\bm{k}}_{\mathbb{P}}}}(\mathbb{S}_{n}^{w^{\dagger}},\mathbb{P})\leq\mmd_{{{\bm{k}}_{\mathbb{P}}}}(\mathbb{S}_{n}^{{w_{\textsc{OPT}}}},\mathbb{P})+\sqrt{\left(\frac{1+\log n^{\prime}}{n^{\prime}}\right)\|{{{\bm{k}}_{\mathbb{P}}}}\|_{n}}. $$

Fix $\delta\in(0,1)$ . By Cor. D.1 with ${\bm{k}}={{\bm{k}}_{\mathbb{P}}}$ and $\mathfrak{t}=\log_{2}\frac{n^{\prime}}{m}$ , with probability at least $1-\delta$ , we have, for any $i\in[2^{\mathfrak{t}}]$ ,

$$ \textstyle\mmd_{{{\bm{k}}_{\mathbb{P}}}}(\mathbb{S}^{w^{\dagger}}_{n},\mathbb{S}^{(i)}_{\textup{out}})\leq\frac{1}{m}\left(2+\sqrt{\frac{8}{3}\|{{\bm{k}}}\|_{n}\log(\frac{6(\log_2\frac{n'}{m})m}{\delta})\left(\log\mathcal{N}_{{\bm{k}}}(\mathcal{B}_{2}(R_{n}),m^{-1})+\log\frac{8}{\delta}\right)}\right), $$

where $\mathbb{S}_{\textup{out}}^{(i)}$ is the $i$ -th coreset output by kt-split. Since KT-Swap can only decrease the MMD to $\mathbb{P}$ , we have, by the triangle inequality of $\mmd_{{{\bm{k}}_{\mathbb{P}}}}$ ,

$$ \textstyle\mmd_{{{\bm{k}}_{\mathbb{P}}}}(\mathbb{S}_{n}^{w_{\textup{SKT}}},\mathbb{P}) \textstyle\leq\mmd_{{{\bm{k}}_{\mathbb{P}}}}(\mathbb{S}_{\textup{out}}^{(1)},\mathbb{P})\leq\mmd_{{{\bm{k}}_{\mathbb{P}}}}(\mathbb{S}_{\textup{out}}^{(1)},\mathbb{S}_{n}^{w^{\dagger}})+\mmd_{{{\bm{k}}_{\mathbb{P}}}}(\mathbb{S}_{n}^{w^{\dagger}},\mathbb{P}), $$

which gives the desired bound. ∎

Thm. 3 now follows from Thm. D.1, the kernel growth definitions in Assum. ( α , β )-kernel, $n\leq n^{\prime}\leq 2n$ , and that $\log_{2}(\frac{n^{\prime}}{m})m\leq n^{\prime}$ . ∎

## Appendix E Resampling of Simplex Weights

Integral to many of our algorithms is a resampling procedure that turns a simplex-weighted point set of size $n$ into an equal-weighted point set of size $m$ while incurring at most $O(1/\sqrt{m})$ MMD error. The motivation for wanting an equal-weighted point set is two-fold: First, in LSKT, we need to provide an equal-weighted point set to KT-Compress++, but the output of LD is a simplex weight. Secondly, we can exploit the fact that non-zero weights are bounded away from zero in equal-weighted point sets to provide a tighter analysis of WeightedRPCholesky. While i.i.d. resampling also achieves the $O(1/\sqrt{m})$ goal, we choose Resample (Alg. E.3), a stratified residual resampling algorithm [Douc and Cappé, 2005, Sec. 3.2, 3.3]. In this section, we derive an MMD bound for Resample and show that it is better in expectation than using i.i.d. resampling or residual resampling alone.

Let $D_{w}^{\textup{inv}}$ be the inverse of the cumulative distribution function of the multinomial distribution with weight $w$ , i.e.,

$$ \textstyle D_{w}^{\textup{inv}}(u)\triangleq\min\left\{i\in[n]:u\leq\sum_{j=1}^{i}w_{j}\right\}. $$

*Algorithm E.1 i.i.d. resampling*

```
Input: Weights $w\in\Delta_{n-1}$ , output size $m$
$w^{\prime}\leftarrow\bm{0}\in\mathbb{R}^{n}$
for $j=1$ to $m$ do
Draw $U_{j}\sim\textup{Uniform}([0,1))$
$\mathtt{I}_{j}\leftarrow D_{w}^{\textup{inv}}(U_{j})$
$w^{\prime}_{\mathtt{I}_{j}}\leftarrow w^{\prime}_{\mathtt{I}_{j}}+\frac{1}{m}$
end for
Return: $w^{\prime}\in\Delta_{n-1}\cap(\frac{\mathbb{N}_{0}}{m})^{n}$
```

*Algorithm E.2 Residual resampling*

```
Input: Weights $w\in\Delta_{n-1}$ , output size $m$
$w^{\prime}_{i}\leftarrow\frac{\lfloor mw_{i}\rfloor}{m}$ , $\forall i\in[n]$
$r\leftarrow m-\sum_{i\in[n]}\lfloor mw_{i}\rfloor\in\mathbb{N}$
$\eta_{i}\leftarrow\frac{mw_{i}-\lfloor mw_{i}\rfloor}{r}$ , $\forall i\in[n]$
for $j=1$ to $r$ do
Draw $U_{j}\sim\textup{Uniform}([0,1))$
$\mathtt{I}_{j}\leftarrow D_{\eta}^{\textup{inv}}(U_{j})$
$w^{\prime}_{\mathtt{I}_{j}}\leftarrow w^{\prime}_{\mathtt{I}_{j}}+\frac{1}{m}$
end for
Return: $w^{\prime}\in\Delta_{n-1}\cap(\frac{\mathbb{N}_{0}}{m})^{n}$
```

*Algorithm E.3 Stratified residual resampling (Resample)*

```
Input: Weights $w\in\Delta_{n-1}$ , output size $m$
$w^{\prime}_{i}\leftarrow\frac{\lfloor mw_{i}\rfloor}{m}$ , $\forall i\in[n]$
$r\leftarrow m-\sum_{i\in[n]}\lfloor mw_{i}\rfloor\in\mathbb{N}$
$\eta_{i}\leftarrow\frac{mw_{i}-\lfloor mw_{i}\rfloor}{r}$ , $\forall i\in[n]$
for $j=1$ to $r$ do
Draw $U_{j}\sim\textup{Uniform}([\frac{j}{r},\frac{j+1}{r}))$
$\mathtt{I}_{j}\leftarrow D_{\eta}^{\textup{inv}}(U_{j})$
$w^{\prime}_{\mathtt{I}_{j}}\leftarrow w^{\prime}_{\mathtt{I}_{j}}+\frac{1}{m}$
end for
Return: $w^{\prime}\in\Delta_{n-1}\cap(\frac{\mathbb{N}_{0}}{m})^{n}$
```

#### Proposition E.1 (MMD guarantee of resampling algorithms).

Consider any kernel ${\bm{k}}$ , points $\mathcal{S}_{n}=(x_{1},\ldots,x_{n})\subset\mathbb{R}^{d}$ , and a weight vector $w\in\Delta_{n-1}$ .

- (a) Using the notation from Alg. E.1, let $X,X^{\prime}$ be independent random variables with law $\mathbb{S}_{n}^{w}$ . Then, the output weight vector $w^{\textup{i.i.d.{}}}\triangleq w^{\prime}$ of Alg. E.1 satisfies $\textstyle\mathbb{E}[\mmd^{2}_{{\bm{k}}}(\mathbb{S}^{w^{\textup{i.i.d.{}}}}_{n},\mathbb{S}_{n}^{w})]=\frac{\mathbb{E}{\bm{k}}(X,X)-\mathbb{E}{\bm{k}}(X,X^{\prime})}{m}.$ (240)

- (b) Using the notation from Alg. E.2, let $R,R^{\prime}$ be independent random variables with law $\mathbb{S}_{n}^{\eta}$ . Then, the output weight vector $w^{\textup{resid}}\triangleq w^{\prime}$ of Alg. E.2 satisfies $\textstyle\mathbb{E}[\mmd^{2}_{{\bm{k}}}(\mathbb{S}_{n}^{w^{\textup{resid}}},\mathbb{S}_{n}^{w})]=\frac{r(\mathbb{E}{\bm{k}}(R,R)-\mathbb{E}{\bm{k}}(R,R^{\prime}))}{m^{2}}.$ (241)

- (c) Using the notation from Alg. E.3, let $R_{j}\triangleq x_{\mathtt{I}_{j}}$ and $R^{\prime}_{j}$ be an independent copy of $R_{j}$ . Let $R$ be an independent random variable with law $\mathbb{S}_{n}^{\eta}$ . Then, the output weight vector $w^{\textup{sr}}\triangleq w^{\prime}$ of Alg. E.3 satisfies $\textstyle\mathbb{E}[\mmd^{2}_{{\bm{k}}}(\mathbb{S}^{w^{\textup{sr}}}_{n},\mathbb{S}_{n}^{w})]=\frac{r\mathbb{E}{\bm{k}}(R,R)-\sum_{j\in[r]}\mathbb{E}{\bm{k}}(R_{j},R_{j}^{\prime})}{m^{2}}.$ (242)

#### Proof of Prop. E.1(a).

Let $X_{i}\triangleq x_{\mathtt{I}_{i}}$ . As random signed measures, we have

$$ \textstyle\mathbb{S}_{n}^{w^{\prime}}-\mathbb{S}_{n}^{w} \textstyle=\frac{1}{m}\sum_{i\in[m]}\delta_{X_{i}}-\sum_{i\in[n]}w_{i}\delta_{x_{i}}. $$

Hence

$$ \textstyle\mmd^{2}_{\bm{k}}(\mathbb{S}^{w^{\prime}}_{n},\mathbb{S}_{n}^{w}) \textstyle=((\mathbb{S}_{n}^{w^{\prime}}-\mathbb{S}_{n}^{w})\times(\mathbb{S}_{n}^{w^{\prime}}-\mathbb{S}_{n}^{w})){\bm{k}} \textstyle=\frac{1}{m^{2}}\sum_{i,i^{\prime}\in[m]}{\bm{k}}(X_{i},X_{i^{\prime}})-\frac{2}{m}\sum_{i\in[m],i^{\prime}\in[n]}w_{i^{\prime}}{\bm{k}}(X_{i},x_{i^{\prime}})+\sum_{i,i^{\prime}\in[n]}w_{i}w_{i^{\prime}}{\bm{k}}(x_{i},x_{i^{\prime}}). $$

Since each $X_{i}$ is distributed to $\mathbb{S}_{n}^{w}$ and $X_{i}$ and $X_{i^{\prime}}$ are independent for $i\neq{i^{\prime}}$ , taking expectation, we have
